lead: Tobit, the man who risked everything to bury the dead, is struck blind, and in his bitterness he suspects his own wife of theft. Anna answers him with a question that cuts deep: “Where are your acts of charity?” In the Gospel the Pharisees and Herodians try to trap Jesus with a question about paying taxes to the emperor. He answers by pointing to the image on the coin, and reminds them that something else bears the image of God. On the memorial of St Justin, a philosopher who gave his life for Christ in Rome, Psalm 112 sings of the righteous whose hearts are firm, secure in the Lord.

r.h: Where are your acts of charity?
set: The Book of Tobit is set among the exiles of the northern tribes in Nineveh, the capital of Assyria. Tobit, of the tribe of Naphtali, tells his own story: he gave alms, fed the hungry, and buried the bodies of his fellow Israelites when the king left them unburied. Just before our passage, at the feast of Pentecost, he left his dinner to bury a murdered man (2:1–8). Having touched a corpse, he was ritually unclean and slept outside in the courtyard.

The book was written in Aramaic or Hebrew, probably two or three centuries before Christ; fragments in both languages were found among the Dead Sea Scrolls at Qumran. The Catholic Church receives it among the books of the Old Testament (CCC 120). The passage shows a good man in the dark: blind, poor, dependent on his wife, and quick to suspect.
str: vv. 9–10: Tobit sleeps in the courtyard; bird droppings blind him; physicians make it worse; four years of blindness.
vv. 11–12: Anna works at weaving and is given a young goat with her wages.
vv. 13–14: Tobit accuses her; Anna answers, “Where are your acts of charity?”
kw: A key word of the whole book (compare 4:7–11; 12:8–9). It comes from eleos, mercy. Anna turns Tobit’s favourite virtue back on him: where is his mercy now, toward her?
Righteousness here means deeds that are right before God and neighbour. Tobit had them in abundance (1:3), yet he fails in the one place where it is hardest: at home.
vv: For four years I remained unable to see.
Tobit does not explain his suffering. The book never says that God sent the blindness as a punishment. It is the trial of a just man, as with Job.
It is surely not stolen, is it? Return it to the owners; for we have no right to eat anything stolen.
His honesty is real, but it has turned hard. Suffering has made him suspicious of the one person who is caring for him.
Where are your acts of charity? Where are your righteous deeds? These things are known about you!
Anna’s words sting because they are partly true. Charity to strangers must also become patience and trust toward those closest to us.
ch: The Church reads Tobit as a story of providence: God is at work even when his servants cannot see. Tobit is a great teacher of almsgiving (4:7–11; 12:8–9), and the Catechism names almsgiving among the three chief forms of penance (CCC 1434). Tobit’s burying of the dead is remembered among the corporal works of mercy, and the Catechism notes that burying the dead is a work of mercy that honours the children of God (CCC 2300). Today’s passage adds a quieter lesson: mercy begins at home. Pope Francis, commenting on St Paul’s hymn to love in Amoris Laetitia, speaks of the patience and trust that love needs within the family (in substance).

set: Jesus is in the Temple at Jerusalem in the last days before his Passion. The chief priests, scribes and elders have just heard the parable of the wicked tenants and understood that it was told against them (12:12). Now they send some Pharisees and Herodians. The two groups were usually far apart: the Pharisees resented Roman rule, while the Herodians supported the house of Herod, which ruled with Rome’s consent.

Background. The tax in question was the poll tax paid directly to Rome by the people of Judea. It was bitterly resented, and some years before, a rising under Judas the Galilean had opposed it. If Jesus said “pay”, he would offend the people; if he said “do not pay”, he could be denounced to the Romans.
str: vv. 13–15a: flattering words and a trap: is it lawful to pay taxes to the emperor?
vv. 15b–16: Jesus asks for a denarius: whose head and whose title?
v. 17: “Give to the emperor the things that are the emperor’s, and to God the things that are God’s.” They are amazed.
kw: A Roman silver coin, a day’s wage for a labourer. The coin of the emperor Tiberius bore his head and a title calling him son of the divine Augustus. Jesus does not carry one; he asks for it.
The word used for the image of God in the Greek of Genesis 1:26–27. The coin bears Caesar’s image; the human person bears God’s.
Not simply “give” but “give back what is owed”. The coin already belongs, in a sense, to the one whose image it carries.
vv: Teacher, we know that you are sincere, and show deference to no one;
The flattery is true, though it is meant as a trap. Jesus is indeed not swayed by anyone’s rank.
Bring me a denarius and let me see it.
His questioners produce the coin themselves, in the Temple courts. They already use Caesar’s money.
Give to the emperor the things that are the emperor’s, and to God the things that are God’s.

The State has a real but limited claim. God’s claim is total, because we carry his image. Tertullian drew the lesson: give to Caesar the image of Caesar on the coin, and to God the image of God in yourself (in substance, On Idolatry 15).
ch: The Catechism teaches that it is a moral duty to pay taxes, to vote and to defend one’s country (CCC 2240), and that citizens are obliged in conscience not to follow the directives of civil authorities when they are contrary to the demands of the moral order; here the Catechism quotes this saying of Jesus (CCC 2242). St Justin, whose memorial we keep, wrote to the emperor that Christians pay their taxes more readily than anyone, because Christ taught them to, but worship God alone (in substance, First Apology 17). The coin goes to Caesar; the heart and the whole person go to God.

qa: Does Jesus divide life into two separate parts, one for God and one for the State?

No. Everything belongs to God, including the emperor. Jesus accepts that the State has a real role and real claims, such as taxes and just laws. But it may never claim what belongs only to God: worship, conscience and the whole person made in his image. When a law commands what is against God’s law, the Christian must obey God rather than men (Acts 5:29; CCC 2242).
rite: St Justin was born about the year 100 at Flavia Neapolis (present-day Nablus) in Samaria. He searched for truth among the philosophers and found it in Christ, whom he called the Word, a seed of whose truth was scattered among all peoples. He taught in Rome and wrote two Apologies and the Dialogue with Trypho. His First Apology contains the oldest full description of the Sunday Eucharist (chapters 65–67), quoted in the Catechism (CCC 1345). He was beheaded in Rome about 165 with several companions, under the prefect Rusticus.
study: Tobit was generous to strangers and harsh at home. Where am I more patient with outsiders than with my own family?
What in my life bears God’s image and needs to be given back to him?

lead: On the same day, far apart, two people pray from the depth of their sorrow: blind Tobit in Nineveh and young Sarah in Ecbatana, insulted and grieving her seven dead husbands. Both ask to die. At that very moment, says the book, both prayers are heard, and Raphael is sent to heal them. In the Gospel the Sadducees mock the hope of resurrection with the story of a woman married to seven brothers. Jesus answers that God is not God of the dead, but of the living. Psalm 25 gives the prayer of the day: “To you, O Lord, I lift up my soul.”

r.h: Two prayers heard at the same moment
set: Stung by Anna’s rebuke, Tobit turns to God. Then the scene moves to Ecbatana, a city in Media far to the east, where Sarah, the only daughter of Raguel, is suffering in a different way. Seven times she was married, and each husband was killed on the wedding night by the demon Asmodeus. A servant mocks her, and she goes up to her father’s room meaning to hang herself.
The author tells the two stories side by side, like two threads that God will soon weave together. The Lectionary leaves out the rest of Sarah’s prayer (vv. 11b–15) and the last lines of v. 17.
str: vv. 1–6: Tobit’s prayer: God is just; Israel has sinned; let me die rather than hear insults.
vv. 7–10: Sarah, mocked by a maid, thinks of her father and turns from despair to prayer.
v. 11a: Sarah prays with hands outstretched toward the window.
vv. 16–17a: both prayers are heard; Raphael is sent to heal them both.
kw: The name of the demon, probably from a Persian word meaning “demon of wrath”. In the story he stands for the power of evil that destroys life and love.
A Hebrew name meaning “God heals”. The angel’s name tells his task: to heal Tobit’s eyes and to deliver Sarah. He will later say that he is one of the seven angels who stand before the Lord (12:15).
vv: You are righteous, O Lord, and all your deeds are just; all your ways are mercy and truth;
Tobit begins not with his complaint but with praise. Even in darkness, he confesses that God is just and merciful.
But she thought it over and said, “Never shall they reproach my father,
Love for her father turns Sarah back from death. She chooses prayer instead of despair.
Blessed are you, merciful God! Blessed is your name forever;
Like Tobit, Sarah begins with blessing. Jewish prayer to this day begins in the same way: “Blessed are you, Lord.”
At that very moment, the prayers of both of them were heard in the glorious presence of God.
Neither of them knows about the other. God hears both and answers both with one plan.
ch: The Church sees in Tobit and Sarah a school of prayer in suffering. Their honest cry, even the wish to die, is not condemned; it is brought to God, and God answers better than they asked. The Catechism teaches that God’s providence works through the actions of creatures and that he can draw good even from evil (CCC 306–308, 312). The angel Raphael has given Christians a lasting image of the guardian angel, a companion on the road (CCC 336).

r.h: Not God of the dead, but of the living
set: The questions in the Temple continue. Now it is the Sadducees, a group closely linked with the priestly families. They accepted the five books of Moses as their chief authority and did not believe in the resurrection of the dead, which they found nowhere in the Law. The Pharisees, and many ordinary Jews, did believe in it (compare Daniel 12:2; 2 Maccabees 7).

Background. The law of levirate marriage (Deuteronomy 25:5–10) required a man to marry his brother’s widow if the brother died childless, so that his name would not be lost. The Sadducees build an absurd case on it to make resurrection look foolish. Readers have noticed that, like Sarah in Tobit, the woman in the story has seven husbands.
str: vv. 18–23: the Sadducees’ case: seven brothers, one wife; whose wife will she be?
v. 24: “you know neither the scriptures nor the power of God”.
v. 25: the risen do not marry; they are like angels.
vv. 26–27: the burning bush: “I am the God of Abraham …”; he is God of the living.
kw: Literally “standing up again”. Not the return to the same earthly life, but a new life given by God to the whole person, body and soul.
Jesus does not say that the risen become angels, but that, like them, they no longer marry or die. Life in the age to come is not a copy of this one.
Jesus refers to the passage “about the bush” (Exodus 3), the way passages were then named before there were chapter numbers.
vv: Is not this the reason you are wrong, that you know neither the scriptures nor the power of God?
Two mistakes: they read the Scriptures too narrowly, and they imagine God’s power too small, as if he could only repeat the present world.
For when they rise from the dead, they neither marry nor are given in marriage, but are like angels in heaven.
Earthly marriage serves this life and the handing on of life. In the resurrection love is not lost but fulfilled in God.
I am the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob
Jesus argues from the Law the Sadducees accept. God speaks of the patriarchs long dead as his own. A bond with the living God cannot be broken by death.
He is God not of the dead, but of the living; you are quite wrong.
The friendship God offers is faithful. Those he loves live to him.
ch: The Catechism quotes this Gospel when it teaches that Jesus firmly upheld faith in the resurrection of the dead against the Sadducees and that faith in the resurrection rests on faith in God, who is the God of the living (CCC 993). At every Mass, in the Creed, we say: “I look forward to the resurrection of the dead and the life of the world to come.”

rite: Today the Church may remember Sts Marcellinus, a priest, and Peter, an exorcist, martyred in Rome about the year 304 under Diocletian. Pope St Damasus later wrote their epitaph, saying that he had heard the story of their death as a boy from the executioner himself. Their names are in the Roman Canon, the First Eucharistic Prayer of the Mass.
study: Tobit and Sarah both begin their prayer with praise. How do I begin my prayer in difficult times?
Do I imagine heaven as a copy of this life? What does “God of the living” teach me about those I have lost?

lead: The story of Tobit reaches its wedding night. Guided by Raphael, Tobias comes to the house of Raguel, receives Sarah as his wife, and before anything else, the two of them rise and pray together. In the Gospel a scribe asks Jesus which commandment is the first of all, and Jesus answers with the love of God and the love of neighbour. Psalm 128 blesses the home of the one who fears the Lord. On the memorial of St Charles Lwanga and his companions, young martyrs of Uganda, the readings speak of a love that is pure and faithful to the end.

r.h: That we may grow old together
set: Tobit has sent his son Tobias to Media to recover money he left there. A travelling companion has joined him, calling himself Azariah; the reader knows he is the angel Raphael. On the road, Raphael tells Tobias about Sarah, his relative, and says that he has the right to marry her. Tobias is afraid, because seven husbands have died, but Raphael tells him what to do and promises that she was set apart for him before the world was made (6:18).

Background. Marriage within the wider family was the custom for Israel in exile, to keep the people faithful amid foreign nations (compare 4:12). The book’s verse numbers differ between translations, which is why the Lectionary and our Bible give slightly different references.
str: 6:10–11: approaching Ecbatana, Raphael tells Tobias about Sarah.
7:1, 9–12: welcome at Raguel’s house; Tobias asks for Sarah; Raguel gives her to him according to the law of Moses.
7:13–16: the marriage contract; the meal; Edna prepares the room and comforts her daughter.
8:4–9: Tobias and Sarah rise and pray; the prayer recalls Adam and Eve; “Amen, Amen.”
kw: Tobias calls his bride “sister” (8:4), and Raguel says “from now on you are her brother and she is your sister” (7:11). The language of the Song of Songs uses the same tender word (Song 4:9).
Tobias takes Sarah not for selfish desire but “with sincerity”, literally “in truth”. Love in marriage seeks the good of the other.
The whole hope of the prayer: not only a wedding night, but a life lived side by side to old age.
vv: Take courage, my daughter; the Lord of heaven grant you joy in place of your sorrow.
Edna weeps, remembering the seven deaths, but she blesses her daughter in faith. A mother’s prayer accompanies the new marriage.
Sister, get up, and let us pray and implore our Lord that he grant us mercy and safety.
Before they come together, husband and wife stand before God. The marriage begins in prayer.
You made Adam, and for him you made his wife Eve as a helper and support.
Tobias goes back to the beginning (Genesis 2:18). Their marriage is part of God’s plan from creation.
Grant that she and I may find mercy and that we may grow old together.
A simple prayer that every couple can make their own.
ch: The Church loves this passage as a picture of Christian marriage. The prayer of Tobias is among the readings offered for the celebration of marriage, and the Catechism quotes it when it speaks of the fidelity and holiness of married love (CCC 2361). Marriage is a gift from God, blessed from the beginning, and protected by prayer against the forces that would destroy it. Raphael’s help shows that God is not absent from the most personal moments of human life.

set: After the hostile questions of the Pharisees, Herodians and Sadducees, a scribe comes with a sincere question. He has heard Jesus answer well. The teachers of the Law counted many commandments in the Torah (later tradition says 613) and discussed which were the weightiest.

Jesus answers with two texts every Jew knew. The first is the Shema, “Hear, O Israel” (Deuteronomy 6:4–5), recited every morning and evening. The second is from Leviticus 19:18: “you shall love your neighbor as yourself.”
str: v. 28: the scribe’s question: which commandment is first of all?
vv. 29–31: Jesus: the Shema and the love of neighbour; no commandment is greater.
vv. 32–33: the scribe agrees: this is more than all burnt offerings and sacrifices.
v. 34: “You are not far from the kingdom of God.”
kw: The first word of Deuteronomy 6:4. To hear, in Hebrew, is also to obey. The love of God begins with listening.
A command to love: not a passing feeling, but a choice of the whole person, heart, soul, mind and strength.
Literally “the one near”. In Leviticus it means first a fellow Israelite; Jesus will show, in Luke’s parable of the Good Samaritan, that the neighbour is anyone in need.
vv: Hear, O Israel: the Lord our God, the Lord is one;
Jesus begins with faith in the one God. Love of neighbour grows from this root.
you shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, and with all your soul, and with all your mind, and with all your strength.
Mark’s form has four words where the Hebrew of Deuteronomy has three, adding “mind”. God asks for the whole person, including our thinking.
You shall love your neighbor as yourself.
The two commandments are distinct but never separated. Jesus joins them into one answer.
You are not far from the kingdom of God.
The scribe is praised. In Mark, this is a warm word to a teacher of the Law, a reminder that not all the scribes opposed Jesus.
ch: The Catechism opens its teaching on the Ten Commandments with this Gospel: Jesus sums up the whole Law in the double commandment of love (CCC 2055). The first three commandments concern the love of God and the other seven the love of neighbour (CCC 2067). The Second Vatican Council taught that love of God and of neighbour is the first and greatest commandment, and that the two cannot be separated (Gaudium et Spes 24, in substance).

qa: The scribe says love is more than sacrifices. Does this make the Mass less important?

No. The scribe, like the prophets (Hosea 6:6), means that worship without love is empty. Jesus himself offers the perfect sacrifice of love on the Cross, made present in the Mass. That is why the Mass is the source of the love the commandment asks for, and why we are sent from it to love our neighbour.
rite: St Charles Lwanga and his twenty-one companions were young Catholic men of the royal court of Buganda, in present-day Uganda. Under King Mwanga II they refused to give up their faith and to submit to the king’s demands against chastity. Between 1885 and 1887 they were put to death, most of them burned alive at Namugongo on 3 June 1886. Anglican Christians died with them. Pope St Paul VI canonised them in 1964 and in 1969 became the first pope to visit Africa, at Kampala. The shrine at Namugongo draws great crowds of pilgrims every year on this day.
study: Do husbands and wives I know pray together? How could our family pray together more often?
Which of the two great commandments do I find harder to live this week, and why?

lead: On the Solemnity of the Most Sacred Heart of Jesus the readings of Year B lead us from the heart of God in the Old Testament to the pierced heart of Christ on the Cross. In Hosea, God speaks as a father who taught his little son to walk and cannot bear to give him up: “My heart recoils within me; my compassion grows warm and tender.” St Paul kneels before the Father and prays that we may know the love of Christ that surpasses knowledge. In the Gospel a soldier pierces the side of the dead Jesus, and blood and water flow out.

The response is the song of Isaiah 12: “With joy you will draw water from the wells of salvation.” Pope Pius XII took the first words of this verse in Latin, Haurietis aquas, as the title of his letter on devotion to the Sacred Heart (1956). The solemnity is kept on the Friday after the Second Sunday after Pentecost, which this year falls on 4 June.

r.h: How can I give you up?
set: Hosea preached in the northern kingdom of Israel in the eighth century before Christ, in the years before it fell to Assyria in 722. His own painful marriage became a parable of God’s love for an unfaithful people (chapters 1–3). Chapter 11 turns from the image of husband and wife to that of father and child.

The Lectionary leaves out the verses of judgment (vv. 2, 5–8b): Israel ran after the Baals, refused to return, and would go into exile. Our verses keep the two ends of the poem: the tender love of the beginning and God’s refusal to destroy at the end.
str: v. 1: Israel as a child: “out of Egypt I called my son”.
vv. 3–4: God the parent: teaching to walk, carrying, healing, leading with cords of kindness, bending down to feed.
v. 8c: the turning point: God’s own heart recoils.
v. 9: “I am God and no mortal, the Holy One in your midst.”
kw: In Hebrew the heart is not only feelings but the centre of thought, decision and love. When God says “my heart”, he speaks of his innermost self.
From the same root as the “overthrow” of Sodom and Gomorrah. Instead of overthrowing Israel like the cities of the plain, God’s own heart is turned over within him.
God’s holiness is his being utterly other. Here it is surprising: precisely because he is God and not a man, he does not act in anger. His holiness shows itself as mercy.
vv: When Israel was a child, I loved him, and out of Egypt I called my son.
The Exodus was an act of fatherly love. St Matthew sees this verse fulfilled when the child Jesus returns from Egypt (Matthew 2:15): the true Son relives the story of Israel.
Yet it was I who taught Ephraim to walk, I took them up in my arms;
Ephraim is a name for the northern kingdom. God pictures himself holding the hands of a toddler. Few passages in the Old Testament are so tender.
I led them with cords of human kindness, with bands of love.

Not the ropes used to drive animals, but the bonds of love that draw a child. Textual note: in the next line the Hebrew words for “infant” and “yoke” are written with the same consonants, so some translations read “like those who lift infants to their cheeks” and others “like those who ease the yoke on their jaws”. Both pictures speak of tender care.
My heart recoils within me; my compassion grows warm and tender.
Admah and Zeboiim, named just before, were destroyed with Sodom (Deuteronomy 29:23). God’s justice would allow it, but his heart will not.
for I am God and no mortal, the Holy One in your midst,
A human father might give up a rebellious son. God does not. His love is more faithful than any human love.
ch: The Church reads Hosea on this day because the heart of God, revealed to the prophets, has taken flesh in Jesus. Pope Pius XII taught in Haurietis Aquas that the Old Testament already speaks of God’s love in such tender human terms, and that these images prepare for the human heart of the Word made flesh (in substance). God’s covenant love for Israel is not withdrawn (Romans 11:29). The Catechism teaches that Jesus has loved us all with a human heart (CCC 478).

r.h: The love of Christ that surpasses knowledge
set: The Letter to the Ephesians presents itself as written by Paul in prison. Many scholars think it was written by a disciple of Paul after his death, in his name and spirit; others defend Paul’s own authorship. Either way the Church receives it as inspired Scripture. Its great theme is the mystery of God’s plan: to unite all things in Christ, and to bring Jews and Gentiles together into one body, the Church.
Our passage has two parts. First Paul speaks of the grace given to him, the least of all the saints, to preach the riches of Christ to the Gentiles. Then he kneels and prays for his readers.
str: vv. 8–9: the grace given to Paul: to preach the boundless riches of Christ and to make known the hidden plan.
vv. 10–12: through the Church God’s wisdom is made known even to the heavenly powers; in Christ we have access to God.
vv. 14–15: Paul kneels before the Father, from whom every family takes its name.
vv. 16–19: his prayer: strength in the inner being, Christ dwelling in the heart, the knowledge of a love beyond knowledge, the fullness of God.
kw: Literally “that cannot be tracked”, whose footprints cannot be traced to the end. The riches of Christ are beyond exploring.
A play on words: patēr, father, and patria, family or clan. Every family in heaven and on earth takes its name from the Father.
The goal of the prayer is that we be filled with all the fullness of God: not a little of God, but God himself living in us.
vv: this grace was given to me to bring to the Gentiles the news of the boundless riches of Christ,
Paul, who once persecuted the Church, calls himself the very least of the saints. Grace, not his merit, made him an apostle.
in whom we have access to God in boldness and confidence through faith in him.
Through Christ we may approach God not as frightened strangers but as children who speak openly to their Father.
For this reason I bow my knees before the Father,
Jews usually prayed standing. Kneeling shows special humility and urgency.
that Christ may dwell in your hearts through faith, as you are being rooted and grounded in love.
Two images: a plant rooted in soil and a house built on a foundation. Love is both the soil and the foundation.
and to know the love of Christ that surpasses knowledge,
A deliberate paradox: we are to know what is beyond knowing. This knowledge is not information but experience, the knowledge of the heart.
ch: The Church has seen in “the breadth and length and height and depth” the dimensions of the Cross, on which Christ’s love stretched out to the whole world; St Augustine read the verse in this way (in substance). Pope Francis, in his letter on the love of the heart of Christ, Dilexit Nos (2024), invited the Church to rediscover this love that surpasses knowledge, and to let it reach the wounded heart of the world.

r.h: Blood and water from his side
set: Jesus has just died on the cross with the words “It is finished” (19:30). It is Friday afternoon, the day of Preparation, and that evening a solemn sabbath begins; in John’s Gospel it is also the eve of the Passover. The Law said that a hanged body must not remain overnight (Deuteronomy 21:22–23). So the authorities ask Pilate to have the legs of the crucified men broken, which hastened death, and the bodies taken down.

Background. When John speaks of “the Jews” in this passage, he means the religious authorities who were dealing with Pilate, not the Jewish people as a whole. Jesus, his mother, the disciples and the evangelist were themselves Jews. The Church firmly teaches that the death of Christ cannot be charged against all the Jews then living, nor against the Jews of today (Nostra Aetate 4; CCC 597).
str: v. 31: the request to break the legs and remove the bodies before the sabbath.
vv. 32–33: the soldiers break the legs of the two others, but Jesus is already dead.
v. 34: a soldier pierces his side; blood and water come out.
v. 35: the eyewitness testifies so that you may believe.
vv. 36–37: two Scriptures fulfilled: “None of his bones shall be broken”; “They will look on the one whom they have pierced.”
kw: The same word is used in the Greek Old Testament for the rib taken from Adam’s side to form Eve (Genesis 2:21–22). The Fathers saw the Church, the new Eve, formed from the side of the new Adam.

The Greek word means to prick or pierce. St Augustine, reading the Latin “opened”, said that a door of life was opened there, from which the sacraments of the Church flowed (in substance, Tractates on John 120).
The eyewitness, understood by the Church as the beloved disciple, stresses that he saw this. It is not a legend but a witness given so that we may believe.
vv: But when they came to Jesus and saw that he was already dead, they did not break his legs.
Jesus has given up his spirit willingly. His death is real and complete.
Instead, one of the soldiers pierced his side with a spear, and at once blood and water came out.
Blood and water: the sign of a real human death, and, for the evangelist, a sign of the life that flows from it. Jesus had promised rivers of living water from his heart (7:37–39).
His testimony is true, and he knows that he tells the truth.
The evangelist turns directly to the reader: “so that you also may believe”. This scene is at the heart of John’s witness.
None of his bones shall be broken.
The rule for the Passover lamb (Exodus 12:46; Numbers 9:12), and also the psalm of the righteous one whom God protects (Psalm 34:20). Jesus is the true Passover Lamb.
They will look on the one whom they have pierced.
From Zechariah 12:10, where the people mourn over one they pierced, and a spirit of compassion is poured out. To look on the Pierced One is to begin to be converted.
ch: The Catechism teaches that the blood and water that flowed from the pierced side of the crucified Jesus are types of Baptism and the Eucharist, the sacraments of new life (CCC 1225), and that the Church was born from the pierced heart of Christ, as Eve was formed from the side of the sleeping Adam (CCC 766, quoting St Ambrose in substance). St John Chrysostom told the newly baptised that the water and the blood are symbols of Baptism and the Eucharist, and that from these the Church is born (in substance, Catecheses 3).

Devotion to the Sacred Heart is not devotion to an organ apart from the person. The heart of Jesus is the sign of the whole love of the Son of God, divine and human, for the Father and for us. The Catechism says that the Sacred Heart of Jesus, pierced by our sins and for our salvation, is the chief sign and symbol of that love with which the divine Redeemer continually loves the eternal Father and all human beings without exception (CCC 478, in substance).

qa: Why do we honour the heart of Jesus? Is it not enough to love Jesus himself?

We do honour Jesus himself. The heart is the biblical sign of the person’s innermost self and love. To honour the Sacred Heart is to worship the person of the Word made flesh, under the sign of his human heart, pierced for us. Because his human heart belongs to the divine person of the Son, the Church honours it with the worship given to Christ himself (compare CCC 478).
What are the promises connected with the Sacred Heart, such as the nine first Fridays?

They come from the private revelations given to St Margaret Mary Alacoque at Paray-le-Monial in France between 1673 and 1675. The Church approved the devotion and recommends the practice of receiving Communion on the first Friday of the month in reparation and love. Private revelations do not add to the faith (CCC 67); the heart of the devotion is the love of Christ shown on the Cross and in the Eucharist, and our response of love and reparation.
Does Hosea’s tenderness mean that God does not judge sin?

No. The chapter itself speaks of exile as the result of Israel’s refusal to return (vv. 5–7). But judgment is not God’s last word. His mercy is greater than his anger, and he punishes in order to heal and bring back. On the Cross the justice and the mercy of God meet: the Son bears the sin of the world, and the heart pierced by sin pours out forgiveness.
rite: Devotion to the heart of Jesus grew in the Middle Ages among saints such as St Bernard, St Gertrude and St Mechtilde. St John Eudes composed the first liturgical texts for the feast in the seventeenth century, and after the revelations to St Margaret Mary Alacoque, with the support of St Claude de la Colombière, the devotion spread throughout the Church. Blessed Pius IX extended the feast to the whole Latin Church in 1856, and Pope Leo XIII consecrated the human race to the Sacred Heart in 1899. In many Catholic homes in India a picture of the Sacred Heart has a place of honour, with a lamp burning before it, and families renew the enthronement of the Sacred Heart in the home. This day is also kept as a day of prayer for the holiness of priests, as Pope St John Paul II asked.
study: Hosea pictures God teaching a child to walk. When have I felt God carrying me or bending down to me?
Paul prays that Christ may dwell in our hearts through faith. What would need to change in my heart for him to be at home there?
The evangelist says, “They will look on the one whom they have pierced.” How can I look at a crucifix today with new eyes?
How can our family honour the Sacred Heart in our home, in prayer, and in reparation for the wounds of the world?

lead: The day after the Sacred Heart of Jesus, the Church honours the Immaculate Heart of his mother. In Isaiah, the people God has blessed rejoice like a bride adorned with jewels: “I will greatly rejoice in the Lord.” In the Gospel the twelve-year-old Jesus stays behind in the Temple, and Mary and Joseph search for him for three days. When they find him, he speaks of his Father, and Mary treasures all these things in her heart. The canticle of Hannah gives the response: “My heart exults in the Lord.”

r.h: Clothed with the garments of salvation
set: Chapters 56–66 of Isaiah come from the time after the return from exile in Babylon, when Jerusalem was being rebuilt in poverty and hope. Many scholars call this part of the book “Third Isaiah”. Chapter 61 begins with the words Jesus read in the synagogue at Nazareth: “The spirit of the Lord God is upon me, because the Lord has anointed me; he has sent me to bring good news to the oppressed” (61:1; Luke 4:18).
Our verses close the chapter. God promises that his people will be known among the nations as blessed, and the city, or the prophet in her name, answers with a song of joy.
str: v. 9: the blessed people will be known among the nations.
v. 10: the song of joy: clothed with salvation, like a bridegroom and a bride.
v. 11: as a garden makes seeds spring up, so God will make righteousness spring up before the nations.
kw: A doubled verb for great joy. The same joy will sound in Mary’s Magnificat: “my spirit rejoices in God my Savior” (Luke 1:47).
Salvation is pictured as clothing that God himself puts on his people. It is his gift, not their own making.
God’s faithful, saving justice, which makes things right. Here it grows like a plant from the soil.
vv: I will greatly rejoice in the Lord, my whole being shall exult in my God;
The Church hears in these words the voice of Mary, who rejoiced in God her Saviour.
he has covered me with the robe of righteousness, as a bridegroom decks himself with a garland, and as a bride adorns herself with her jewels.
Bride and bridegroom: the image of the covenant between God and his people. Mary, adorned with grace from the first moment of her life, is the first fruits of this wedding joy.
so the Lord God will cause righteousness and praise to spring up before all the nations.
What God sows in secret grows into praise that all can see.
ch: The Church applies this song to Mary, who was clothed with the garment of salvation from the first moment of her conception, preserved from every stain of original sin by the merits of Christ her Son (CCC 491–492). The opening words of the entrance antiphon of the Mass of the Immaculate Conception on 8 December are taken from this verse. Mary’s holiness is God’s gift, and her joy is the joy of one who knows that everything she has is grace.

r.h: His mother treasured all these things in her heart
set: This is the last scene of Luke’s infancy story and the only story in the Gospels from the hidden years of Jesus between his infancy and his public ministry. Devout Jewish families went up to Jerusalem for the great feasts, above all Passover. At twelve, a boy was approaching the age when he would take on the duties of the Law.
Pilgrims travelled in large groups of relatives and neighbours, which explains how Mary and Joseph could travel a day without noticing that Jesus was not with them.
str: vv. 41–42: the yearly pilgrimage; Jesus is twelve.
vv. 43–45: Jesus stays behind; his parents search for him.
vv. 46–47: after three days they find him among the teachers.
vv. 48–50: Mary’s question; Jesus speaks of his Father; they do not understand.
v. 51: Jesus returns to Nazareth and is obedient; Mary treasures all in her heart.
kw: Literally “in the things of my Father”. It can mean his Father’s house or his Father’s affairs. Both are true: the first words of Jesus in Luke speak of God as his Father.
A strong word for anguish. Mary and Joseph feel real pain; holiness does not make them stop being parents.
To keep carefully, to hold on to. Mary keeps the events and the words in her heart, even when she does not understand them, and ponders them (compare 2:19).
vv: After three days they found him in the temple, sitting among the teachers, listening to them and asking them questions.
Many readers since early times have seen in the “three days” a foreshadowing of the three days in which Jesus was lost to his mother in death and found again in the Resurrection.
Look, your father and I have been searching for you in great anxiety.
Mary calls Joseph his father. Jesus’ answer gently points to his other Father. Both are true: Joseph is his father in the eyes of the law and in love; God is his Father by nature.
Did you not know that I must be in my Father’s house?
The little word “must” will return in Luke for the divine plan that leads to the Cross (9:22; 24:26).
Then he went down with them and came to Nazareth, and was obedient to them. His mother treasured all these things in her heart.
The Son of God lives thirty years of obedience in an ordinary home. Mary’s heart is the place where the mystery is kept and pondered.
ch: The Catechism teaches that the finding in the Temple is the only event that breaks the silence of the Gospels about the hidden years of Jesus, and that in it he lets us glimpse the mystery of his total consecration to a mission flowing from his divine sonship (CCC 534). His hidden life at Nazareth allows everyone to enter into fellowship with Jesus by the most ordinary events of daily life (CCC 533). The Second Vatican Council sees Mary as the one who “kept these things in her heart”, advancing in her pilgrimage of faith (Lumen Gentium 57–58). Her Immaculate Heart is a heart wholly open to God, keeping his word and bringing it to fruit.

qa: What does the Church mean by the “Immaculate Heart” of Mary?

The heart, in the Bible, is the centre of the person. Mary’s heart is called immaculate because she was preserved from all sin from the first moment of her existence and lived wholly for God. Devotion to her Immaculate Heart honours her inner life of faith, love and pondering, and asks her to lead us to her Son. It always points to Christ, as her own words did: “Do whatever he tells you” (John 2:5).
rite: Devotion to the heart of Mary was promoted in the seventeenth century by St John Eudes. After the appearances of Our Lady at Fatima in 1917, Pope Pius XII consecrated the world to the Immaculate Heart of Mary in 1942 and extended the feast to the whole Church in 1944. Pope St John Paul II made it an obligatory memorial, kept on the Saturday after the Solemnity of the Sacred Heart. This year it falls on the same day as the memorial of St Boniface (died 754), the English monk Wynfrith who became the apostle of Germany and was martyred at Dokkum in Frisia while preparing new Christians for confirmation. Both may be remembered today.
study: Mary did not understand, yet she kept the words in her heart. What word of God am I being asked to keep and ponder, without understanding it yet?
Jesus lived obediently at Nazareth for many years. How can the ordinary duties of my home become a place of holiness?

lead: After the great feasts of Easter, Pentecost and the Body and Blood of Christ, the Sundays in Ordinary Time resume. The Tenth Sunday of Year B sets side by side the first sin in the garden and the conflict around Jesus in Galilee. In Genesis God seeks the man who hides, “Where are you?”, and promises that the offspring of the woman will strike the serpent’s head. In the Gospel Jesus is accused of working by the power of Satan; he answers that he is the stronger one who binds the strong man. His family comes to take him home, and he declares that whoever does the will of God is his brother and sister and mother.

St Paul, in the second reading, speaks from his own sufferings: “So we do not lose heart … our inner nature is being renewed day by day.” Psalm 130, the De profundis, joins the readings together: out of the depths we cry to the Lord, for with him there is steadfast love and great power to redeem.

set: The first chapters of Genesis teach, in the language of story and image, truths about God, the world and humanity. The Church teaches that the account of the fall uses figurative language but affirms a real event, a fault committed at the beginning of human history (CCC 390). In chapter 2 God placed the man and the woman in the garden and gave them one command. In chapter 3 the serpent persuades them to doubt God’s goodness, and they eat.
Our passage begins just after the sin. The man and the woman, who were naked and not ashamed (2:25), now hide among the trees when they hear God walking in the garden in the cool of the day.
str: v. 9: God calls: “Where are you?”
v. 10: the man: “I was afraid, because I was naked; and I hid myself.”
vv. 11–13: God questions; the man blames the woman, and God who gave her; the woman blames the serpent.
v. 14: the curse on the serpent.
v. 15: enmity between the serpent and the woman, between his offspring and hers; “he will strike your head”.
¶ God does not curse the man or the woman here; he curses the serpent and the ground (3:17). The promise of victory comes before the words of punishment to the man and the woman.
kw: God knows where the man is. The question is an invitation to come out of hiding and to tell the truth. It is the first question God asks in the Bible.
A lasting hostility. God himself sets it between the woman and the serpent, so that the human race will not remain on the side of evil.
A word that can mean one descendant or many. The promise speaks of a long struggle between the two lines, and of one from the woman’s line who will strike the serpent’s head.
vv: But the Lord God called to the man, and said to him, “Where are you?”
Sin makes man hide; God comes looking. The whole story of salvation begins here, with God seeking the one who is lost.
I was afraid, because I was naked; and I hid myself.
Before the sin there was trust and no shame. Now there is fear. The first fruit of sin is broken relationship with God.
The woman whom you gave to be with me, she gave me fruit from the tree, and I ate.
The man blames the woman and, indirectly, God. Sin divides husband and wife and makes us shift the blame.
I will put enmity between you and the woman, and between your offspring and hers; he will strike your head, and you will strike his heel.

The serpent’s blow to the heel is painful; the blow to the head is fatal. Textual note: the Hebrew says “he” or “it”, meaning the offspring; the Greek translation has “he”. The Latin Vulgate of St Jerome read “she”, which shaped much Christian art showing Mary crushing the serpent. Both readings point to the same victory: Christ wins it, and Mary, his mother, shares in it.
ch: The Catechism calls this verse the “Protoevangelium”, the first announcement of the Gospel: the Messiah and Redeemer, the battle between the serpent and the woman, and the final victory of a descendant of hers (CCC 410). It adds that many Fathers and Doctors of the Church have seen the woman as Mary, the mother of Christ, the “new Eve” (CCC 411). St Irenaeus wrote that the knot of Eve’s disobedience was loosed by Mary’s obedience (in substance, Against Heresies 3.22.4).

The Church also reads the passage as the revelation of original sin: the first parents lost the original holiness and justice they had received from God, not only for themselves but for all human beings (CCC 416–417). But the first word after the sin is God’s search and God’s promise. Pope St Leo the Great said that Christ’s grace gave us blessings better than those the demon’s envy had taken away (in substance; quoted in CCC 412).

r.h: So we do not lose heart
set: Paul wrote Second Corinthians after painful conflicts with the community in Corinth, some of whom despised him as weak and unimpressive. In chapters 4 and 5 he answers by speaking of the treasure of the Gospel carried “in clay jars” (4:7): the frailty of the apostle shows that the power belongs to God.
Our passage follows his list of sufferings: afflicted, perplexed, persecuted, struck down, but not crushed or destroyed (4:8–9). He explains why he keeps going: faith in the resurrection.
str: v. 13: “I believed, and so I spoke”: faith that speaks.
v. 14: God who raised Jesus will raise us too.
v. 15: everything is for your sake, so that thanksgiving may increase.
vv. 16–18: the outer nature wastes away, the inner is renewed; slight affliction, eternal glory; seen and unseen.
5:1: the earthly tent and the eternal house from God.
kw: I believed, and so I spoke
Paul quotes Psalm 116:10 in its Greek form (in the Greek numbering, Psalm 115:1). The psalm is a song of thanksgiving by one rescued from death.
Literally “the inner man”. Not a soul trapped in a body, but the person as renewed by the Spirit, growing day by day toward the resurrection.
In Hebrew the word for glory, kābôd, also means weight. Paul, who knew Hebrew, sets the “weight” of glory against the lightness of present affliction.
vv: we also believe, and so we speak,
Faith cannot keep silent. The apostle preaches because he believes.
because we know that the one who raised the Lord Jesus will raise us also with Jesus,
The resurrection of Jesus is the pledge of ours. Paul’s courage rests not on his strength but on this certainty.
So we do not lose heart. Even though our outer nature is wasting away, our inner nature is being renewed day by day.
Age, illness and labour wear the body down. The life of grace grows at the same time. Every sick and elderly Christian can make these words their own.
For this slight momentary affliction is preparing us for an eternal weight of glory beyond all measure,
Paul’s afflictions were not slight (11:23–28). He calls them slight only when weighed against the glory to come.
For we know that if the earthly tent we live in is destroyed, we have a building from God, a house not made with hands, eternal in the heavens.
A tent is temporary, a house lasting. Paul, a tentmaker by trade (Acts 18:3), knew both well.
ch: The Church prays with this hope in the Preface for the Dead: for your faithful, Lord, life is changed, not ended, and when this earthly dwelling turns to dust, an eternal dwelling is made ready in heaven (in substance). The Catechism teaches that Christ will raise us up on the last day, and that by Baptism we already share in his heavenly life (CCC 1002–1003). Christian suffering is not meaningless: united with Christ it becomes a way to glory (compare CCC 1521).

r.h: Whoever does the will of God
set: Jesus has begun his ministry in Galilee. He has healed many, cast out demons, and just chosen the Twelve (3:13–19). Crowds press around him, so that he and his disciples cannot even eat. Two groups react: his own family, who think he has gone out of his mind, and scribes come down from Jerusalem, who say he works by the power of Beelzebul.

Background. Mark often places one story inside another, so that each explains the other. Here the family sets out (vv. 20–21), the scribes accuse (vv. 22–30), and the family arrives (vv. 31–35). Both groups misjudge Jesus, but in different ways: the family out of worry, the scribes out of hostility.
str: vv. 20–21: the crowd; his family set out to restrain him: “He has gone out of his mind.”
v. 22: the scribes from Jerusalem: “He has Beelzebul.”
vv. 23–27: the parables: a kingdom divided; a house divided; the strong man bound.
vv. 28–30: every sin can be forgiven, but not blasphemy against the Holy Spirit.
vv. 31–35: his mother and brothers outside; “Whoever does the will of God is my brother and sister and mother.”
kw: Literally “those from his side”, his relatives. The phrase is deliberately general. Mark does not say that Mary shared their opinion.
An old name of a Canaanite god, “Baal the prince”, used in Jesus’ day as a name for the chief of the demons. The scribes cannot deny the exorcisms, so they explain them as the work of evil.
Satan is the strong man; Jesus is the stronger one whom John the Baptist announced (1:7). His exorcisms show that the strong man is already being bound.
vv: When his family heard it, they went out to restrain him, for people were saying, “He has gone out of his mind.”
Jesus’ zeal seemed excessive even to those who loved him. Matthew and Luke leave this verse out; Mark keeps the hard memory.
How can Satan cast out Satan?
Jesus answers with simple logic. If his work destroys the power of evil, it cannot come from evil.
But no one can enter a strong man’s house and plunder his property without first tying up the strong man;
The parable of Jesus’ whole mission. He has come to set captives loose from the power of evil.
Truly I tell you, people will be forgiven for their sins and whatever blasphemies they utter;
A word of immense mercy comes first: there is no sin God cannot forgive.
Whoever does the will of God is my brother and sister and mother.
Jesus does not reject his family; he opens it wide. The bond of faith and obedience to God creates a new family around him.
ch: On the sin against the Holy Spirit the Catechism teaches that there are no limits to the mercy of God, but anyone who deliberately refuses to accept his mercy by repenting rejects the forgiveness of sins and the salvation offered by the Holy Spirit (CCC 1864). The sin is unforgivable not because God refuses, but because the sinner refuses to be forgiven.

On the “brothers” of Jesus the Catechism explains that the Church has always understood these as close relations, according to a common way of speaking in the Old Testament; James and Joseph, called brothers of Jesus, are the sons of another Mary (CCC 500; compare Mark 6:3; 15:40). Mary remained ever virgin (CCC 499). The Second Vatican Council says that Mary received these words of her Son in faith, for she heard and kept the word of God faithfully (Lumen Gentium 58). St Augustine taught that Mary was more blessed in receiving the faith of Christ than in conceiving the flesh of Christ (in substance, On Holy Virginity 3). She is the first of those who do the will of God.

qa: Does this Gospel mean that Jesus rejected his mother?

No. Jesus is not pushing Mary away; he is showing where true closeness to him lies. No one did the will of God more fully than Mary, who said, “Here am I, the servant of the Lord; let it be with me according to your word” (Luke 1:38). She is doubly his mother: by giving him flesh and by her faith. The Church honours her as the model disciple.
What is the unforgivable sin? Could I have committed it without knowing?

It is not a single word said in anger or a sin of weakness. It is the deliberate, lasting refusal to accept God’s mercy, calling good evil and refusing to repent (CCC 1864). Anyone who is worried about having committed it shows by that very worry that they have not hardened their heart. The door of confession is open.
Did God really make a serpent speak? How should we read Genesis 3?

The Church teaches that the account uses figurative language but affirms a real event at the beginning of human history (CCC 390). The serpent stands for the tempter, whom Scripture later calls “that ancient serpent, who is called the Devil and Satan” (Revelation 12:9; CCC 391). What matters is the truth taught: human beings, created good, misused the liberty God gave them by distrusting him, and God at once promised salvation.
rite: With this Sunday the Sundays of the Latin Church return to the green of Ordinary Time, already worn on weekdays since Pentecost, until the end of the liturgical year. In Year B the Sunday Gospels follow Mark; today’s passage is one of the earliest in his account of the Galilean ministry. The Church in India, which celebrated the Body and Blood of Christ last Sunday, kept the Sacred Heart of Jesus on Friday and the Immaculate Heart of Mary on Saturday. Genesis 3:15 and Mark 3:35 together give a fitting close to that week: the woman whose offspring defeats the serpent is also the first disciple who does the will of God. The opening prayer of today’s Mass asks God, from whom all good things come, that by his inspiration we may discern what is right and by his guidance do it.
study: God asks Adam, “Where are you?” Where am I hiding from God, and what would it mean to answer him honestly?
Adam blamed Eve and Eve blamed the serpent. In what situations do I find it hard to take responsibility for my own wrongs?
Paul says, “we do not lose heart”. Who among the sick or elderly in our parish could be encouraged by these words, and how?
Jesus calls those who do God’s will his family. How can our parish feel more like a family to those who have no family?

lead: This week the weekday Mass begins two great readings side by side: St Paul’s Second Letter to the Corinthians and the Sermon on the Mount. Today Paul opens his letter with a blessing of “the God of all consolation”, who comforts us in affliction so that we may comfort others. In the Gospel Jesus sits on the mountain and calls blessed the poor in spirit, those who mourn, the meek and the persecuted. Paul shows what the Beatitudes look like in a real life, and Psalm 34 sums up the day: the Lord is close to the brokenhearted; taste and see that he is good.

set: Paul wrote this letter from Macedonia, most likely in the mid fifties of the first century, after a hard time with the church he had founded at Corinth. There had been a painful visit and a letter written “with many tears” (2:4). Some in Corinth doubted his authority and mocked his weakness. Many scholars think that 2 Corinthians as we have it gathers more than one of Paul’s letters to Corinth; others defend its unity. Either way, its voice is Paul at his most personal.

Ancient letters began with a greeting and usually a thanksgiving. Paul turns the thanksgiving into a blessing of God, in the form of the Jewish prayer “Blessed are you, Lord”. In five verses the word “consolation” and its verb come again and again.
str: vv. 1–2: greeting from Paul and Timothy to the church in Corinth and all Achaia.
vv. 3–4: God is blessed as the Father of mercies, who consoles us so that we can console others.
vv. 5–7: the sufferings of Christ overflow to us, and so does his consolation; Paul and the Corinthians share both.
kw: The word means comfort, but also strengthening and urging on: someone called to stand beside you. It belongs to the same family as Paraclete, the name Jesus gives the Holy Spirit in John’s Gospel (John 14:16).
Literally pressure, being crushed. Paul uses it for persecution, hardship and inner distress. The next verses speak of an affliction in Asia so heavy that he “despaired of life itself” (1:8).
The Corinthians are partners in Paul’s sufferings and in his consolation (v. 7). The same root gives koinōnia, communion.
vv: the Father of mercies and the God of all consolation,
Two names for God built on the Old Testament. In Hebrew, mercies (raḥamim) are linked with the word for a mother’s womb. God’s mercy is tender, close and active.
who consoles us in all our affliction, so that we may be able to console those who are in any affliction
Consolation is not meant to stop with us. The comfort we receive becomes a gift we can pass on. Those who have been through grief often become the best comforters of others.
For just as the sufferings of Christ are abundant for us, so also our consolation is abundant through Christ.
The sufferings of the apostle are joined to Christ’s own. Paul does not say that faith removes suffering; he says that in Christ suffering and comfort both overflow.
Our hope for you is unshaken;
After all the tension with Corinth, Paul begins with hope, not with complaint. This is a lesson for every pastor and parent.
ch: The Church sees in this passage the Christian meaning of suffering. St John Paul II, in his apostolic letter on suffering, Salvifici Doloris (1984), wrote that those who share in the sufferings of Christ also share in his consolation and in the work of redemption. The Catechism teaches that the Holy Spirit is the Paraclete, the Consoler (CCC 692). Every visit to the sick, every word of comfort at a funeral and every patient bearing of pain can become what Paul describes: consolation received from God and handed on.

r.h: Blessed are the poor in spirit
set: Matthew gathers Jesus’ teaching into five great discourses, and the Sermon on the Mount (chapters 5–7) is the first. Jesus goes up the mountain and sits down to teach, as a rabbi sat. Many commentators see Jesus here as a new Moses, who received the Law on Sinai; but Jesus does not receive the word, he speaks it with his own authority.
The Beatitudes follow a form well known from the Psalms and the wisdom books: “Happy are those who …” (Psalm 1:1). Jesus fills that old form with the good news of the kingdom.
str: vv. 1–2: Jesus goes up the mountain, sits down and teaches the disciples, with the crowds listening.
vv. 3–10: eight Beatitudes, framed by the same promise, “theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (vv. 3 and 10).
vv. 11–12: a ninth, spoken directly to the disciples: blessed are you when you are persecuted for my sake.
kw: Not a wish but a declaration. Jesus announces that these people are already in God’s favour, because the kingdom is coming to them.

In the Old Testament the poor (‘anawim) are those who have nothing to rely on but God (Psalm 34:6; Zephaniah 3:12). Matthew’s “in spirit” shows the inner attitude: humble dependence on God, which material poverty often teaches.
Matthew’s usual phrase. Following the Jewish custom of reverence, “heaven” stands for God. It means God’s reign, not only a place after death.
vv: he went up the mountain; and after he sat down, his disciples came to him.
The scene recalls Sinai. The disciples come close, and the crowds also hear him (7:28). The Sermon is first of all for those who follow him.
Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven.
The first Beatitude is the door to all the others. Only an empty hand can receive the kingdom as a gift.
Blessed are the meek, for they will inherit the earth.
Almost word for word from Psalm 37:11. The meek are not weak; they do not seize by force what God will give.
Blessed are the pure in heart, for they will see God.
In the Bible the heart is the centre of the person, where decisions are made. Purity of heart means an undivided heart, wanting God alone. Its promise is the highest of all: the vision of God.
Rejoice and be glad, for your reward is great in heaven,
Joy in persecution is possible because the disciple stands in the line of the prophets and belongs to Christ.
ch: The Catechism calls the Beatitudes the heart of Jesus’ preaching; they depict the face of Jesus Christ and portray his love (CCC 1716–1717). Christ himself is the poor, meek, merciful and persecuted one. St Augustine, in his commentary on the Sermon on the Mount, called it a perfect standard of the Christian life, and he linked the Beatitudes with the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit (in substance). The saints are simply the Beatitudes lived out in very different lives.

qa: Are the Beatitudes commands or promises?

Both, in a way. In form they are promises: Jesus declares people blessed and tells what God will give them. But they also describe the kind of person a disciple becomes, and so they call us to conversion. The Catechism says they respond to the desire for happiness that God has placed in every human heart (CCC 1718).
study: When did someone console me in a hard time? Whom can I console this week with the comfort I received?
Which Beatitude do I find hardest to believe? Why?

lead: Paul had changed his travel plans, and some in Corinth said he was a man of “Yes and No”, unreliable. He answers that his word is not double, because the Son of God he preached is God’s great “Yes” to all his promises. In the Gospel Jesus tells his disciples who they are: salt of the earth, light of the world. Both readings speak of a life that is reliable and visible. Psalm 119 prays: let your face shine on your servant.

set: Paul had promised a double visit to Corinth, on the way to Macedonia and back again (1:15–16). He changed his plan, to spare them another painful visit (1:23). His critics used the change to say that he could not be trusted. Paul replies not only with an explanation but with theology: the faithfulness of God stands behind the preacher and his message.
str: v. 18: God is faithful; our word to you has not been “Yes and No”.
vv. 19–20: Jesus Christ, whom Paul, Silvanus and Timothy preached, is God’s “Yes”; through him we say “Amen”.
vv. 21–22: God establishes us in Christ, anoints us, seals us and gives us the Spirit as a first installment.
kw: A Hebrew word meaning firm, sure, reliable. To say Amen is to lean one’s whole weight on God’s word. Christ is God’s Yes; the Church answers Amen.
Paul plays on words: God establishes us “in Christ” (Christos, the Anointed One) and has “anointed” us (chrisas). Christians share in the anointing of the Messiah.
A word from trade, borrowed from the Semitic languages: a down payment that guarantees the full price will follow. The Spirit given now is the pledge of the glory to come.
vv: As surely as God is faithful, our word to you has not been “Yes and No.”
Paul swears, in effect, by God’s faithfulness. The reliability of the messenger matters because he carries the word of a faithful God.
For in him every one of God’s promises is a “Yes.”
All the promises made to Abraham, to David and through the prophets find their fulfilment in Christ. God has not changed his mind about any of them.
For this reason it is through him that we say the “Amen,” to the glory of God.
Probably a reference to the Amen of the community at worship. When the people answer “Amen” at the end of the Eucharistic Prayer, they say this same word through Christ to the Father.
by putting his seal on us and giving us his Spirit in our hearts as a first installment.
A seal marked ownership and protection. Paul does not name a rite here, but the Church has always heard in these words Baptism and the anointing with the Spirit.
ch: The Catechism quotes these verses when it explains the seal of Confirmation: Christians are marked with the seal of the Spirit, who establishes them in Christ (CCC 1296). It also teaches that Jesus Christ himself is the “Amen” (Revelation 3:14), the definitive Amen of the Father’s love for us (CCC 1065). So the simple Amen said at Mass, and especially before receiving Holy Communion, is a small act of faith with a long history: a Yes to the One who is God’s Yes.

r.h: Salt of the earth, light of the world
set: Right after the Beatitudes Jesus turns to the disciples and says “you are”. He does not say “try to become” salt and light. Those who live the Beatitudes already are salt and light, and they must not lose what they are. Salt and light were ordinary things in every Galilean house: salt to preserve and to season, an oil lamp to light the one room where the family lived.
str: v. 13: you are the salt of the earth; salt that loses its taste is thrown out.
v. 14: you are the light of the world; a city on a hill cannot be hidden.
vv. 15–16: a lamp is put on a lampstand; let your light shine so that others give glory to the Father.
kw: Salt preserved food from decay and gave it flavour. In Israel’s worship every offering was seasoned with “the salt of the covenant” (Leviticus 2:13).

The Greek verb literally means “become foolish”. The salt of the Dead Sea region, mixed with other minerals, could lose its saltiness. A disciple who loses the wisdom of the Gospel becomes useless in the same way.
A grain measure holding about nine litres. Putting it over a lamp would put the lamp out.
vv: You are the salt of the earth;
A small group of fishermen and ordinary people are told that they matter for the whole earth. The mission is universal from the start.
You are the light of the world. A city built on a hill cannot be hid.

Jesus calls himself the light of the world in John 8:12; here he shares the title with his disciples. Their light is his light reflected. Many commentators also hear Isaiah’s vision of Zion on the mountain, to which the nations come (Isaiah 2:2–3).
In the same way, let your light shine before others, so that they may see your good works and give glory to your Father in heaven.
The aim is not that people praise us, but that they praise the Father. Later in the Sermon Jesus warns against doing good in order to be seen (6:1); the difference is where the glory goes.
ch: The Second Vatican Council took its great document on the Church from this image: Christ is the light of the nations, Lumen Gentium, and that light shines on the face of the Church. The Catechism, describing the People of God, says that its mission is to be salt of the earth and light of the world (CCC 782). The Council also teaches that lay people make Christ known to others above all by the witness of their lives (Lumen Gentium 31). A Christian home, an honest office, a kind classroom are lamps on the lampstand.

qa: Does “let your light shine” contradict Jesus’ warning not to practise our piety before others (Matthew 6:1)?

No. Both sayings ask the same question: for whose glory? Good works are to be seen so that people give glory to the Father. Piety done in order to be admired by others has already received its reward. The disciple neither hides the light nor puts himself in the spotlight.
study: Where do I need to keep my word more faithfully, so that my “Yes” means yes?
In what place of my daily life is God asking me to be salt or light?

lead: Paul contrasts the ministry of Moses, written on stone, with the ministry of the new covenant, written by the Spirit: “the letter kills, but the Spirit gives life.” In the Gospel Jesus says that he has come not to abolish the Law and the prophets but to fulfil them. The two readings must be read together: the Spirit does not throw away the Law; he writes it on the heart. On the memorial of St Ephrem, Psalm 99 proclaims: holy is the Lord our God.

set: Some preachers had come to Corinth with letters of recommendation and questioned Paul’s credentials. Paul answers that the Corinthians themselves are his letter, written by the Spirit on human hearts (3:1–3). He then compares his ministry with that of Moses, using the story of Moses’ shining face when he came down from Sinai (Exodus 34:29–35).

Paul argues “from the lesser to the greater”, a method well known among the Jewish teachers of his time: if the first ministry had glory, how much more the second. He is not saying that the Law was bad. Elsewhere he calls it “holy and just and good” (Romans 7:12). He is saying that the new covenant, promised by Jeremiah (Jeremiah 31:31–34), surpasses it.
str: vv. 4–6: our competence is from God, who made us ministers of a new covenant, of spirit and not of letter.
vv. 7–8: the old ministry came in glory, so that Moses’ face shone; much more the ministry of the Spirit.
vv. 9–11: the ministry of condemnation had glory; the ministry of justification abounds in glory; what is permanent surpasses what was set aside.
kw: The phrase of Jeremiah 31:31, and of Jesus at the Last Supper: “This cup is the new covenant in my blood” (1 Corinthians 11:25). Paul is its servant.

The written text by itself, carved on stone. Paul does not mean the literal sense of Scripture as opposed to the spiritual sense; he means a law written outside a person, which tells what to do but cannot give the power to do it.
The visible radiance of God’s presence, Hebrew kabod. It shone on Moses’ face. In the new covenant it shines in Christ and, through the Spirit, in believers.
vv: our competence is from God,
Paul’s confidence is not self-confidence. Every minister of the Church, and every Christian, works from a gift received.
not of letter but of spirit; for the letter kills, but the Spirit gives life.
The Law shows sin but cannot heal it; only the Spirit pours God’s love into our hearts (Romans 5:5). This is how St Augustine read the verse in his work On the Spirit and the Letter (in substance).
how much more will the ministry of the Spirit come in glory?
If a reflection of God’s glory on one man’s face made the people afraid to look, what will the gift of the Spirit to all believers be?
for if what was set aside came through glory, much more has the permanent come in glory!
The old covenant came “through glory”: Paul honours it. The new is permanent because it is founded on Christ’s death and resurrection.
ch: The Catechism teaches that, in Christian tradition, the Law is holy, spiritual and good, yet still imperfect; it is a first stage on the way to the kingdom (CCC 1963). The New Law is the grace of the Holy Spirit given through faith in Christ (CCC 1966). The Church also holds that God’s covenant with Israel has never been revoked (Romans 11:29; CCC 121). So Paul’s contrast is never a cause for pride or contempt. It is a call to let the Spirit write God’s will on our hearts.

r.h: Not to abolish but to fulfil
set: These verses are the key to the whole Sermon on the Mount. In the next part Jesus will say six times, “You have heard that it was said … But I say to you” (5:21–48). Some might think he was setting the Law aside. Matthew, writing for a community with deep Jewish roots, shows at the start that Jesus fulfils the Law and the prophets.
str: v. 17: I have come not to abolish but to fulfil.
v. 18: not one letter, not one stroke will pass from the Law until all is accomplished.
v. 19: whoever breaks and teaches others to break the least commandment will be least; whoever does and teaches them will be great.
kw: To fill up, to bring to full measure. Matthew uses it again and again for the prophecies fulfilled in Jesus. Jesus fulfils the Law by obeying it perfectly and by revealing its deepest meaning.

The iota is the smallest Greek letter, corresponding to the Hebrew yod; the “stroke” is a tiny hook that distinguishes one Hebrew letter from another. Not even the smallest detail of God’s word is without value.
Jewish teachers distinguished “light” and “heavy” commandments. Jesus says that even the least must be kept and taught.
vv: I have come not to abolish but to fulfill.
“I have come” is a phrase of mission: Jesus speaks of why he was sent. He is the goal towards which the Law and the prophets were moving.
not one letter, not one stroke of a letter, will pass from the law until all is accomplished.

The Law endures, but it is now read in the light of Christ. The Church does not keep the ritual laws of the Old Testament, because Christ has accomplished what they foreshadowed; the moral law remains.
but whoever does them and teaches them will be called great in the kingdom of heaven.
Doing comes before teaching. A teacher of the faith is measured first by his own life.
ch: The Catechism teaches that the Law of the Gospel fulfils, refines, surpasses and leads the Old Law to its perfection (CCC 1967), and that Jesus fulfilled the Law so perfectly that he took upon himself its curse for our sake (CCC 580). The Second Vatican Council, following St Augustine, taught that the New Testament lies hidden in the Old and the Old is made plain in the New (Dei Verbum 16). This is why the Church reads the Old Testament at Mass: it is not an old book left behind, but God’s word fulfilled in Christ.

qa: If Jesus did not abolish the Law, why do Christians not keep the food laws or circumcision?

The Church distinguishes within the Law. The moral law, summed up in the Ten Commandments, remains and is deepened by Christ. The ritual and ceremonial laws prepared for Christ and are fulfilled in him; the apostles at the Council of Jerusalem decided that Gentile believers were not bound by them (Acts 15). Christ has fulfilled them, and they now teach us about him.
rite: Today is the optional memorial of St Ephrem the Syrian, deacon and Doctor of the Church. Born at Nisibis about 306, he taught there and later at Edessa, where he died in 373. He wrote hymns, poetic homilies and commentaries in Syriac, and taught the faith to his people through song; tradition calls him the Harp of the Holy Spirit. Pope Benedict XV declared him a Doctor of the Church in 1920. Ephrem loved to find Christ hidden in the symbols of the Old Testament, which is today’s Gospel lived as prayer: the Law and the prophets fulfilled in Christ. The Syriac Churches of Kerala sing his hymns to this day.
study: Do I treat any commandment as too small to matter? What would it mean to keep it with love?
Which Old Testament passage has helped me to understand Christ better?

lead: Paul continues his reflection on Moses’ veil: when one turns to the Lord, the veil is removed, and all of us, with unveiled faces, are being transformed into Christ’s image from glory to glory. In the Gospel Jesus asks for a righteousness that goes deeper than outward observance: not only no murder, but no anger and no insult, and reconciliation before worship. The glory Paul describes becomes visible in a reconciled community. Psalm 85 sings: the glory of the Lord will dwell in our land.

set: Paul takes up the detail of Exodus 34: after speaking with God, Moses put a veil over his shining face, and removed it when he went in before the Lord. Paul uses the veil as an image. He speaks of his own people, many of whom had not accepted the gospel, and says that a veil lies over their reading of Moses. These are words of a man who loved his people deeply (Romans 9:1–5) and who believed that God would not abandon them (Romans 11:1–2, 29). They must never be used to look down on the Jewish people.
The Lectionary leaves out 4:2, where Paul defends his honesty, and continues with the gospel veiled to those who are perishing and the light shining in our hearts.
str: 3:15–16: a veil lies over minds when Moses is read; when one turns to the Lord, the veil is removed.
3:17–18: the Lord is the Spirit; with unveiled faces we are transformed from glory to glory.
4:1: by God’s mercy we have this ministry and do not lose heart.
4:3–6: the gospel veiled to some; we proclaim Christ, the image of God; God has shone in our hearts.
kw: The word can mean both beholding as in a mirror and reflecting like a mirror. Both meanings fit: we look at the glory of the Lord, and our faces begin to shine with it.
The same verb is used for the Transfiguration of Jesus (Matthew 17:2; Mark 9:2). What happened to Christ on the mountain is to happen slowly in us.
Christ is the image of God (4:4). Humanity was created in God’s image (Genesis 1:27); in Christ that image is restored and made perfect.
vv: but when one turns to the Lord, the veil is removed.
Paul echoes Exodus 34:34, where Moses removed the veil when he turned to the Lord. Conversion, not cleverness, opens Scripture.
Now the Lord is the Spirit, and where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is freedom.
The freedom of the Spirit is freedom for love and for God, not freedom from every rule.
And all of us, with unveiled faces, seeing the glory of the Lord as though reflected in a mirror, are being transformed into the same image from one degree of glory to another;
Moses alone saw the glory; now “all of us”. The change is gradual: holiness is growth, day by day, prayer by prayer, Communion by Communion.
who has shone in our hearts to give the light of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ.
An echo of the first day of creation (Genesis 1:3). Many commentators also hear Paul’s own conversion on the road to Damascus, when a light flashed around him (Acts 9:3). Faith is a new creation.
ch: The Eastern and Western Fathers loved this text. St Athanasius wrote that the Son of God became man so that we might become God (CCC 460), that is, share in the divine nature by grace (2 Peter 1:4). The Church teaches that God’s gifts and call to Israel are irrevocable, and that the Jewish people are not to be presented as rejected (Nostra Aetate 4; CCC 839). The Pontifical Biblical Commission, in its document The Jewish People and their Sacred Scriptures in the Christian Bible (2001), noted that the Jewish reading of the Bible is a possible reading, in continuity with the Jewish Sacred Scriptures of the Second Temple period. Christians read Moses in the light of Christ; they pray that the veil be lifted from their own hearts first.

set: Verse 20 states the theme of everything that follows: a righteousness that exceeds that of the scribes and Pharisees. The scribes and Pharisees were respected teachers who took the Law seriously; Jesus is not mocking their zeal but asking for something deeper, a righteousness of the heart. Then comes the first of six contrasts: “You have heard … but I say to you.”
str: v. 20: the greater righteousness.
vv. 21–22: not only murder, but anger and insult bring judgment.
vv. 23–24: leave your gift at the altar; first be reconciled.
vv. 25–26: come to terms quickly with your accuser on the way.
kw: In Matthew, right living before God, doing his will. It comes from a heart changed by grace, not from outward correctness alone.
An Aramaic insult kept in the Greek text of v. 22; the NRSV renders it “insult”. Jesus treats contemptuous words as seriously as the courts treated murder.
The valley of Hinnom south of Jerusalem, once a place of idolatrous child sacrifice (Jeremiah 7:31), became an image of final punishment.
vv: unless your righteousness exceeds that of the scribes and Pharisees, you will never enter the kingdom of heaven.
“Exceeds” means not more rules but more depth: the Law kept from within.
But I say to you that if you are angry with a brother or sister, you will be liable to judgment;
Jesus speaks with an authority greater than that of a teacher interpreting the Law. He goes to the root: murder begins in anger and contempt.
leave your gift there before the altar and go; first be reconciled to your brother or sister, and then come and offer your gift.
Jesus imagines a pilgrim in the Temple who remembers a quarrel. Worship and reconciliation belong together; God does not want gifts from a heart that refuses peace.
Truly I tell you, you will never get out until you have paid the last penny.

The “penny” is the quadrans, the smallest Roman coin. The plain sense is urgency: settle quarrels while there is time. Some Fathers and later writers also heard in it an echo of the purification after death.
