ch: The Catechism teaches that in the Sermon on the Mount the Lord recalls the commandment “You shall not kill” and adds to it the forbidding of anger, hatred and vengeance (CCC 2262). It also lists reconciliation with one’s brother before presenting an offering at the altar among the marks of the conversion of heart Jesus asks for in prayer (CCC 2608). The early Christian teaching called the Didache told those who had a quarrel not to join the Sunday Eucharist until they were reconciled (Didache 14). In the Roman Mass the sign of peace before Communion keeps this Gospel before our eyes.

qa: Is all anger sinful?

No. The Catechism teaches that anger becomes sin when it desires harm for someone (CCC 2302); Scripture also knows a just anger at evil (Ephesians 4:26). Jesus himself showed anger at the hardness of hearts (Mark 3:5). What Jesus forbids here is anger that holds on to resentment and turns into contempt and insult.
study: Is there someone with whom I need to be reconciled before I next come to the altar? What first step can I take?
How does the sign of peace at Mass change, or fail to change, the way I treat people at home?

lead: Today the Church honours St Barnabas, whom the Acts of the Apostles calls “a good man, full of the Holy Spirit and of faith”. The first reading tells how the church in Jerusalem sent him to Antioch, how he rejoiced to see God’s grace among the Gentile believers, brought Saul from Tarsus, and was finally sent out with him on mission. The Gospel gives Jesus’ instructions to the Twelve as he sends them out: proclaim the kingdom, heal, and give as you have received. Psalm 98 sings that the Lord has revealed his saving power to the nations.

r.h: A good man, full of the Holy Spirit
set: Barnabas first appears in Acts 4:36–37. His name was Joseph, a Levite from Cyprus; the apostles called him Barnabas, which Luke explains as “son of encouragement”. He sold a field and laid the money at the apostles’ feet. Later, when the disciples in Jerusalem were afraid of the newly converted Saul, it was Barnabas who took him and brought him to the apostles (9:27).

After the death of Stephen, believers scattered by persecution came to Antioch in Syria, one of the great cities of the Roman Empire. Some of them, men of Cyprus and Cyrene, began to preach the Lord Jesus to Greeks as well (11:20). This was something new, and the church in Jerusalem sent Barnabas to see. Two chapters later, the church of Antioch sends Barnabas and Saul on what is usually called Paul’s first missionary journey, beginning with Cyprus, Barnabas’ homeland.
str: 11:21b–24: many Gentiles turn to the Lord; Barnabas is sent from Jerusalem, rejoices and encourages them.
11:25–26: Barnabas brings Saul from Tarsus; a year of teaching; the disciples are first called Christians at Antioch.
13:1–3: prophets and teachers at Antioch; the Holy Spirit sets apart Barnabas and Saul; fasting, prayer, laying on of hands, sending.
kw: Barnabas “exhorted them all” (11:23). Luke’s verb echoes the meaning he gives to Barnabas’ name, “son of encouragement” (4:36). He lived up to his name.

The word is formed like a Latin name for the followers of a leader: “Christ’s people”. Many scholars think it was first given by outsiders in Antioch. The believers came to bear it without shame (1 Peter 4:16).
The Greek word gives us “liturgy”. The great decision to begin the mission to the nations was taken during worship and fasting, in obedience to the Holy Spirit.
vv: When he came and saw the grace of God, he rejoiced, and he exhorted them all to remain faithful to the Lord with steadfast devotion;
Barnabas could have come to inspect and to find fault. Instead he saw grace and rejoiced. That is the first gift of a good pastor.
for he was a good man, full of the Holy Spirit and of faith.
A rare and simple praise in Acts. Goodness, the Spirit and faith go together; his goodness was the fruit of the Spirit.
Then Barnabas went to Tarsus to look for Saul,
Tarsus was about two hundred kilometres away by land and sea. Barnabas went himself to find the man others had feared. Without Barnabas, Paul might have stayed unknown.
it was in Antioch that the disciples were first called “Christians.”
A mixed community of Jewish and Gentile believers is the first to bear the name of Christ.
Set apart for me Barnabas and Saul for the work to which I have called them.
The Holy Spirit chooses, the community confirms. Barnabas is named first; later in Acts the order becomes “Paul and Barnabas”, and Barnabas does not seem to mind.
ch: The Church honours Barnabas as an apostle, though he was not one of the Twelve, because Luke himself calls him and Paul apostles (Acts 14:14), and because he was sent by the Spirit and the Church to found churches. Tradition holds that he died as a martyr in Cyprus, at Salamis. The laying on of hands with prayer at Antioch is not described as an ordination in the later sense, but the Church sees in it the pattern of every sending: the Spirit calls, the community prays and fasts, and hands are laid on those who are sent (compare CCC 699 on the laying on of hands as a sign of the Spirit). Barnabas also teaches the virtue of encouragement: to see grace in others before seeing their faults, and to give a second chance, as he did again later with his cousin John Mark (Acts 15:37–39; Colossians 4:10).

set: Chapter 10 is the second of the five great discourses in Matthew, the missionary discourse. Jesus has just called the Twelve by name (10:1–4) and now sends them out to the lost sheep of the house of Israel. After the resurrection, the mission will open to all nations (28:19). The Church reads this Gospel on the feast of Barnabas because he lived exactly this way: poor, generous and on the move.
str: v. 7: proclaim that the kingdom of heaven has come near.
v. 8: heal, raise, cleanse, cast out; you received without payment, give without payment.
vv. 9–10: take no money, bag, spare tunic, sandals or staff; the labourer deserves his food.
vv. 11–13: stay with a worthy household; greet the house; your peace will rest on it or return to you.
kw: The same message John the Baptist and Jesus proclaimed (3:2; 4:17). The apostles do not bring a new message of their own; they carry Jesus’ message.
What the apostles received from Christ was a gift; it must be handed on as a gift. From this verse the Church learned to condemn the buying and selling of spiritual things.
Behind it stands the Hebrew shalom, the ordinary greeting, which means wholeness and well-being from God. The apostles’ greeting carries real power: it rests on the house or returns to them.
vv: As you go, proclaim the good news, ‘The kingdom of heaven has come near.’
Proclaiming happens “as you go”, along the way. Mission is not only an event; it is a way of life.
You received without payment; give without payment.
The rule of every ministry in the Church. Grace cannot be sold.
for laborers deserve their food.
Giving without payment does not mean the community has no duty to support those who serve it. The same principle appears in 1 Corinthians 9:14 and 1 Timothy 5:18.
If the house is worthy, let your peace come upon it; but if it is not worthy, let your peace return to you.
The messenger’s peace is never wasted. If it is refused, it returns to the one who gave it.
ch: The Catechism defines simony, the buying or selling of spiritual things, and quotes this Gospel against it: “You received without pay, give without pay” (CCC 2121). It adds that the minister should ask nothing for the sacraments beyond the offerings set by the competent authority, since the labourer deserves his food (CCC 2122). Barnabas, who sold his field and gave the money to the apostles, shows what this looks like in a life.

qa: Did Barnabas write the “Letter of Barnabas”?

There is an early Christian writing called the Letter of Barnabas, but almost all scholars agree that it was not written by the Barnabas of Acts. It dates from about the end of the first century or early second, and the name was attached to it later. The true Barnabas is known to us from the Acts of the Apostles and the letters of Paul.
rite: The memorial of St Barnabas is kept in the Roman calendar on 11 June, with proper readings. Barnabas reminds the Church that the mission to the nations began in a mixed, joyful community at Antioch, through a man who knew how to encourage. Parishes can honour him by thanking catechists, sponsors and mentors who, like Barnabas, have taken someone by the hand and brought them into the life of the Church.
study: Who has been a Barnabas for me, seeing grace in me and bringing me forward? Have I thanked them?
Whom could I encourage this week, especially someone others have given up on?
What have I received “without payment” from God that I can give in the same way?

lead: Paul reaches one of the summits of his letter: the love of Christ urges us on; if anyone is in Christ, there is a new creation; God has reconciled us to himself and given us the ministry of reconciliation. “Be reconciled to God.” In the Gospel Jesus asks for words so true that oaths are not needed: let your “Yes” mean yes and your “No” mean no. A reconciled person becomes a truthful person. Psalm 103 sings: the Lord is kind and merciful.

set: Paul is still defending his ministry. Why does he work so hard, endure so much, and refuse to boast about outward things? Because the love of Christ has taken hold of him. These verses gather Paul’s whole gospel into a few lines: Christ’s death for all, a new creation, and reconciliation as God’s gift and the Church’s mission.
str: vv. 14–15: the love of Christ urges us on; one died for all, so that all may live for him.
vv. 16–17: we no longer regard anyone from a human point of view; in Christ, a new creation.
vv. 18–19: God reconciled us to himself through Christ and gave us the ministry of reconciliation.
vv. 20–21: we are ambassadors; be reconciled to God; he made him to be sin who knew no sin.
kw: The verb means to press, to hold together, to control. Christ’s love for us, shown on the cross, presses on Paul and directs his whole life.
From ordinary life: the making up of a broken relationship. Notice who acts: God reconciles us to himself. We do not win God back; he comes to us.
An ambassador speaks with the authority of the one who sent him. Through the apostles God himself is making his appeal.
vv: For the love of Christ urges us on, because we are convinced that one has died for all;
Christ died for all, without exception. The love that moved him is the love that now moves his apostle.
So if anyone is in Christ, there is a new creation: everything old has passed away; see, everything has become new!
Paul does not say only that the person is renewed but that “there is a new creation”. Baptism opens a new world. Isaiah had heard God say, “I am about to do a new thing” (Isaiah 43:19).
in Christ God was reconciling the world to himself,
The whole world is the horizon of God’s mercy. The cross is not God changing his mind about us, but God himself coming to make peace.
So we are ambassadors for Christ, since God is making his appeal through us; we entreat you on behalf of Christ, be reconciled to God.
Paul writes to Christians. Even the baptised need to hear again and again: be reconciled.
For our sake he made him to be sin who knew no sin, so that in him we might become the righteousness of God.

Christ was sinless, but he took the place of sinners. Several Fathers, including St Augustine, read “sin” here as “a sacrifice for sin”, since the same Hebrew word can mean both sin and sin offering (in substance).
ch: The Catechism quotes this verse in teaching that Christ, without sin, took our place: “For our sake God made him to be sin who knew no sin” (CCC 602). It teaches that Christ entrusted the ministry of reconciliation to his apostles, and quotes Paul’s appeal, “be reconciled to God” (CCC 1442). Every Christian becomes a new creature in Baptism (CCC 1265). In the sacrament of Penance the priest still speaks as an ambassador of Christ: the words of absolution begin, “God, the Father of mercies, through the death and resurrection of his Son has reconciled the world to himself.”

set: This is the fourth of the six contrasts in Matthew 5. The Law forbade false oaths and required vows made to the Lord to be kept (Leviticus 19:12; Numbers 30:2; Deuteronomy 23:21). In practice people sometimes swore by heaven, by earth or by Jerusalem, thinking that such oaths, which avoided God’s name, were less binding. Jesus answers that all of these belong to God, and goes further: a disciple’s plain word should be so reliable that no oath is needed.
str: v. 33: you have heard: do not swear falsely; keep your vows.
vv. 34–36: do not swear at all: not by heaven, earth, Jerusalem or your own head.
v. 37: let your word be “Yes, Yes” or “No, No”; anything more comes from the evil one.
kw: To call God or something sacred as witness to the truth of what one says. An oath assumes that ordinary words cannot be trusted.
Jesus quotes Isaiah 66:1: “Heaven is my throne and the earth is my footstool.” Every so-called lesser oath still touches God.
Grammatically it can mean “evil” or “the evil one”. The need for oaths arises from a world where lying is common, the work of the father of lies (John 8:44).
vv: You shall not swear falsely, but carry out the vows you have made to the Lord.
Jesus does not deny the Law; he takes it to its goal. If no word is false, the oath becomes unnecessary.
But I say to you, Do not swear at all,
The aim is truthfulness in every word, not only in words spoken under oath.
And do not swear by your head, for you cannot make one hair white or black.
Even our own life is not in our control; it belongs to God.
Let your word be ‘Yes, Yes’ or ‘No, No’; anything more than this comes from the evil one.

St Paul uses the same language for his own honesty and for God’s faithfulness: in Christ “every one of God’s promises is a ‘Yes’” (2 Corinthians 1:20). The disciple’s truthfulness reflects the faithfulness of God.
ch: The Catechism explains that Jesus’ teaching on oaths belongs to the second commandment (CCC 2153). Following St Paul, who calls God as witness (2 Corinthians 1:23; Galatians 1:20), the tradition of the Church has understood Jesus’ words as not excluding oaths made for grave and right reasons, for example in court (CCC 2154). An oath may be refused when it is demanded for purposes contrary to the dignity of persons or to the communion of the Church (CCC 2155). The heart of the teaching is simple: Christians are to be people whose word can be trusted.

qa: Is it wrong for a Christian to take an oath in court or at an ordination?

No. The Church teaches that an oath for a grave and just reason, such as in a court of law or when taking up an office, is permitted, because it honours God as the witness of truth (CCC 2154). What Jesus forbids is careless or false swearing, and a double standard where only sworn words are true.
study: Where do I need to be reconciled with God? When did I last receive the sacrament of Penance?
Do people know that my “Yes” means yes? Where do I exaggerate, shade the truth or make promises I do not keep?

lead: After the great feasts of Easter, Pentecost, the Trinity and Corpus Christi, the green Sundays of Ordinary Time return, and the readings of this Eleventh Sunday of Year B are about growth. In Ezekiel God himself takes a tender sprig from the top of a cedar and plants it on a high mountain, where it becomes a noble cedar with birds of every kind in its branches. In the Gospel Jesus tells two parables of the kingdom: the seed that grows while the farmer sleeps, and the mustard seed that becomes the greatest of shrubs, with birds nesting in its shade. Both readings say the same thing: God plants, God gives the growth, and what begins small becomes a shelter for many.

Psalm 92 gives the picture to every faithful person: “The righteous flourish like the palm tree, and grow like a cedar in Lebanon.” St Paul, in the Second Letter to the Corinthians, speaks of the growth we cannot yet see: “we walk by faith, not by sight”, until the harvest when all appear before the judgment seat of Christ. This year 13 June, the day of St Antony of Padua, falls on the Sunday, so his memorial gives way to the Lord’s Day.

set: Ezekiel was a priest of Jerusalem who was taken to Babylon with King Jehoiachin and the first exiles in 597 before Christ. There, by the river Chebar, he received his call (1:1–3). For years he warned the exiles that Jerusalem would fall; after it fell in 587 he became the prophet of hope and restoration.

Background. Chapter 17 is a riddle or allegory. A great eagle breaks off the top of a cedar of Lebanon and carries it to a land of trade (vv. 3–4): this is Nebuchadnezzar taking King Jehoiachin, the top of the royal tree of David, to Babylon (v. 12). A vine planted in his place turns to another eagle, Egypt: this is King Zedekiah, who broke his oath and sought Egypt’s help (vv. 15–21). The house of David seems finished. Then, in our three verses, God speaks in his own name and promises to plant again.
str: v. 22: “I myself” take a tender sprig from the top of the cedar and plant it on a high and lofty mountain.
v. 23: on the mountain height of Israel it becomes a noble cedar; birds of every kind live under it.
v. 24: all the trees of the field shall know the Lord, who brings low the high tree and makes the low tree high.
¶ The passage answers the riddle. The eagles of the nations broke off the top of the cedar; only God can plant it again, and he does it with the most tender shoot.
kw: The cedar of Lebanon was the noblest tree of the ancient Near East; Solomon built the Temple and his palace with it (1 Kings 5:6). In the prophets it stands for kings and kingdoms, sometimes proud and cut down (Isaiah 2:13), here a sign of God’s own planting.

The young, soft shoot at the very top. God does not choose a strong branch. The royal hope will begin again from something weak and small, as Isaiah also says of the shoot from the stump of Jesse (Isaiah 11:1).
The Hebrew adds the pronoun “I” to the verb for emphasis, and repeats it in v. 22. What the great powers could only break, God alone will plant.
vv: I myself will take a sprig from the lofty top of a cedar; I will set it out.
The sprig comes from the same cedar, the line of David. God does not start with a new family; he keeps his promise to David (2 Samuel 7:16).
On the mountain height of Israel I will plant it,
The mountain is Zion, the place of the Temple. Ezekiel sees the restored kingdom bound up with the worship of God.
Under it every kind of bird will live; in the shade of its branches will nest winged creatures of every kind.
In the Old Testament birds sheltering in a great tree are a picture of nations finding protection under a kingdom (Ezekiel 31:6; Daniel 4:12). God’s planting will be a home for many peoples.
I bring low the high tree, I make high the low tree; I dry up the green tree and make the dry tree flourish.
This is the law of God’s way of acting, sung again by Hannah (1 Samuel 2:7–8) and by Mary in the Magnificat (Luke 1:52).
ch: The Church has read this tender sprig as a promise of the Messiah from David’s line. Jesus himself is the shoot that seemed small and weak, born in Bethlehem, raised in Nazareth, cut down on the Cross, and raised by God to be a home for all nations. The birds of every kind are the peoples who come to the Church. The Second Vatican Council teaches that the Church, the kingdom of Christ already present in mystery, grows visibly in the world through the power of God (Lumen Gentium 3).

r.h: We walk by faith, not by sight
set: Paul founded the church in Corinth, a busy port city of Greece, around the year 50, and wrote to it several times. The Second Letter to the Corinthians is the most personal of his letters. In chapters 4 and 5 he speaks of the treasure of the Gospel carried “in clay jars” (4:7), of the outer nature wasting away while the inner nature is renewed day by day (4:16), and of the earthly tent of the body that will be exchanged for a building from God (5:1).
Our passage follows. Paul is not afraid of death, but he does not despise life in the body either. He lives between the two, confident, and with one aim: to please the Lord.
str: vv. 6–8: always confident: at home in the body we are away from the Lord; we walk by faith, not by sight; we would rather be at home with the Lord.
v. 9: whether at home or away, our aim is to please him.
v. 10: all must appear before the judgment seat of Christ.
kw: To be of good courage. Paul uses it twice (vv. 6, 8). His confidence does not come from his strength but from the Spirit, whom God has given as a guarantee (5:5).
Literally what is seen, the visible form. We do not yet see the Lord face to face; we live by trust in his word (compare 1 Corinthians 13:12).

The raised platform from which a magistrate gave judgment. In the forum of Corinth Paul had himself stood before the bēma of the proconsul Gallio (Acts 18:12). Now he speaks of the judgment seat of Christ.
vv: while we are at home in the body we are away from the Lord
Paul uses the picture of people living in their own country or away from it. Life in the body is good, but it is not yet the homeland.
for we walk by faith, not by sight.
“Walk” in the Bible means to live, to conduct one’s life. Faith is not a feeling for special moments but the way we move through every day.
So whether we are at home or away, we make it our aim to please him.
Whether he lives or dies, Paul’s aim is the same. This releases the Christian from fear of death and from making comfort the goal of life.
so that each may receive recompense for what has been done in the body, whether good or evil.
What we do in the body matters. Paul, the apostle of grace, still speaks of judgment according to deeds. Grace does not make our deeds unimportant; it makes them able to bear fruit for God.
ch: The Catechism quotes v. 7 when it teaches that faith is a foretaste of the vision we shall have: now “we walk by faith, not by sight” (CCC 164). It also quotes v. 8 on Christian death: to be away from the body and at home with the Lord (CCC 1005). The Church teaches that each person receives his eternal recompense in his immortal soul at the moment of death, in a particular judgment (CCC 1022), and that at the end Christ will judge the living and the dead (CCC 1038–1039). This is not meant to frighten but to give weight to each day, lived by grace, with the aim of pleasing the Lord.

r.h: The seed grows, he does not know how
set: Mark 4 is Mark’s collection of parables, told by the Sea of Galilee from a boat (4:1). It begins with the sower (4:1–20) and the lamp (4:21–25). Then come today’s two parables: the seed growing secretly, which only Mark records, and the mustard seed, which Matthew and Luke also tell.

Background. In Jesus’ ministry the kingdom looked very small: a teacher from Nazareth, a few fishermen and tax collectors, some women who followed him, crowds who came and went, and opposition growing (3:6). The parables answer the question: can this really be the kingdom of God?
str: vv. 26–29: the seed growing by itself: the farmer sows, sleeps and rises; the earth produces of itself; at harvest he puts in the sickle.
vv. 30–32: the mustard seed: the smallest of seeds becomes the greatest of shrubs, and birds nest in its shade.
vv. 33–34: Jesus spoke the word in parables as they were able to hear, and explained everything to his disciples in private.
kw: The word from which “automatic” comes. It does not mean that the kingdom grows without God, but that it grows without the farmer’s control. The power of growth is in the seed and the soil that God has made.
Black mustard grows around the Lake of Galilee. Its seed is tiny, yet in one season the plant can grow taller than a man. “Small as a mustard seed” was a common saying for the smallest thing.

From a Greek word meaning to set side by side. A parable sets an everyday scene beside the kingdom and invites the hearer to think. Behind it stands the Hebrew māšāl, which covers proverbs, riddles and stories, like Ezekiel’s riddle of the cedar.
vv: and would sleep and rise night and day, and the seed would sprout and grow, he does not know how.
The farmer does his part, but the growth is not his work. Every farmer in Kerala who sows paddy with the monsoon knows this: you cannot pull the shoots up to make them grow faster.
first the stalk, then the head, then the full grain in the head.
Growth has its stages and its time. The kingdom ripens patiently, in a soul, a family or a parish, by night as well as by day.
at once he goes in with his sickle, because the harvest has come.
These words echo Joel 3:13, “Put in the sickle, for the harvest is ripe.” The harvest is God’s final judgment, which Paul also speaks of in the second reading.
It is like a mustard seed, which, when sown upon the ground, is the smallest of all the seeds on earth;
Jesus does not choose a mighty cedar like Ezekiel, but a humble garden plant. The kingdom begins in lowliness.
so that the birds of the air can make nests in its shade.
His hearers would have caught the echo of Ezekiel 17:23 and Daniel 4:12. The small beginning will become a shelter for the nations.
With many such parables he spoke the word to them, as they were able to hear it;
Jesus is patient with his hearers. He does not force the truth on them; he gives it as they can receive it.
ch: The Second Vatican Council, quoting this chapter, teaches that the word of the Lord is compared to a seed sown in a field; those who hear it with faith and are numbered among the little flock of Christ have received the kingdom itself; then, by its own power, the seed sprouts and grows until harvest time (Lumen Gentium 5; CCC 764). The Catechism says that the kingdom is already present in mystery in the Church, its seed and beginning (CCC 669; Lumen Gentium 3, 5).

St Ambrose saw Christ himself in the mustard seed: small and despised when buried in the earth like a grain, but when he rose he grew into a tree whose branches shelter the whole world (in substance, Commentary on Luke). St Thérèse of Lisieux, who chose the “little way”, is a modern witness that God does great things with small seeds.

qa: Is the mustard seed really the smallest of all seeds?

Jesus speaks as a Galilean to Galileans, using a well-known saying about the smallest seed they sowed. There are smaller seeds in the world, such as orchid seeds, but the point of the parable is not botany. It is the contrast between a tiny beginning and a great result, which every listener could see in his own field.
If the seed grows “of itself”, does it matter what we do?

Yes. The farmer sows and the farmer reaps; without sowing there is no harvest. But he cannot make the seed grow. The parable guards us against two errors: laziness, which does nothing, and anxiety, which thinks everything depends on us. The Church teaches that God works in us and with us, and that our cooperation is itself his gift (CCC 2001, 2008).
What does “judgment seat of Christ” mean for a Christian who trusts in grace?

Paul knows that we are saved by grace (Ephesians 2:8), and he also says we will receive recompense for what we did in the body. The two belong together. Grace is not a reason to do nothing; it is the power that makes our works good. The Catechism teaches that our merits are themselves gifts of God’s goodness (CCC 2009, 2011). So we look to the judgment with hope, not with fear.
rite: On the Sundays of Ordinary Time the Latin Church reads Mark’s Gospel in Year B, and today begins a series from Mark 4 and 5. This year the feast day of St Antony of Padua falls on the Sunday and is not celebrated at Mass. Antony was born in Lisbon about 1195, became a Franciscan, was a great preacher, and died near Padua on 13 June 1231. He was canonised within a year, and Pope Pius XII declared him a Doctor of the Church in 1946. In many parishes in Kerala and across India, the Tuesday devotions, the novenas and the distribution of St Antony’s bread to the poor may go on outside the Mass. Antony himself was a tender sprig: a little-known friar whose preaching became, after his death, a shelter for countless people.
study: Ezekiel’s God chooses a tender sprig and Jesus a mustard seed. Where in my life or parish do I despise a small beginning?
What “seed” have I sown in my family or my work that I must now leave to God to grow?
Paul says “we walk by faith, not by sight”. In what situation this week do I most need to walk by faith?
Psalm 92 says the righteous “in old age still produce fruit”. How can our parish honour and use the gifts of its elderly?

lead: St Paul urges the Corinthians not to accept the grace of God in vain: now is the acceptable time, now is the day of salvation. He describes his own ministry, full of hardships yet full of joy, “as having nothing, and yet possessing everything.” In the Gospel Jesus goes beyond the old rule of “an eye for an eye”: do not resist an evildoer, turn the other cheek, go the second mile. Paul’s life shows what Jesus’ words look like in practice.

set: Paul has just written that God was in Christ reconciling the world to himself, and that he is an ambassador for Christ: “be reconciled to God” (5:19–20). Now he presses the point. Some in Corinth were doubting him as an apostle because he was poor, suffering and not impressive in speech. He answers by describing his ministry with a list of hardships and a series of paradoxes.
str: vv. 1–2: do not accept God’s grace in vain; now is the acceptable time (quoting Isaiah 49:8).
vv. 3–7: servants of God commend themselves through endurance, hardships and the gifts of the Spirit.
vv. 8–10: paradoxes: unknown yet well known, dying yet alive, poor yet making many rich.
kw: Not simply clock time but the right moment, the time God gives. Paul reads Isaiah’s “acceptable time” as fulfilled now, in the preaching of the Gospel.
Paul and his companions are God’s co-workers (compare 1 Corinthians 3:9). God does the saving; he still wants human servants to carry his word.
Patient staying power under pressure. It heads the list (v. 4). For Paul it is the first mark of a true servant of God.
vv: we urge you also not to accept the grace of God in vain.
Grace can be received and yet left without fruit. The Corinthians had believed; Paul wants that faith to change their lives.
See, now is the acceptable time; see, now is the day of salvation!
The Church reads these words on Ash Wednesday. Every day God gives is a “now” in which we can turn to him.
as sorrowful, yet always rejoicing; as poor, yet making many rich; as having nothing, and yet possessing everything.
The world sees only the outside: poverty and sorrow. Faith sees what is within: joy and the riches of Christ, which Paul shares with many.
ch: The Church hears in “now is the acceptable time” the call to daily conversion (CCC 1427–1429). Paul’s paradoxes have inspired many saints. St Francis of Assisi, having nothing, possessed everything; and countless missionaries, priests and sisters have lived Paul’s list of hardships with joy. The Catechism also teaches that the ministry is service: the ministers of the Church are servants of Christ (CCC 876).

set: This is the fifth of the six “antitheses” of the Sermon on the Mount, where Jesus says, “You have heard that it was said… But I say to you” (5:21–48). He does not abolish the law but fulfils it (5:17), bringing it to its deepest meaning.
str: v. 38: the old rule: an eye for an eye, a tooth for a tooth.
v. 39a: “Do not resist an evildoer.”
vv. 39b–41: three examples: the cheek, the coat and cloak, the second mile.
v. 42: give to the one who begs and the one who wants to borrow.
kw: The law of equal retribution (Exodus 21:24; Leviticus 24:20; Deuteronomy 19:21). It was given to limit revenge to what was just, and it was applied by judges, not by private persons. Jesus goes further: not only limit revenge, but give it up.
Do not meet evil with evil. Jesus does not forbid justice or defence of the innocent; he forbids personal revenge.
A word for the right of Roman soldiers and officials to require a local person to carry their baggage for a set distance. Jesus says: go a second mile, willingly.
vv: But if anyone strikes you on the right cheek, turn the other also;
A blow to the right cheek with the right hand would be with the back of the hand, an insult more than an injury. Jesus asks us not to answer insult with insult.
and if anyone forces you to go one mile, go also the second mile.
The first mile is forced; the second is a gift. Love changes a burden into service.
Give to everyone who begs from you,
The disciple has an open hand. Christian tradition has read this as a call to a generous heart, guided by wisdom about what truly helps.
ch: The Catechism teaches that in the Sermon on the Mount the Lord recalls the commandment “You shall not kill” and adds the forbidding of anger, hatred and vengeance; he asks his disciples to turn the other cheek and to love their enemies (CCC 2262). It also teaches that legitimate defence of oneself and of others is not against this commandment (CCC 2263–2265). St Augustine noted that when Jesus himself was struck, he did not literally turn his cheek but answered with truth and meekness (John 18:22–23); what he commands is a heart ready to bear wrong rather than return it (in substance).

qa: Does “turn the other cheek” mean a wife or child must accept abuse?

No. Jesus speaks against revenge, not against protecting the weak. The Church teaches that legitimate defence is right and can even be a serious duty for those responsible for others (CCC 2265). Victims of abuse should seek safety and help. Turning the other cheek means refusing to hate and to take revenge, not letting evil continue.
study: Is there a good work I keep putting off for “later”? What would it mean to hear “now is the day of salvation” today?
When someone wrongs me, what would “going the second mile” look like in my home or workplace?

lead: St Paul holds up the poor churches of Macedonia, who gave beyond their means for the poor of Jerusalem, and points to the deepest reason for giving: Jesus Christ, “though he was rich, yet for your sakes he became poor.” In the Gospel Jesus asks the hardest love of all: love your enemies and pray for those who persecute you, so that you may be children of your Father, who sends sun and rain on all. Both readings ask a love that gives without counting, as God gives.

r.h: Though he was rich, he became poor
set: For several years Paul organised a collection among his Gentile churches for the poor Christians of Jerusalem (Romans 15:25–27; 1 Corinthians 16:1–4; Galatians 2:10). It was a sign of unity between Jewish and Gentile believers. The Corinthians had begun eagerly a year before, but had not finished. Chapters 8 and 9 are Paul’s appeal to complete it.
Macedonia was the northern province of Greece, with the churches of Philippi, Thessalonica and Beroea. They were poorer than Corinth and had suffered for the faith (1 Thessalonians 2:14).
str: vv. 1–5: the example of the Macedonians: in affliction and poverty, overflowing generosity; they gave themselves first to the Lord.
vv. 6–8: Titus is sent to complete the work; excel in this too; not a command but a test of love.
v. 9: the reason: the generous act of our Lord Jesus Christ.
kw: Paul uses this one word many times in these chapters: for God’s grace given to the Macedonians (v. 1), for the collection itself (vv. 6–7), and for the self-giving of Christ (v. 9). Giving is grace received and grace passed on.
Literally singleness, simplicity. A generous person gives with an undivided heart, without second thoughts. The same word family appears in tomorrow’s and Friday’s readings.
The verb for falling into real poverty. Paul is thinking of the whole mystery of Christ: the eternal Son who became man, lived poor and died on a cross.
vv: their abundant joy and their extreme poverty have overflowed in a wealth of generosity on their part.
Joy and poverty together produce generosity. It is often the poor who give most gladly.
they gave themselves first to the Lord and, by the will of God, to us,
The gift of money came after the gift of self. Christian giving begins in prayer and self-offering.
though he was rich, yet for your sakes he became poor, so that by his poverty you might become rich.
In one sentence Paul tells the whole Gospel. Compare the hymn of Philippians 2:6–8: he emptied himself, taking the form of a slave.
ch: The Catechism quotes this verse to teach that the mystery of redemption is at work in Christ’s whole life, already in his Incarnation, through which by becoming poor he enriches us with his poverty (CCC 517). St John Chrysostom, quoted in the Catechism, says that not to enable the poor to share in our goods is to steal from them (CCC 2446). The Church’s love for the poor is part of her constant tradition (CCC 2444).

set: This is the last of the six antitheses of the Sermon on the Mount. It gathers all the others into one command: love as the Father loves. The section ends with the call to be perfect as the heavenly Father is perfect.
str: v. 43: “love your neighbor and hate your enemy”.
vv. 44–45: love your enemies and pray for persecutors, so as to be children of the Father, who gives sun and rain to all.
vv. 46–47: loving only those who love us is what everyone does.
v. 48: be perfect as your heavenly Father is perfect.
kw: The love that wills the good of the other, even when there is no feeling of affection. It can be commanded because it is a choice and a prayer, not first an emotion.
Personal and public enemies alike. Jesus does not define the enemy narrowly; he leaves no one outside love.
Complete, whole, mature. The perfection asked is the wholeness of a love that excludes no one, like the Father’s. Luke gives the saying as “Be merciful, just as your Father is merciful” (Luke 6:36).
vv: You shall love your neighbor and hate your enemy.

The first half is Leviticus 19:18. The words “hate your enemy” are not found in the law. The law itself told Israel to help an enemy’s animal (Exodus 23:4–5), and Proverbs to feed a hungry enemy (Proverbs 25:21). Jesus may be answering a narrow popular understanding of “neighbour”.
Love your enemies and pray for those who persecute you,
Prayer is where love of enemies begins. It is hard to keep hating someone for whom we pray by name.
for he makes his sun rise on the evil and on the good, and sends rain on the righteous and on the unrighteous.
Jesus points to creation. Every morning God’s goodness falls on all. Children show the family likeness by acting as their Father acts.
Be perfect, therefore, as your heavenly Father is perfect.
This is not a call for a few. The Second Vatican Council quotes it to teach that all the faithful are called to the fullness of the Christian life (Lumen Gentium 40; CCC 2013).
ch: The Catechism teaches that Christ’s teaching goes so far as to require the forgiveness of offences, and extends the commandment of love to all enemies (CCC 1933). Christian prayer extends to the forgiveness of enemies and so makes the disciple like the Master (CCC 2844). Jesus prayed from the Cross, “Father, forgive them” (Luke 23:34), and St Stephen prayed for those who stoned him (Acts 7:60). In many lands today Christians suffer for their faith; the Church prays for them, and for those who wrong them.

qa: Does loving my enemy mean I must trust him or pretend nothing happened?

No. Love wills the good of the other and refuses hatred and revenge. It does not require us to deny the truth or to put ourselves or others in danger. Forgiveness and trust are different: forgiveness can be given at once, by grace; trust may need time and change. The first step is the one Jesus names: pray for them.
study: The Macedonians “gave themselves first to the Lord”. Before I give money or time this week, how will I first give myself to him?
Who is the hardest person for me to pray for? Can I pray for them by name today?

lead: St Paul uses the language of the farmer: the one who sows bountifully will reap bountifully, and God loves a cheerful giver. In the Gospel Jesus speaks of the three good works of Jewish piety: almsgiving, prayer and fasting. Do them for the Father who sees in secret, not to be seen by others. Both readings ask the same question: for whom am I giving?

set: Paul continues his appeal for the collection for the poor of Jerusalem. He has praised the Macedonians and sent Titus and two brothers ahead, so that the Corinthians’ gift may be ready as a gift and not as something extorted (9:5). Now he gives the spiritual principle behind giving.
str: v. 6: sow sparingly, reap sparingly; sow bountifully, reap bountifully.
v. 7: give as you have decided in your heart, not reluctantly or under compulsion.
vv. 8–10: God is able to provide every blessing; he supplies seed to the sower (quoting Psalm 112:9).
v. 11: enriched for generosity, which produces thanksgiving to God.
kw: From it comes our word “hilarious”. The line echoes the Greek Old Testament of Proverbs 22:8, which says God blesses a cheerful giver. God looks at the heart as well as at the gift.
Literally “with blessings”. A generous gift is a blessing for the poor and draws down blessing on the giver.
Having enough, contentment (v. 8). God gives not so that we may hoard, but so that, having enough, we may share abundantly in every good work.
vv: the one who sows sparingly will also reap sparingly, and the one who sows bountifully will also reap bountifully.
Giving is not loss but sowing. What is given in love is not wasted; God makes it grow.
not reluctantly or under compulsion, for God loves a cheerful giver.
Paul does not set an amount. He asks for a decision of the heart, made willingly and with joy.
He who supplies seed to the sower and bread for food
These words recall Isaiah 55:10. All we have to give is first given to us by God.
ch: From the very beginning Christians have brought, along with the bread and wine for the Eucharist, gifts to share with those in need (CCC 1351). The collection at Mass continues Paul’s collection. The Catechism lists almsgiving among the chief works of mercy and a witness to fraternal charity (CCC 2447).

r.h: Your Father who sees in secret
set: After the six antitheses about the law, the Sermon on the Mount turns to three practices of devotion that Jesus’ hearers knew well: almsgiving, prayer and fasting (compare Tobit 12:8). Jesus does not reject them; he assumes his disciples will do them (“whenever you give… whenever you pray… whenever you fast”). He warns only against doing them to be seen. The Lectionary leaves out the Lord’s Prayer (vv. 7–15), which is read tomorrow.
str: v. 1: the principle: do not practise your piety to be seen by others.
vv. 2–4: almsgiving: no trumpet; let not the left hand know.
vv. 5–6: prayer: not at street corners, but in your room with the door shut.
vv. 16–18: fasting: oil on your head, wash your face.
kw: Literally “righteousness”: the right way of living before God. Here it names the acts of devotion.
In Greek, a stage actor who plays a part behind a mask. Jesus warns against making devotion a performance. The warning is for his own disciples, and for every religious person.
Used again and again in this passage. God sees what no one else sees, and his reward is himself.
vv: do not let your left hand know what your right hand is doing,
A vivid picture: give so quietly that you yourself hardly notice. Do not keep a record of your own goodness.
go into your room and shut the door and pray to your Father who is in secret;

The word for “room” meant an inner storeroom, often the only room with a door. Jesus does not forbid public prayer, which he himself shared in the synagogue and the Temple; he asks that all prayer come from a heart turned to the Father.
But when you fast, put oil on your head and wash your face,
Oil and washing were signs of ordinary daily care, even of joy. Fasting should not become a show of sadness.
ch: The Catechism teaches that the New Law practises the acts of religion, almsgiving, prayer and fasting, directing them to the “Father who sees in secret”, in contrast with the desire to be seen by men (CCC 1969). It names fasting, prayer and almsgiving as the three forms of penance that express conversion in relation to oneself, to God and to others (CCC 1434). The Church reads this Gospel on Ash Wednesday, at the start of Lent.

qa: If good works should be secret, why does Jesus also say “let your light shine before others” (Matthew 5:16)?

The two sayings answer different temptations. In 5:16 the light is seen so that people “give glory to your Father in heaven”. In 6:1 the work is done “in order to be seen”, for one’s own glory. The question is not whether people see, but for whom we act. St Gregory the Great said: let the work be public, but the intention remain hidden (in substance).
study: Do I give gladly or reluctantly? What would make my giving more cheerful this week?
Which of the three, almsgiving, prayer or fasting, do I most need to practise “in secret” for the Father alone?

lead: In the last chapters of the Second Letter to the Corinthians, Paul defends his ministry against visiting preachers he calls “super-apostles”. He speaks as a father who has promised his church to Christ as a chaste bride, and fears she may be led astray. In the Gospel Jesus teaches his disciples the Our Father. A sincere and pure devotion to Christ, which Paul longs for, is taught and nourished in the prayer Jesus gave us.

set: Chapters 10–13 of the letter are sharper in tone than what comes before. Some scholars think they were once a separate letter; others read the whole as one letter written in stages. In either case Paul is answering preachers who came to Corinth, boasted of their gifts and eloquence, accepted payment, and belittled him.
Paul, who dislikes boasting, decides to “boast a little” in order to win the Corinthians back. He calls it “a little foolishness”.
str: vv. 1–3: “bear with me”: Paul’s divine jealousy; the church betrothed to Christ; the fear of the serpent’s deceit.
vv. 4–6: another Jesus, another spirit, another gospel; Paul not inferior to the super-apostles.
vv. 7–11: why Paul preached without payment in Corinth: out of love.
kw: Literally “the jealousy of God”: the zeal of the God of the covenant for his people, his bride (Hosea 2:19–20). Paul shares God’s own zeal for the Corinthians.
A word for arranging a betrothal. Paul is like the friend or father who betroths the bride and must present her pure on the wedding day.
An ironic name: literally “the very-extra apostles”. Paul uses it for the visiting preachers, probably not for the Twelve.
vv: I feel a divine jealousy for you, for I promised you in marriage to one husband, to present you as a chaste virgin to Christ.
The image of God’s people as a bride runs from the prophets to Revelation (Isaiah 62:5; Revelation 21:2). The whole Church, and each soul, is betrothed to Christ.
as the serpent deceived Eve by its cunning,
Paul recalls Genesis 3. The danger is not open hostility but a clever voice that draws the heart away from simple devotion.
And why? Because I do not love you? God knows I do!
Paul’s refusal of payment was not coldness but love. He did not want anything to stand between the Corinthians and the Gospel.
ch: The Second Vatican Council calls the Church the spotless spouse of the spotless Lamb (Lumen Gentium 6). The Church sees in this verse the meaning of consecrated virginity: virgins consecrated to God are a sign of the Church as the Bride of Christ, and of the world to come (CCC 922–923, 1619). But every Christian, married or single, is called to “a sincere and pure devotion to Christ”.

set: In the middle of his teaching on almsgiving, prayer and fasting, Jesus pauses to give his disciples a model of prayer. Matthew’s form of the Our Father, with seven petitions, is the one the Church prays. Luke gives a shorter form, taught when a disciple asks, “Lord, teach us to pray” (Luke 11:1–4).
str: vv. 7–8: do not heap up empty phrases; the Father knows what you need.
v. 9: “Our Father in heaven, hallowed be your name.”
v. 10: your kingdom come, your will be done.
vv. 11–13: bread, forgiveness, protection in trial and from the evil one.
vv. 14–15: forgive others, and the Father will forgive you.
kw: A rare word, perhaps meaning to babble. Jesus does not forbid long prayer or repetition (he himself prayed the same words three times in Gethsemane, Matthew 26:44); he forbids thinking we will be heard because of many words.

A rare Greek word, found almost nowhere outside the Lord’s Prayer. It can mean “for this day”, “for tomorrow”, or “super-substantial”. The Fathers heard in it both our daily food and the Bread of Life, the Eucharist (CCC 2837).
Sin is pictured as a debt owed to God. Luke’s form says “sins” (Luke 11:4). In v. 14 Matthew uses “trespasses”.
vv: for your Father knows what you need before you ask him.
We do not pray to inform God, but to open our hearts to him as children.
Our Father in heaven, hallowed be your name.
Jesus lets us call God what he calls him: Father. “Our”, not “my”: we never pray alone.
Give us this day our daily bread.
A prayer for each day, like the manna in the desert, given day by day (Exodus 16:4).
And forgive us our debts, as we also have forgiven our debtors.
The only petition Jesus comments on afterwards (vv. 14–15). Our forgiving does not earn God’s mercy, but a heart closed to others cannot receive it.
And do not bring us to the time of trial, but rescue us from the evil one.
The Greek ponēros can mean evil or the evil one. The Church understands it of Satan, the one who opposes God (CCC 2851).
ch: Tertullian called the Lord’s Prayer a summary of the whole Gospel, and St Augustine said that if we run through all the prayers of Scripture we will find nothing that is not contained in it (CCC 2761–2762, in substance). The Didache told Christians to pray it three times a day (CCC 2767). In the Mass it is prayed before Communion, and the priest’s prayer and the people’s doxology “For the kingdom, the power and the glory are yours” follow it. That doxology is not in the oldest manuscripts of Matthew, but it is very ancient, and a shorter form of it is found in the Didache. The Catechism teaches that the mercy of God cannot penetrate our hearts as long as we have not forgiven those who have trespassed against us (CCC 2840).

qa: Why do some Christians end the Our Father with “For thine is the kingdom”, while Catholics do not say it at the end?

The doxology is an ancient addition found in some manuscripts and in the Didache, but not in the oldest manuscripts of Matthew. Catholics do pray it at Mass, after the priest’s prayer that follows the Our Father. So it is not a difference of faith, only of where the words are placed.
study: Pray the Our Father slowly, pausing after each line. Which petition is hardest for me to mean?
Is there someone I must forgive before I can pray “as we also have forgiven our debtors” honestly?

lead: Paul’s rivals in Corinth boasted of their pedigree and their gifts. Paul answers them, “speaking as a fool”, with a list of sufferings for Christ, and ends: “If I must boast, I will boast of the things that show my weakness.” In the Gospel Jesus tells his disciples not to store up treasures on earth but in heaven, for where your treasure is, there your heart will be. Paul shows a heart whose treasure is Christ and the churches.

r.h: I will boast of my weakness
set: This is the centre of what is often called Paul’s “fool’s speech” (11:1–12:13). The visiting preachers in Corinth claimed to be better apostles. Paul unwillingly matches them claim for claim, but then turns the boasting upside down: instead of successes he lists hardships.

Background. Many of these sufferings are not told in Acts, which shows how much of Paul’s life we do not know. Acts mentions a beating with rods at Philippi (Acts 16:22–23), a stoning at Lystra (Acts 14:19), and later the shipwreck on the way to Rome (Acts 27), which happened after this letter was written.
str: v. 18: since many boast, Paul will boast too.
vv. 21–23a: Hebrew, Israelite, descendant of Abraham, minister of Christ.
vv. 23b–27: a list of labours, beatings, journeys, dangers, hunger and cold.
vv. 28–29: daily anxiety for all the churches.
v. 30: if I must boast, I will boast of my weakness.
kw: A key word of this part of the letter. Paul uses it many times, always with irony. True boasting is “in the Lord” (10:17, quoting Jeremiah 9:24).

The law limited a beating to forty strokes (Deuteronomy 25:3), and the custom of giving thirty-nine kept a margin of mercy. This was a discipline of the synagogue. Many scholars note that Paul’s receiving it five times shows that he remained within the synagogue community and kept preaching there.
The word Paul chooses to boast of. In the next chapter he will hear the Lord say, “power is made perfect in weakness” (12:9).
vv: Are they Hebrews? So am I. Are they Israelites? So am I. Are they descendants of Abraham? So am I.
Paul is proud of his people. He never stopped being a son of Israel (Romans 9:3–5; 11:1).
Three times I was beaten with rods. Once I received a stoning. Three times I was shipwrecked;
Beating with rods was a Roman punishment. Paul suffered at the hands of many: his own people, Gentiles, robbers, the sea, even false brothers (v. 26).
I am under daily pressure because of my anxiety for all the churches.
After all the outward sufferings comes the inward one: the care of a pastor for his people. This is often the heaviest burden.
If I must boast, I will boast of the things that show my weakness.
Paul turns the world’s values upside down. His weakness lets Christ’s strength be seen.
ch: The Catechism quotes Paul’s experience, “power is made perfect in weakness” (12:9), when it teaches that only faith can embrace the mysterious ways of God’s almighty power, shown most fully in Christ crucified (CCC 273). Paul’s anxiety for all the churches has become a model for bishops and priests; the Second Vatican Council asks bishops to have care for all the churches, as members of the college of bishops (Christus Dominus 6). Paul’s words about suffering should never be read against the Jewish people: he speaks of trials from many sides, and he loved his own people to the end.

set: The Sermon on the Mount now turns from devotion to possessions. In a land where wealth was kept in fine clothes, stored grain and buried coins, every listener understood the dangers Jesus names: moths eat clothes, “rust” (literally “eating”) destroys stores, and thieves dig through mud-brick walls.
str: vv. 19–20: do not store up treasures on earth, but in heaven.
v. 21: where your treasure is, there your heart will be.
vv. 22–23: the eye is the lamp of the body; healthy eye, body full of light; unhealthy eye, darkness.
kw: A store or treasury. Jesus does not condemn having goods, but making them the treasure the heart rests on.
Literally single, simple, the word family of Paul’s “generosity” (2 Corinthians 8:2). The single eye looks at God alone, and is also generous.
In Jewish speech an “evil eye” meant envy or meanness (Deuteronomy 15:9; Proverbs 28:22). The one who looks at others’ goods with greed fills himself with darkness.
vv: but store up for yourselves treasures in heaven,
Treasure in heaven is stored by love, mercy and almsgiving (compare Matthew 19:21). It cannot be stolen.
For where your treasure is, there your heart will be also.
A simple test of the heart: what do I think about most, worry about most, protect most?
The eye is the lamp of the body.
The eye lets in the light. If our way of looking is generous and single, our whole life is lit up; if it is greedy, our whole life darkens.
ch: The Catechism teaches that Jesus asks his disciples to prefer him to everything and everyone, and to renounce all that they have for his sake and that of the Gospel (CCC 2544). The Lord grieves over the rich, because they find their consolation in the abundance of goods (CCC 2547). The treasure that no thief can take is Christ himself, given to us in the Eucharist and found again in every act of love.

study: Paul’s deepest anxiety was “for all the churches”. Whom will I pray for today: my parish priest, my bishop, a persecuted church?
If a thief broke into my house tonight, what would I most fear to lose? What treasure can no thief take?

lead: Paul, pushed by rivals in Corinth into a contest of boasting, tells of a vision in which he was caught up into Paradise. Yet the one thing he will really boast of is his weakness, because the Lord said to him, “My grace is sufficient for you.” In the Gospel Jesus tells his disciples not to worry about food and clothing, for their heavenly Father knows what they need. Both readings teach the same trust: not in our own strength, and not in wealth, but in God who gives. Psalm 34 sings the invitation: “O taste and see that the Lord is good.” Today the Church may also remember St Romuald, who left everything to seek God alone.

set: In chapters 10–13 of this letter Paul defends his ministry against visiting preachers whom he calls, with some irony, “super-apostles” (11:5; 12:11). They impressed the Corinthians with their eloquence, their letters of recommendation and their spiritual experiences, and they looked down on Paul as weak. Paul answers with what is often called his “fool’s speech” (11:1–12:13). If boasting is demanded, he will boast, but of the wrong things: his beatings, shipwrecks and dangers (11:23–29), his escape from Damascus in a basket let down a wall (11:32–33), and now a vision he hardly dares to describe. Some scholars think chapters 10–13 were first a separate letter, later joined to the others; the Church receives the whole as Scripture.

Background. The letter was written in the middle of the 50s, so “fourteen years ago” takes us to the early 40s, years of Paul’s life about which Acts tells us very little. Jewish writings of the time spoke of several heavens; “the third heaven” and “Paradise” here name the place of God’s own presence.
str: vv. 1–4: a man in Christ caught up to the third heaven, into Paradise, who heard things that cannot be told.
vv. 5–6: Paul will boast of that man, but of himself only of his weaknesses.
vv. 7–9a: the thorn in the flesh; three prayers; the Lord’s answer.
vv. 9b–10: so he will gladly boast of his weaknesses: when he is weak, then he is strong.
¶ The passage turns on v. 9. Everything before it climbs up to the third heaven; everything after it comes down to weakness, insults and hardships, and finds Christ there.
kw: Skolops can mean a thorn, a splinter, or a pointed stake. Paul never says what it was. Suggestions include an illness (compare Galatians 4:13–15), the opponents who harassed him, or a lasting temptation. St John Chrysostom understood it of the adversaries who attacked Paul’s work (in substance). What is clear is that it was painful, it lasted, and it kept him humble.
God’s favour given as a gift, and the strength that comes with it. The Lord does not remove the thorn. He gives something greater: his own presence and help in the weakness.
The two words meet in v. 9. The verb translated “is made perfect” (teleitai) means brought to its goal, completed. Christ’s power does its full work where human strength runs out.
vv: I know a person in Christ who fourteen years ago was caught up to the third heaven
Paul speaks of himself in the third person, as v. 7 makes plain. He will not turn this experience into a credential. What matters is not what he has seen but whom he serves.
Three times I appealed to the Lord about this, that it would leave me,
The prayer recalls Jesus in Gethsemane, who prayed three times (Mark 14:32–41). Paul’s prayer was answered, though not in the way he asked.
My grace is sufficient for you, for power is made perfect in weakness.
The Lord’s answer is in the present tense: the grace is enough, now and always. Paul does not say he enjoys weakness; he has learned that it is the place where Christ’s power dwells.
for whenever I am weak, then I am strong.
This is not a love of suffering for its own sake. It is the experience of an apostle whose sufferings for Christ made room for Christ to act.
ch: The Catechism teaches that only faith can embrace the mysterious ways of God’s almighty power, and that this faith glories in its weaknesses in order to draw to itself Christ’s power; the Virgin Mary is its supreme model (CCC 273). Speaking of the sick, the Catechism also recalls this passage: even the most intense prayers do not always obtain the healing of every illness, and Paul learned from the Lord that his grace is sufficient (CCC 1508). The Church therefore never treats illness or weakness as a sign that God has turned away. Joined to Christ, it can become a place of his strength.

set: These verses belong to the Sermon on the Mount (chapters 5–7). Jesus has just spoken of treasure in heaven and of the healthy eye (6:19–23). Now he draws the conclusion: a person cannot belong to two masters. Then he speaks to the anxiety that money so often brings.

The pictures come from the Galilean countryside: birds that do not sow or reap, wild flowers in the fields, and the dry grass that was gathered to heat clay ovens. The listeners were mostly poor farmers and fishermen, for whom food and clothing were daily worries, not distant ideas.
str: v. 24: no one can serve two masters; God and wealth.
vv. 25–30: do not worry about life and body: the birds, the lilies, the grass of the field.
vv. 31–32: your heavenly Father knows that you need these things.
v. 33: strive first for the kingdom of God and his righteousness.
v. 34: do not worry about tomorrow.
kw: An Aramaic word kept in the Greek; older translations say “mammon”. It means money and property, perhaps from a root meaning that in which one puts one’s trust. Jesus speaks of it almost as a rival lord.

The verb comes six times in these verses (vv. 25, 27, 28, 31, and twice in v. 34). Jesus does not forbid work or care; the birds are fed, but they still look for their food. He forbids the anxious care that forgets the Father.
A word Matthew likes (6:30; 8:26; 14:31; 16:8). Jesus says it to disciples: not to unbelievers, but to believers whose faith is still too small for their troubles.
vv: You cannot serve God and wealth.
To “serve” here is to be a slave. Money is a useful servant but a hard master, and the heart cannot give itself wholly to both.
Look at the birds of the air; they neither sow nor reap nor gather into barns, and yet your heavenly Father feeds them.
Jesus argues from the lesser to the greater. If God cares for birds, how much more for his children.
But strive first for the kingdom of God and his righteousness, and all these things will be given to you as well.

The heart of the passage. “First” does not mean “only”: food and clothing still matter, but they find their right place when God’s reign comes first. In Matthew “righteousness” is the faithful life the kingdom asks for (5:6, 20).
Today’s trouble is enough for today.
A word of plain wisdom. Grace is given for today; tomorrow will have its own grace.
ch: The Catechism sees here the childlike abandonment Jesus asks for, to the providence of a Father who cares for his children’s smallest needs (CCC 305, quoting 6:31–33). It also lists the love of money among the forms of idolatry: “You cannot serve God and mammon” (CCC 2113). The Church does not read this Gospel as a call to carelessness. Parents must provide for their children, and work is a duty and a dignity. What Jesus removes is the anxiety that makes money a god.

qa: Does this Gospel mean we should not save money or plan for the future?

No. Scripture praises the ant that stores its food in summer (Proverbs 6:6–8), and Jesus himself speaks of the builder who first sits down to estimate the cost (Luke 14:28). Prudent planning is a virtue. What Jesus warns against is worry that takes the place of trust, and saving that becomes hoarding while others are in need. The question is who is master: God, with money as a servant, or money, with God pushed aside.
rite: St Romuald was born at Ravenna about the year 951. As a young man he saw his father kill a relative in a quarrel, and he went to do penance at the monastery of Sant’Apollinare in Classe, where he became a monk. He spent his life founding hermitages and monasteries in Italy; the best known is Camaldoli in Tuscany, from which the Camaldolese monks take their name. He joined the silence of the hermit to the common life of the monastery. A short rule handed down under his name says, in substance: sit in your cell as in paradise. By the traditional reckoning he died on 19 June 1027, so this year marks a thousand years since his death. His life is a commentary on today’s Gospel: he had one Master.
study: What worries fill most of my thoughts? What would it mean, this week, to “strive first for the kingdom” in one of them?
Paul learned that grace is sufficient in his weakness. Where in my life have I found God’s help most clearly when my own strength ran out?

lead: The readings of this Sunday are held together by the sea. In the first reading God answers Job out of the whirlwind and reminds him who shut in the sea and said to it, “Thus far shall you come, and no farther.” Psalm 107 sings of sailors caught in a storm who cried to the Lord, and “he made the storm be still, and the waves of the sea were hushed.” In the Gospel Jesus, asleep in the boat, rises, rebukes the wind and says to the sea, “Peace! Be still!” The disciples ask the question the whole of Mark’s Gospel wants us to answer: “Who then is this, that even the wind and the sea obey him?” The first reading has already given the clue: only the Creator commands the sea.

The second reading, from Paul’s second letter to the Corinthians, gives the reason a Christian can face the storms of life without fear: the love of Christ, who died for all, so that those who live might live for him. In him there is a new creation. The Sundays of Ordinary Time in Year B read Mark’s Gospel, and this passage closes the chapter of parables with an act that reveals who Jesus is.

set: The Book of Job tells of a righteous man who loses his children, his wealth and his health. Through a long debate (chapters 3–37) his three friends insist that suffering must be punishment for sin. Job protests his innocence and calls on God to answer him. At last, in chapter 38, God speaks “out of the whirlwind”. He does not explain why Job has suffered. Instead he asks Job a long series of questions about creation (chapters 38–41), opening before him a world far larger than human sight. Job’s answer at the end is humble trust (42:1–6).

Background. Many peoples of the ancient Near East pictured the sea as a power of chaos, and some of their stories told of gods who fought against it. In the Bible the sea is no rival god. It is a creature. In today’s verses God handles the mighty sea as a mother handles a newborn child: it bursts from the womb, and he wraps it in clouds and swaddling bands, and then sets it within limits. The Lectionary leaves out vv. 2–7, where God asks Job where he was when the foundations of the earth were laid.
str: v. 1: the Lord answers Job out of the whirlwind.
v. 8: who shut in the sea with doors when it burst from the womb?
v. 9: the clouds its garment, thick darkness its swaddling band.
vv. 10–11: bounds, bars and doors; “Thus far shall you come, and no farther.”
¶ The questions are not meant to crush Job but to enlarge him. The God who knows the limits of the sea also knows the limits of Job’s suffering.
kw: God speaks from the storm, the very power that frightens human beings. The storm is not outside his rule; it is the place from which he speaks.
For Israel, a people of the land, the sea was a place of danger and the picture of everything wild and threatening. That God sets its limits means that no chaos is beyond his reach.
A word for a fixed limit or a statute. The God who gives laws to Israel gives a law to the sea (compare Proverbs 8:29; Jeremiah 5:22).
vv: Then the Lord answered Job out of the whirlwind:
After thirty-five chapters of human words, God speaks. The answer is first of all a presence: Job is no longer talking about God, but hearing him.
Or who shut in the sea with doors when it burst out from the womb?
The sea is pictured as a newborn bursting into the world. Its strength is real, but it is the strength of a creature, not of a god.
when I made the clouds its garment, and thick darkness its swaddling band,
A tender image. The ocean that terrifies sailors is, to its Maker, like an infant wrapped in cloth.
Thus far shall you come, and no farther, and here shall your proud waves be stopped
The waves are “proud”: they rise as if they could overrun everything. God’s word stops them. The Gospel will show the same word on the lips of Jesus.
ch: The Church reads this passage as a confession of God the Creator, who does not abandon his creatures but upholds them in being and guides them (CCC 301). It does not solve the mystery of suffering with a formula. The Catechism says that there is no quick answer to the question why evil exists; only the Christian faith as a whole constitutes the answer (CCC 309). At its heart stand the Cross and Resurrection of Christ. St Gregory the Great wrote a great commentary on Job, the Moralia, in which he read Job’s patience as a figure of Christ and of the Church in its trials.

set: In chapters 1–7 of this letter Paul explains to the Corinthians the ministry he has received. Some accused him of acting for his own advantage. In 5:11–21 he tells them what really drives him: not self-interest, but the love of Christ, and the conviction that Christ’s death has changed everything. Just after our verses he will speak of God “reconciling the world to himself” in Christ, and of the ministry of reconciliation (5:18–20).
str: v. 14: the love of Christ urges us on: one has died for all, therefore all have died.
v. 15: he died for all, so that the living might live no longer for themselves but for him.
v. 16: from now on we regard no one from a human point of view.
v. 17: if anyone is in Christ, there is a new creation.
kw: The verb means to hold tightly, to press in on every side, to control. The love of Christ grips Paul and leaves him no other way. “The love of Christ” here is first Christ’s love for us, which then awakens our love for him.
from a human point of view

Literally “according to the flesh”: judging by outward and worldly standards, such as status, eloquence, or success. Paul once judged Jesus that way, as a failed and crucified man. Now he sees him as the risen Lord.
Not only a new start but a new act of the Creator. Isaiah had heard God say, “I am about to do a new thing” (Isaiah 43:19). In Christ that new thing has begun.
vv: For the love of Christ urges us on,
The engine of Paul’s whole ministry. He does not serve out of fear or for reward, but because he has been loved.
And he died for all, so that those who live might live no longer for themselves,
Christ’s death has a purpose in us: a life turned outward, toward him and toward others.
From now on, therefore, we regard no one from a human point of view;
A new way of seeing people follows. No one is judged by wealth, caste, language or rank; each is someone for whom Christ died.
So if anyone is in Christ, there is a new creation: everything old has passed away; see, everything has become new!
“See” is the voice of wonder. The world is the same, yet for the one in Christ it is seen and lived anew.
ch: The Church teaches, with the apostles, that Christ died for all people without exception (CCC 605, citing this passage). Baptism makes the newly baptised “a new creature” (CCC 1265), and the baptised person belongs no longer to himself but to him who died and rose for us (CCC 1269). This is why a Christian can face the storms of life without despair: life is no longer lived for oneself alone, but in the hands of the One who has already passed through death.

set: It is the evening of the day on which Jesus taught the crowds in parables from a boat by the shore (4:1–34). Now he says, “Let us go across to the other side.” The other side is the eastern shore of the lake, a largely Gentile region, where he will heal the man possessed by many demons (5:1–20).

Background. The Sea of Galilee is a lake about twenty-one kilometres long, lying some two hundred metres below sea level and ringed by hills. Cold winds can drop suddenly into the basin and whip up dangerous waves within minutes. Several of the disciples were fishermen who knew the lake well; their terror tells us how violent this storm was.
str: vv. 35–36: evening; “Let us go across”; they take him in the boat “just as he was”.
v. 37: a great windstorm; the boat is being swamped.
v. 38: Jesus asleep on the cushion; “Teacher, do you not care?”
v. 39: he rebukes the wind and speaks to the sea; a dead calm.
vv. 40–41: “Why are you afraid?” and “Who then is this?”

¶ The story ends with two questions, one from Jesus and one from the disciples. Jesus asks about their faith; they ask about his identity. The two belong together: to have faith is to know who is in the boat.
kw: The same verb Mark uses when Jesus rebukes unclean spirits (1:25; 3:12; 9:25). Jesus speaks to the storm as to a hostile power that must yield to him.
Literally “Be silent! Be muzzled!” The second verb is the one Jesus used to the unclean spirit in the synagogue at Capernaum: “Be silent” (1:25). One word from him, and the chaos is silenced.

Mark uses this word three times: a great windstorm (v. 37), a great calm (v. 39, “dead calm”), and, literally, “they feared a great fear” (v. 41). The great fear of the storm becomes the greater awe before Jesus himself.
vv: But he was in the stern, asleep on the cushion;

Only Mark mentions the cushion, a vivid detail that early tradition linked with the preaching of Peter. Jesus is truly human and tired after a long day. His sleep is also the sleep of perfect trust (compare Psalm 4:8).
Teacher, do you not care that we are perishing?
The cry of every believer in a storm. Mark does not hide the disciples’ rough words; Matthew and Luke soften them (Matthew 8:25; Luke 8:24).
He woke up and rebuked the wind, and said to the sea, “Peace! Be still!”
Psalm 107, today’s psalm, says of the Lord: “he made the storm be still”. Jesus does with a word what the psalms say only God does.
Why are you afraid? Have you still no faith?
Jesus does not blame them for waking him, but for thinking that, with him in the boat, they could be lost.
Who then is this, that even the wind and the sea obey him?
The question is left open for the reader. The Old Testament has already answered it: God, of whom the psalm says, “You silence the roaring of the seas” (Psalm 65:7).
ch: The Catechism teaches that the signs worked by Jesus attest that the Father has sent him, and invite belief in him (CCC 548). The fathers loved this story. St Augustine told his people that when the storm of temptation or anger rises in us, it is because Christ is asleep in our heart, that is, we have forgotten our faith; we must wake him by remembering him, and the sea will grow calm (in substance). Tertullian already saw in the little boat a figure of the Church, tossed by the waves of the world but carrying the Lord (On Baptism 12, in substance). Many commentators also hear an echo of Jonah, asleep in the ship during the storm while the sailors feared greatly (Jonah 1). But here is one greater than Jonah: he does not need to be thrown into the sea; he commands it.

qa: Did the stilling of the storm really happen, or is it only a picture?

The Gospel tells it as an event that the disciples remembered, with vivid details such as the cushion in the stern. The Church believes that Jesus truly worked miracles, as signs that the kingdom of God is present in him (CCC 547–548). Because it really happened, it can also become a picture for us: the boat of our life and of the Church, the storms, and the Lord who is present even when he seems to sleep.
Why does God seem to sleep when we are suffering?

The psalms themselves cry, “Rouse yourself! Why do you sleep, O Lord?” (Psalm 44:23). Scripture does not forbid this cry; Jesus does not reject the disciples who wake him. Yet Psalm 121:4 says that he who keeps Israel “will neither slumber nor sleep”. Jesus was asleep in the boat, but he was in the boat. His seeming silence is not absence. Faith learns to hold on in the dark, as Job did, knowing that the one who sets limits to the sea also sets limits to our trials (compare 1 Corinthians 10:13).
Does God ever answer Job’s question about suffering?

Not with an explanation. God answers Job with himself: he speaks, he shows his care for all creation, and Job finds peace in his presence. Only the Christian faith as a whole answers the question of evil (CCC 309), and its heart is Christ, who enters our suffering, dies, and rises again. The disciples in the boat do not get an explanation of the storm either; they get Jesus.
rite: This Twelfth Sunday in Ordinary Time falls in the season of the monsoon, when the sea along the coasts of India is at its roughest. Many Latin Catholic parishes along the western and eastern coasts are communities of fishermen, and they know from long experience what the disciples felt in the boat. On the western coast, in June and July boats are often held back from the deep sea by the weather and the seasonal ban on fishing, and families feel the strain. This Gospel invites us to pray for all who work at sea, and for migrants and refugees who cross dangerous waters in many lands. The Church has a special ministry for seafarers, the Apostleship of the Sea, now called Stella Maris, and in many coastal parishes boats and nets are blessed. At Mass we confess the same Lord whom the disciples met in the boat.
study: God speaks to Job out of the storm. Has a hard time in my life become a place where I heard God more clearly?
Jesus asks, “Why are you afraid?” What storm is frightening me now, and what would it mean to remember that he is in the boat?
Paul says that those who live should live no longer for themselves. In my family, where could I live a little less for myself this week?
How can our parish, or our family, be like a boat that carries the Lord to “the other side”, to people who do not yet know him?

lead: Through these days the first reading follows the story of Abraham. Today God calls Abram to leave his country, his kindred and his father’s house, and promises that in him all the families of the earth shall be blessed; Abram goes, building altars as he travels. In the Gospel Jesus warns against judging others and tells us to take the log out of our own eye first. On the memorial of St Aloysius Gonzaga, a young man who left a prince’s inheritance to follow Christ, Psalm 33 sings: “Happy is the nation whose God is the Lord, the people whom he has chosen as his heritage.”

r.h: Go to the land that I will show you
set: The first eleven chapters of Genesis end with the tower of Babel, where humanity is scattered and divided. Then comes the family of Terah. Abram, with his wife Sarai, who has no child (11:30), has moved with his father from Ur of the Chaldeans to Haran in northern Mesopotamia (11:31). Here God speaks to him. With this call the history of salvation takes a new turn: God begins to heal the whole human family through one man and his descendants.
