Abram’s route runs south through Canaan, through places that will matter greatly in Israel’s story: Shechem, Bethel and the Negeb, the dry south. At each stop he builds an altar. He owns nothing in the land yet; he claims it only by worship.
str: vv. 1–3: God’s call and promise: land, a great nation, blessing, a great name, and blessing for all the families of the earth.
vv. 4–5: Abram goes, at seventy-five, with Sarai, Lot and all they have.
vv. 6–7: at Shechem the Lord appears and promises the land to his offspring; an altar.
vv. 8–9: near Bethel another altar; Abram calls on the name of the Lord and journeys on toward the Negeb.
kw: Literally “go for yourself” or “go by yourself”. The call asks Abram to leave, in three widening circles, his land, his clan and his father’s household. He is told where to leave, but not yet where he will arrive: “the land that I will show you”.

Words from the root “bless” come five times in vv. 2–3. Some commentators note that the story of sin in chapters 3–11 is marked by curses; now the story of salvation begins with blessing, and it is meant for “all the families of the earth”.
The land is promised to Abram’s “offspring” (v. 7). St Paul notes that the word is singular, and reads it of Christ, in whom the promise is fulfilled (Galatians 3:16).
vv: Go from your country and your kindred and your father’s house to the land that I will show you.
Faith begins with a word from God and a road whose end is not yet seen.
and in you all the families of the earth shall be blessed.
Abram is chosen not for himself alone but for the sake of all peoples. Paul calls this verse the gospel proclaimed beforehand to Abraham (Galatians 3:8).
So Abram went, as the Lord had told him;
No speech, no question: only obedience. The Letter to the Hebrews sums it up: “By faith Abraham obeyed when he was called… not knowing where he was going” (Hebrews 11:8).
ch: The Catechism teaches that, in order to gather together scattered humanity, God calls Abram from his country, his kindred and his father’s house, and makes him Abraham, the father of a multitude of nations (CCC 59). The people descended from him were to be the trustee of the promise (CCC 60). The Letter to the Hebrews lays special emphasis on Abraham’s faith (CCC 145), and the Church calls him our father in faith. Christians share this root with the Jewish people, to whom the promises first belong and whose calling God does not revoke (Romans 11:29).

r.h: First take the log out of your own eye
set: The Sermon on the Mount now turns to how disciples treat one another. Jesus has taught the Lord’s Prayer, with its petition to forgive as we are forgiven (6:12). Here he forbids the judging that condemns. He does not forbid all judgment: a few verses later he asks his disciples to recognise false prophets by their fruits (7:15–20). What he forbids is the harsh, self-righteous verdict on another person’s heart. A saying of Hillel in the Mishnah teaches something similar: do not judge your neighbour until you have stood in his place.
str: vv. 1–2: do not judge; the measure you give will be the measure you get.
vv. 3–4: the speck in your neighbour’s eye and the log in your own.
v. 5: “You hypocrite, first take the log out of your own eye.”
kw: Here it means to pass sentence, to condemn. “That you may not be judged” is a way of speaking of God’s judgment without naming God.
A speck of chaff or sawdust against a roof beam. Jesus, the carpenter’s son, uses a deliberately comic picture: a man with a beam in his eye offering to do eye surgery on his brother.
In Greek the word meant an actor, one who plays a part behind a mask. The one who judges harshly is playing the part of the righteous man.
vv: Do not judge, so that you may not be judged.
Not a ban on telling right from wrong, but on taking God’s place as judge of another person.
and the measure you give will be the measure you get.
The picture is of a market measure for grain. The mercy we show others is the measure we ask God to use for us.
You hypocrite, first take the log out of your own eye, and then you will see clearly to take the speck out of your neighbor’s eye.
Jesus does not say we should never help our brother. He says: begin with yourself. Only a humble eye sees clearly enough to help.
ch: The Catechism names rash judgment as a sin against truth and the good name of others: assuming a neighbour’s moral fault without enough foundation (CCC 2477). To avoid it, it quotes St Ignatius of Loyola: every good Christian ought to be more ready to give a favourable interpretation to another’s statement than to condemn it (CCC 2478, in substance). Examination of conscience and the sacrament of penance are the Church’s way of taking the log out of our own eye.

qa: If we must not judge, how can parents or the Church correct anyone?

Jesus forbids condemning another person’s heart, not caring about right and wrong. Correction given in love is a work of mercy; Jesus himself teaches how to correct a brother (Matthew 18:15). The difference lies in the eye and the heart: the one who corrects well has first looked at his own faults, speaks humbly, and wants his brother’s good, not his own victory.
rite: St Aloysius Gonzaga (1568–1591) was the eldest son of the Marquis of Castiglione in northern Italy, and was raised to be a soldier and a prince. While still a boy he resolved to give himself to God. Against his father’s strong opposition he renounced his inheritance in favour of his brother and entered the Society of Jesus in Rome in 1585. His spiritual director was St Robert Bellarmine. In 1591 plague struck Rome, and Aloysius nursed the sick in the hospitals, carrying the dying in his own arms. He caught the disease and died on 21 June, at the age of twenty-three. The Church honours him as a patron of young people. Like Abram, he left his father’s house for a land God would show him.
study: Abram went “not knowing where he was going”. Where is God asking me to take a step of trust before I can see the end of the road?
Whom have I judged harshly in recent days? What might the “log” in my own eye be?

lead: Abram and his nephew Lot have grown so rich that the land cannot hold them both, and their herdsmen quarrel. Abram, the elder, lets Lot choose first, and God then renews the promise to Abram: all the land he can see will be his. In the Gospel Jesus gives the rule that sums up the law and the prophets: “In everything do to others as you would have them do to you,” and he calls his disciples to the narrow gate. Psalm 15 describes the one who may dwell with God: one who walks blamelessly and does no evil to a friend. Today the Church may remember St Paulinus of Nola, and Sts John Fisher and Thomas More, martyrs.

r.h: Let there be no strife between us
set: Abram has returned from Egypt to the Negeb, where he went during a famine (12:10–13:1). He comes back to Bethel, to the altar he built at the beginning (13:3–4). He and Lot now have large flocks, and pasture and water are limited in the hill country. The quarrel of the herdsmen threatens to divide the family.
The Lectionary leaves out vv. 3–4, the return to Bethel. The verse about Sodom (v. 13) prepares for the stories of chapters 18–19.
str: vv. 2, 5–7: Abram and Lot are rich; the land cannot support both; strife among the herdsmen.
vv. 8–9: Abram’s offer: “we are kindred”; let Lot choose left or right.
vv. 10–13: Lot looks, chooses the plain of the Jordan, and settles near Sodom.
vv. 14–17: the Lord tells Abram to raise his eyes: all the land he sees is his and his offspring’s.
v. 18: Abram settles by the oaks of Mamre at Hebron and builds an altar.
kw: The same word family names the place where Israel later quarrelled with God in the desert, Meribah (Exodus 17:7). Abram refuses to let a quarrel over goods break a family bond.
Literally “brothers”, though Lot is Abram’s nephew. In Hebrew the word covers close relatives. For Abram, being kin matters more than having the better land.

Lot “looked about him”, literally lifted up his eyes, and chose for himself (v. 10). After Lot has gone, God tells Abram, “Raise your eyes now” (v. 14). Lot looks with his own desire; Abram looks at God’s word, and receives far more.
vv: Let there be no strife between you and me, and between your herders and my herders; for we are kindred.
The elder and the one who received the promise gives way to the younger. Peace in the family is worth more than his rights.
Lot looked about him, and saw that the plain of the Jordan was well watered everywhere like the garden of the Lord,
The plain looks like Eden. But the narrator adds at once that Sodom was nearby and wicked (v. 13). What looks best is not always best.
Raise your eyes now, and look from the place where you are, northward and southward and eastward and westward;
Abram gave up the choice, and God gives him the whole. The four directions mean everything his eyes can see.
ch: The fathers held up Abram as a model of a peacemaker who yields for the sake of concord. St John Chrysostom, preaching on Genesis, praised his humility: though he was the elder and the one to whom God had spoken, he let the younger choose (in substance). The Church reads here the beatitude of the peacemakers (Matthew 5:9), and the teaching of the Catechism that peace is the work of justice and the fruit of charity (CCC 2304). Families who quarrel over land and inheritance can hear Abram’s words as their own: “we are kindred”.

set: These verses come near the end of the Sermon on the Mount. Verse 6 is a short, hard saying about holy things; vv. 7–11, on asking and receiving, are left out today. Verse 12 gives the summary of the whole Sermon: the “Golden Rule”. Then vv. 13–14 begin the closing call to decision, with its pairs: two gates, two trees, two builders (7:13–27).

Background. The Golden Rule was known in other forms. The Book of Tobit says, “What you hate, do not do to anyone” (Tobit 4:15). The Talmud tells that the great Jewish teacher Hillel summed up the Torah in a similar way: what is hateful to you, do not do to your neighbour. Jesus gives the rule in its positive form: not only avoid harm, but do the good you would wish to receive.
str: v. 6: do not give what is holy to dogs, nor pearls to swine.
v. 12: in everything do to others as you would have them do to you; this is the law and the prophets.
vv. 13–14: the narrow gate and hard road that lead to life; the wide gate and easy road that lead to destruction.
kw: Originally the holy meat of the Temple sacrifices, which could not be thrown to dogs (compare Exodus 29:33). The Didache, an early Christian writing, applies this saying to the Eucharist: only the baptised may receive it (Didache 9).

A way of naming the whole of the Scriptures of Israel. Jesus said at the start of the Sermon that he came not to abolish the law and the prophets but to fulfil them (5:17). Now the Sermon closes the circle: love of neighbour sums them up (compare 22:40).

The gate is narrow, and the road is literally “pressed” or “afflicted” (tethlimmenē), from the same family as the word for tribulation. The way of life is not crowded and comfortable; it asks for decision and effort, sustained by grace.
vv: Do not give what is holy to dogs; and do not throw your pearls before swine,
Coming just after the warning not to judge, this saying asks for discernment. The holy things of God are to be treated with reverence.
In everything do to others as you would have them do to you; for this is the law and the prophets.
“In everything” leaves no exceptions: family, work, money, speech. The rule asks me to imagine myself in the other’s place.
For the gate is narrow and the road is hard that leads to life, and there are few who find it.
Jesus does not tell us how many will be saved; when someone asks him, he answers, “Strive to enter through the narrow door” (Luke 13:24). The saying is a call, not a census.
ch: The Catechism says that the law of the Gospel requires us to choose between the two ways, and that it is summed up in the Golden Rule (CCC 1970). It also lists the Golden Rule among the rules that apply in every case of conscience (CCC 1789). The words on the narrow gate appear where the Catechism speaks of the last things: the teachings on hell are a call to responsibility and to conversion (CCC 1036). God wants all to be saved (1 Timothy 2:4), and his grace makes the narrow way possible.

qa: What does “do not give what is holy to dogs” mean? Is Jesus calling people dogs?

Jesus uses a proverb of his time about holy things and unclean animals. It is not an insult to any people. Its point is reverence: sacred things must not be handled carelessly or given to those who would trample them. The early Church applied it to the Eucharist, which is given to the baptised who are prepared to receive it (Didache 9; compare 1 Corinthians 11:27–29).
rite: St Paulinus of Nola (about 354–431) was born at Bordeaux in Gaul, became a senator and governor in Campania, and then, with his wife Therasia, gave away his great wealth to the poor. He settled at Nola, near the tomb of St Felix, was ordained priest and later became bishop of Nola. He was a poet and the friend by letter of Augustine and others. Sts John Fisher (1469–1535), bishop of Rochester and cardinal, and Thomas More (1478–1535), Lord Chancellor of England, refused to accept King Henry VIII as supreme head of the Church in England and were beheaded: Fisher on 22 June, More on 6 July 1535. More is reported to have said on the scaffold that he died the king’s good servant, but God’s first. Pope St John Paul II named him patron of statesmen and politicians in 2000. They walked the narrow gate.
study: Abram said, “Let there be no strife between you and me.” Is there a quarrel in my family, perhaps over property or inheritance, where I could give way for the sake of peace?
Choose one person I will meet tomorrow. How would I want to be treated in that person’s place?

lead: God tells Abram not to be afraid, and promises him a son and descendants as many as the stars. “And he believed the Lord; and the Lord reckoned it to him as righteousness.” Then, in a strange night rite, God himself passes between the divided animals and makes a covenant with Abram. In the Gospel Jesus warns against false prophets: “You will know them by their fruits.” Abram’s faith bore fruit in obedience; true prophets are known by the same kind of fruit. Psalm 105 sings: “He is mindful of his covenant forever.”

set: God has promised Abram a land and a great nation (12:1–7; 13:14–17), but years have passed and Abram and Sarai still have no child. Abram’s heir would be a servant, Eliezer of Damascus. In this chapter Abram tells God his fear plainly, and God answers with two promises, each followed by a sign: first descendants (vv. 1–6), then the land (vv. 7–21).

Background. In the ancient Near East a covenant could be sealed by cutting animals in two and passing between the pieces, as if to say, “May I be like these animals if I break my word.” The prophet Jeremiah mentions this rite (Jeremiah 34:18). Here only the smoking fire pot and the flaming torch, signs of God’s presence, pass between the pieces. God binds himself; Abram, in a deep sleep, only receives. The Lectionary leaves out vv. 13–16, where God foretells the years of slavery in Egypt.
str: vv. 1–3: “Do not be afraid”; Abram complains that he has no son.
vv. 4–6: “Count the stars”; Abram believes, and it is reckoned to him as righteousness.
vv. 7–12: the promise of the land; the animals divided; birds of prey driven off; deep sleep and darkness.
vv. 17–18: the fire pot and torch pass between the pieces; the covenant and the land from the river of Egypt to the Euphrates.
kw: From the root ʾmn, to be firm, to be sure, the root of our word “Amen”. To believe is to lean one’s whole weight on God and his word.
Right relationship, faithfulness to a bond. God counts Abram’s trust as what makes him right with God. St Paul quotes this verse (Romans 4:3; Galatians 3:6), and so does St James (James 2:23).
Literally “to cut a covenant” (v. 18), a phrase that recalls the cutting of the animals in this rite.
vv: Do not be afraid, Abram, I am your shield; your reward shall be very great.
The first words of God to Abram in this chapter are the words God speaks so often to those he calls: do not be afraid.
Look toward heaven and count the stars, if you are able to count them.
God takes Abram outside, under the night sky of the desert. The promise is as great as the heavens, and Abram has nothing to hold but God’s word.
And he believed the Lord; and the Lord reckoned it to him as righteousness.
One of the great verses of the Bible. Abram’s faith is not a work that earns God’s favour; it is the welcome he gives to God’s promise.
a smoking fire pot and a flaming torch passed between these pieces.
Fire and smoke are signs of God’s presence, as later at Sinai (Exodus 19:18). God himself walks the path of the covenant oath.
ch: The Catechism says that Abraham fulfils the definition of faith in Hebrews 11:1, and quotes this verse: “Abraham believed God, and it was reckoned to him as righteousness” (CCC 146). The Council of Trent taught that faith is the beginning of human salvation, the foundation and root of all justification (Session 6, chapter 8). Paul and James both quote Genesis 15:6 and do not contradict each other: Paul stresses that justification is a gift received by faith, not earned by works of the law; James shows that true faith lives and acts, as Abraham’s did when he offered Isaac. Faith, hope and charity, and the good works that grow from them, are all gifts of grace (CCC 1987–1992, 2008).

r.h: You will know them by their fruits
set: After the narrow gate (7:13–14) Jesus warns against those who would lead people along the wrong road: false prophets. They look harmless, like sheep, but they destroy the flock. The test he gives is simple and practical: look at the fruit of their lives and teaching.
John the Baptist had spoken in almost the same words: “every tree therefore that does not bear good fruit is cut down and thrown into the fire” (3:10). Jesus repeats the warning (7:19).
str: v. 15: beware of false prophets in sheep’s clothing.
v. 16: you will know them by their fruits: no grapes from thorns, no figs from thistles.
vv. 17–18: a good tree bears good fruit, a bad tree bad fruit.
vv. 19–20: the tree without good fruit is cut down; you will know them by their fruits.
kw: One who claims to speak for God but does not. The Old Testament knew them well (Jeremiah 23:16), and the early Church had to discern them too.
Wolves that snatch and tear. Jesus sends his disciples “like sheep into the midst of wolves” (10:16); here the danger is wolves dressed as sheep, inside the flock.

In the Bible fruit means the deeds and character that grow out of a person’s heart. Paul will speak of the fruit of the Spirit: love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, generosity, faithfulness, gentleness and self-control (Galatians 5:22–23).
vv: Beware of false prophets, who come to you in sheep’s clothing but inwardly are ravenous wolves.
The danger is not always obvious. A gentle appearance and pious words are not enough; Jesus asks for discernment.
You will know them by their fruits.
Fruit takes time to appear. The test is the patient look at a whole life: humility, charity, fidelity to the Gospel.
A good tree cannot bear bad fruit, nor can a bad tree bear good fruit.
What we do flows from what we are. To change the fruit, the tree itself must be made good, and that is the work of grace.
ch: The Didache, an early Christian writing, gives a similar rule for testing travelling prophets: not everyone who speaks in the Spirit is a prophet, but only one who lives in the ways of the Lord (Didache 11, in substance). The Catechism speaks of the fruits of the Spirit as perfections that the Holy Spirit forms in us as the first fruits of eternal glory, and lists twelve according to the tradition of the Church (CCC 1832). The Church tests new teachings and private revelations in the same way: by their fidelity to the faith handed down and by the fruits of holiness they bear.

study: Abram brought his fear and complaint to God honestly. What fear do I need to bring to God in prayer today?
Looking at the “fruit” of my life this past month, what does it show about the tree?

lead: Today the Church celebrates the birth of St John the Baptist. Apart from the Lord himself, John and the Blessed Virgin Mary are the only saints whose birthdays the Church keeps in the liturgy, because tradition holds that John was sanctified even before his birth, when he leapt for joy in his mother’s womb at Mary’s greeting (Luke 1:41, 44). The readings speak of a calling that begins before birth. In Isaiah the Servant says, “The Lord called me before I was born”, and God makes him “a light to the nations”. In Acts Paul, preaching in a synagogue, presents John as the one who prepared for Jesus and said, “I am not worthy to untie the thong of the sandals on his feet.” In the Gospel John is born, named, and grows strong in spirit in the wilderness.

Psalm 139 gives thanks to God who knit us together in our mother’s womb: “I praise you, for I am fearfully and wonderfully made.” The feast falls six months before Christmas, because the angel told Mary that Elizabeth was in her sixth month (Luke 1:36). St Augustine noted that John was born when the days begin to grow shorter and Christ when they begin to grow longer, and heard in this John’s own word: “He must increase, but I must decrease” (John 3:30; in substance).

set: This is the second of the four “Servant Songs” in the Book of Isaiah (42:1–9; 49:1–6; 50:4–11; 52:13–53:12). Many scholars think that chapters 40–55 of Isaiah come from the time of the exile in Babylon, in the sixth century before Christ, when Israel needed to hear that God had not forgotten his people.

Background. Who is the Servant? In v. 3 he is called “Israel”, yet in vv. 5–6 he has a mission to Israel, to bring Jacob back. The Servant seems to be both the people and one person who sums up the people’s calling. The Church sees the song fulfilled in Christ, and also, in its own measure, in John, who was called before his birth (Luke 1:15) and was sent to turn many of the people of Israel to the Lord (Luke 1:16).
str: v. 1: “Listen to me, O coastlands”; called and named in the womb.
v. 2: a sharp sword, a polished arrow, hidden in God’s hand and quiver.
v. 3: “You are my servant, Israel.”
v. 4: “I have labored in vain”, yet my reward is with my God.
vv. 5–6: to bring Jacob back, and more: “a light to the nations” to the end of the earth.
kw: A title of honour, given to Abraham, Moses and David. The servant belongs wholly to his master and acts in his name.
The islands and distant shores of the Mediterranean, the furthest lands known. The Servant speaks to the whole world.

God says that bringing back Israel is “too light a thing”; the Servant’s mission reaches all peoples. Simeon will call the child Jesus “a light for revelation to the Gentiles” (Luke 2:32), and Paul and Barnabas will quote this verse at Pisidian Antioch (Acts 13:47).
vv: The Lord called me before I was born, while I was in my mother’s womb he named me.
The calling comes before any merit. Jeremiah heard the same (Jeremiah 1:5). John’s name too was given by God before his birth (Luke 1:13).
he made me a polished arrow, in his quiver he hid me away.
Hidden, then sent. John spent years in the wilderness before he appeared to Israel (Luke 1:80).
I have labored in vain, I have spent my strength for nothing and vanity;
Even God’s servant knows discouragement. John in prison would send to ask Jesus, “Are you the one who is to come?” (Luke 7:19).
I will give you as a light to the nations, that my salvation may reach to the end of the earth.
The circle widens from Israel to the whole world. The mission of the Church is born here.
ch: The Church reads the Servant Songs as fulfilled in Jesus, the true Servant who gives his life (CCC 713, 601). On this day the Church applies the second song also to John, the herald, called from the womb. The Catechism calls John the Lord’s immediate forerunner, the “prophet of the Most High”, who surpasses all the prophets, of whom he is the last (CCC 523). The Second Vatican Council took the phrase “light of the nations” for the opening words of its document on the Church, Lumen Gentium: Christ is the light of the nations, and the Church reflects his light.

set: On their first missionary journey Paul and Barnabas reach Antioch in Pisidia, in the centre of present-day Turkey. On the Sabbath they go to the synagogue, and after the reading of the Law and the Prophets they are invited to speak (13:13–15). Paul’s sermon (13:16–41) is the first long sermon of his that Acts records. He retells Israel’s story from the Exodus to David, and then announces Jesus, the Saviour from David’s line.

Our verses are the hinge of the sermon: from David to Jesus, by way of John. That even in Asia Minor Paul could speak of John to a synagogue audience shows how widely John was remembered (compare Acts 18:25; 19:3).
str: v. 22: God made David king, a man after his heart.
v. 23: from David’s posterity God has brought Israel a Saviour, Jesus.
v. 24: before his coming John proclaimed a baptism of repentance.
v. 25: John: “I am not he… I am not worthy to untie the thong of the sandals on his feet.”
v. 26: “to us the message of this salvation has been sent.”
kw: God himself is Israel’s Saviour in the Old Testament. Now God brings a Saviour, Jesus, whose name means “the Lord saves”.
Metanoia is a change of mind and heart, a turning back to God. John’s baptism prepared hearts; Christian baptism, given in the name of Jesus, gives the Holy Spirit (Acts 19:4–6).
Gentiles who worshipped the God of Israel and attended the synagogue without becoming Jews. Paul addresses both them and the “descendants of Abraham’s family” (v. 26).
vv: I have found David, son of Jesse, to be a man after my heart, who will carry out all my wishes.
Paul combines words from Psalm 89:20 and 1 Samuel 13:14. The promise to David prepares for Jesus, son of David.
Of this man’s posterity God has brought to Israel a Savior, Jesus, as he promised;
God keeps his promises to Israel. Jesus is first of all the fulfilment of what God promised his people.
What do you suppose that I am? I am not he.
John’s greatness is his humility. He knows who he is not.
I am not worthy to untie the thong of the sandals on his feet.
Untying a master’s sandals was a slave’s task. John does not think himself worthy even of that.
ch: The Catechism says that John is “more than a prophet”: in him the Holy Spirit concludes his speaking through the prophets, and he goes before the Lord “in the spirit and power of Elijah” (CCC 718–719). John points away from himself; that is why the Church loves him. Every preacher, catechist and parent is called to the same humility: to bring people to Christ, and then step aside.

set: Luke tells the beginnings of John and of Jesus side by side: two annunciations (1:5–25 and 1:26–38), the meeting of the two mothers (1:39–56), and two births (1:57–80 and 2:1–40). At each step Jesus is shown to be greater, but John is honoured as his forerunner. Zechariah has been unable to speak since he doubted the angel’s word in the Temple (1:20). Now the promise is fulfilled.

Background. A Jewish boy was circumcised on the eighth day (Genesis 17:12; Leviticus 12:3). The naming, which Luke places at the same moment, would normally follow family custom, often a grandfather’s or father’s name. The Lectionary leaves out Zechariah’s song, the Benedictus (vv. 67–79), which the Church sings every morning at Lauds, and jumps to v. 80.
str: vv. 57–58: Elizabeth gives birth; neighbours and relatives rejoice at the Lord’s mercy.
vv. 59–61: the eighth day; “No; he is to be called John.”
vv. 62–64: Zechariah writes, “His name is John”, and his tongue is set loose in praise.
vv. 65–66: fear and wonder through the hill country: “What then will this child become?”
v. 80: the child grows, strong in spirit, in the wilderness.
kw: From the Hebrew Yôḥānān, “the Lord has been gracious”. The name, given by the angel (1:13), is the message of the child: God has shown favour to his people.

Literally “the Lord had made great his mercy” with her (v. 58). It is the same verb as in Mary’s song: “My soul magnifies the Lord” (1:46). Elizabeth’s neighbours echo, without knowing it, the Magnificat.
An Old Testament expression for God’s power at work in a person, especially in a prophet (compare Ezekiel 1:3). The neighbours see that this child is marked by God.
vv: Her neighbors and relatives heard that the Lord had shown his great mercy to her, and they rejoiced with her.
The angel had said, “many will rejoice at his birth” (1:14). The promise begins to come true in a village home.
No; he is to be called John.
Elizabeth speaks first, against custom. Luke does not say how she knew; she trusts the word God gave.
He asked for a writing tablet and wrote, “His name is John.”
Not “his name shall be”, but “is”: the name was already given by God. Zechariah’s obedience to the angel’s word opens his mouth.
Immediately his mouth was opened and his tongue freed, and he began to speak, praising God.
The first use of his returned voice is praise. Silence that began in doubt ends in blessing.
The child grew and became strong in spirit, and he was in the wilderness until the day he appeared publicly to Israel.
Luke will say much the same of Jesus (2:40). The wilderness is where Israel was formed, and where John is formed for his mission.
ch: The Catechism teaches that with John the Baptist the Holy Spirit begins the restoration to humanity of the divine likeness, and that John was filled with the Holy Spirit even from his mother’s womb (CCC 717, 720). The Church’s tradition holds that John was cleansed from original sin before his birth, at the Visitation (St Thomas Aquinas explains this sanctification in the womb); this is why his birth is a feast. Mary alone was preserved from original sin from the first moment of her conception (CCC 491). The Benedictus, the song of Zechariah that follows our passage, is prayed every morning in the Liturgy of the Hours: each day the Church joins Zechariah in thanking God for the dawn from on high.

qa: Why does the Church celebrate John’s birth, when it usually keeps a saint’s day of death?

For most saints the feast is their “birthday into heaven”, the day of their death. John’s birth is celebrated because it was already holy: he was filled with the Holy Spirit before birth (Luke 1:15) and leapt for joy in the womb in the presence of the Lord (Luke 1:41, 44). His martyrdom is also kept, on 29 August. Only Jesus, Mary and John have their birth celebrated in the Roman calendar.
Why 24 June and not 25 June, if it is six months before Christmas?

In the old Roman way of counting days, 25 December was “the eighth day before the Kalends of January”, and 24 June is “the eighth day before the Kalends of July”. So the two feasts fall on matching days in the Roman calendar, even though June has only thirty days.
Why did Zechariah lose his speech, and does God punish doubt?

Zechariah asked the angel for a sign, because he and Elizabeth were old (1:18). The silence was the sign, and also a time of discipline and waiting. It was not a rejection. When the promise was fulfilled and Zechariah obeyed, his voice returned in praise. God is patient with our doubts and leads us through them to faith, as he led Zechariah.
rite: The Nativity of St John the Baptist is a solemnity of the Roman calendar, with the Gloria and the Creed, and its own Vigil Mass on the evening before. An eighth-century Latin hymn for this feast, Ut queant laxis, attributed to Paul the Deacon, gave music the names of its notes: the monk Guido of Arezzo took the first syllables of its lines, ut, re, mi, fa, sol, la. The hymn asks St John to cleanse our lips, so that with loosened voices we may sing God’s wonders, as Zechariah’s tongue was loosened. In Goa the feast, called São João, falls in the monsoon and is kept with joy: young men wear crowns of leaves and flowers and leap into the wells and ponds, recalling the child who leapt for joy in his mother’s womb. Every family that names a child, every parent who asks “What then will this child become?”, can make this feast its own.
study: God called John and named him before he was born. What does this say about the dignity of every child in the womb?
Zechariah’s silence ended in praise when he obeyed. Is there a word of God I have doubted that I need to obey?
John said, “I am not he.” In my family, parish or work, how can I point people to Christ rather than to myself?
The neighbours asked, “What then will this child become?” Which child or young person could I pray for, and encourage, this week?

lead: God renews his covenant with Abraham: he gives Abram and Sarai new names, the sign of circumcision, and the promise of a son, Isaac, though both are old. Abraham falls on his face and laughs. In the Gospel a leper kneels before Jesus and says, “Lord, if you choose, you can make me clean.” Jesus chooses, and touches him. In both readings God keeps his word where human strength has run out, and Psalm 128 sings of the blessing on the house of those who fear the Lord.

r.h: Walk before me, and be blameless
set: Twenty-four years have passed since God first called Abram from Haran (12:4). Ishmael, the son of Hagar, is now thirteen. God appears again and makes the covenant solemn and lasting: Abram becomes Abraham, Sarai becomes Sarah, every male is to be circumcised, and the son of the promise will be born of Sarah within a year. Many scholars think this chapter comes from a priestly tradition in Israel that loved covenants, names and signs. The Lectionary leaves out the verses on the new name of Abraham and the details of the rite.
str: v. 1: God Almighty appears: “walk before me, and be blameless.”
vv. 9–10: Abraham’s side of the covenant: circumcision of every male.
vv. 15–16: Sarai becomes Sarah; she will bear a son and be the mother of nations.
vv. 17–18: Abraham laughs, and prays for Ishmael.
vv. 19–22: the son will be called Isaac; Ishmael too is blessed; the covenant passes through Isaac.
kw: An ancient name of God used to the patriarchs (compare Exodus 6:3). Its exact meaning is uncertain; the Latin translation and later tradition render it “Almighty”. Here it fits: only the Almighty can give a child to a man of ninety-nine and a woman of ninety.
Whole, complete, without defect. The same word is used for an animal fit for sacrifice. God does not ask Abraham for a flawless record but for a whole heart, a life lived entirely before him.
The name means “he laughs”. Abraham laughs here (v. 17), Sarah will laugh at Mamre (18:12), and at the birth Sarah will say, “God has brought laughter for me” (21:6). Doubt becomes joy.
vv: I am God Almighty; walk before me, and be blameless.
The covenant begins with God naming himself, and then with a call. To walk before someone is to live in his sight, as a servant walks before a king.
Every male among you shall be circumcised.
The sign is cut into the body of every family. It marks the people as belonging to God for all generations.
Then Abraham fell on his face and laughed,
He bows in worship and laughs in disbelief at the same moment. God does not withdraw the promise; he names the child after the laughter.
As for Ishmael, I have heard you; I will bless him
Abraham’s prayer for his first son is heard. Ishmael is not the son of the covenant, but he is not forgotten. The name Ishmael means “God hears” (16:11).
ch: The Catechism calls Abraham the model of the obedience of faith, “the father of all who believe” (CCC 145–146), and says that because he walked in God’s presence and in covenant with him he was ready to welcome the mysterious Guest at Mamre (CCC 2571). The Church reads circumcision as a sign that prepared for baptism: Jesus himself was circumcised as a son of Abraham, and his circumcision prefigures the “circumcision of Christ”, which is baptism (CCC 527; Colossians 2:11–12). God’s covenant with Abraham’s descendants remains, for “the gifts and the calling of God are irrevocable” (Romans 11:29).

r.h: I do choose. Be made clean!
set: Jesus comes down from the mountain after the Sermon on the Mount (chapters 5–7). Matthew now gathers ten mighty works in chapters 8–9. Having shown Jesus as teacher with authority, he shows him as healer with authority. The first person healed is a man shut out from ordinary life.

Background. The law of Leviticus 13–14 deals with skin diseases that made a person ritually unclean. The Greek word lepra covered several skin conditions, not only what we call leprosy today. The sick person lived apart, and if healed showed himself to the priest and offered the prescribed sacrifice before returning to the community.
str: v. 1: the crowds follow Jesus down from the mountain.
v. 2: the leper kneels: “Lord, if you choose, you can make me clean.”
v. 3: Jesus stretches out his hand, touches him, and he is cleansed.
v. 4: say nothing; go to the priest; offer the gift Moses commanded.
kw: The word means to bow down in homage, and Matthew uses it for worship of God (4:10) and of Jesus (2:11; 28:9, 17). The leper approaches as one who believes.
The leper does not doubt Jesus’ power, only his will. Jesus answers with the same word: “I do choose.” His will is to heal.
More than healing of the skin: it means restoration to worship and to the community. That is why the man must go to the priest.
vv: Lord, if you choose, you can make me clean.
A prayer of complete trust. The man leaves everything to Jesus’ will. Christians have prayed in these words for centuries.
He stretched out his hand and touched him,
Jesus could have healed with a word, as he will for the centurion’s servant. He chooses to touch the one no one touched. Holiness here does not fear contact with impurity; it overcomes it.
go, show yourself to the priest, and offer the gift that Moses commanded,
Jesus respects the law of Moses. The healing is to be confirmed in the proper way, so that the man can take his place again among his people and in worship.
ch: The Catechism speaks of Christ’s compassion towards the sick and his many healings as a sign that God has visited his people (CCC 1503), and notes that the sick try to touch him, for power comes from him (CCC 1504). The Church continues his touch in the sacrament of the Anointing of the Sick, and in every hand stretched out to those whom illness or stigma has set apart. Many missionaries, such as St Damien of Molokai, gave their lives to people with leprosy because of this Gospel.

qa: Why does Jesus tell the man to say nothing to anyone?

In Matthew, as in Mark, Jesus often asks that his mighty works not be spread about. He does not want to be followed as a wonder-worker or a political Messiah. His identity will be fully shown only on the Cross and in the Resurrection. The first duty of the healed man is to go to the priest and give thanks to God.
study: Abraham was told to “walk before me, and be blameless.” What would it mean for me to live this day consciously before God?
Who in my parish or neighbourhood is “untouchable” in practice? How can I stretch out my hand to them?

lead: At the oaks of Mamre Abraham runs to welcome three strangers in the heat of the day, and receives from them the promise that Sarah will have a son. Sarah laughs, and the Lord asks, “Is anything too wonderful for the Lord?” In the Gospel a centurion, a Gentile, trusts that Jesus can heal his servant with a word, and Jesus heals Peter’s mother-in-law and many others. Instead of a psalm the Church sings Mary’s Magnificat, for Mary is the woman in whom God did the most wonderful thing of all, and who sang that God remembered his mercy, “according to the promise he made to our ancestors, to Abraham and to his descendants forever”.

r.h: Is anything too wonderful for the Lord?
set: Abraham is camped by the oaks of Mamre near Hebron. In the desert world, hospitality to travellers was a sacred duty; a stranger might die without it. Abraham does more than his duty. He runs, bows, has water brought for their feet, and has a feast prepared.

The narrator tells us at once that “the Lord appeared to Abraham”, but Abraham sees three men. Through the story the text moves between “they” and “the Lord”, and the reader is left to wonder at the mystery.
str: vv. 1–2: the Lord appears; Abraham sees three men and runs to meet them.
vv. 3–8: the welcome: water, rest, bread, a calf, curds and milk.
vv. 9–10: “Where is your wife Sarah?” The promise of a son.
vv. 11–15: Sarah laughs; “Is anything too wonderful for the Lord?”; Sarah’s fear and denial.
kw: Verbs of haste appear again and again: Abraham runs (rûṣ), hastens (mahar) to Sarah, runs to the herd, and the servant hastens. An old man in the midday heat rushes to serve.
Sarah laughs “to herself”, out of long disappointment. The same root gives the name Isaac. God does not punish her laughter; he answers it with a question and a promise.
From peleʾ, wonder, a deed beyond human power. The angel Gabriel will echo this to Mary: “nothing will be impossible with God” (Luke 1:37).
vv: He looked up and saw three men standing near him.
Hebrews 13:2 recalls this scene: “by doing that some have entertained angels without knowing it.”
Let a little water be brought, and wash your feet, and rest yourselves under the tree.
Abraham promises “a little” and gives a great deal. True hospitality is generous and humble at once.
Is anything too wonderful for the Lord?
The central verse. The question is addressed to Abraham and Sarah, and to every reader who has given up hope.
Oh yes, you did laugh.
God is gentle with Sarah. He does not reject her; he simply tells her the truth. The promise stands.
ch: The Catechism says that the remarkable hospitality at Mamre is the prelude to the annunciation of the true Son of the promise (CCC 2571). Many Fathers, among them St Ambrose and St Augustine, saw in the three visitors a hint of the mystery of the Holy Trinity (in substance), and the famous icon by Andrei Rublev shows the three seated at Abraham’s table. The Church does not say that Abraham knew the Trinity; she says that God was already preparing his people to receive the full revelation of who he is.

set: Jesus enters Capernaum, the lakeside town where he made his home. A centurion, an officer in charge of about a hundred soldiers, comes to ask for help. Many scholars think he served Herod Antipas, the ruler of Galilee, rather than a Roman legion; either way he was a Gentile. Matthew then adds two more healings, Peter’s mother-in-law and the sick brought at evening, and a fulfilment text from Isaiah.
str: vv. 5–9: the centurion’s request and his word of humble faith.
vv. 10–13: Jesus marvels at his faith; many will come from east and west; the servant is healed.
vv. 14–15: Peter’s mother-in-law is healed and serves him.
vv. 16–17: many are healed at evening; Isaiah 53:4 is fulfilled.
kw: A commander of a hundred men. In the Gospels and Acts centurions often appear in a good light: at the Cross (27:54) and Cornelius (Acts 10).
Literally “fit” or “sufficient”. The centurion knows that a Jew might not enter a Gentile’s house without becoming unclean, and he does not want to burden Jesus. His humility opens him to grace.
From the same root as diakonos, servant. The healed woman at once uses her restored strength to serve Jesus. Healing leads to service.
vv: Lord, I am not worthy to have you come under my roof; but only speak the word, and my servant will be healed.

The Church has made these words her own. At every Mass, before Communion, the faithful say: “Lord, I am not worthy that you should enter under my roof, but only say the word and my soul shall be healed.”
in no one in Israel have I found such faith.
Jesus marvels at a Gentile’s faith. This is a sign of the mission to the nations that the Gospel will open at its end (28:19).
many will come from east and west and will eat with Abraham and Isaac and Jacob in the kingdom of heaven,
The image of the great banquet of the nations, foretold in Isaiah 25:6. The patriarchs of Israel sit at that table with them.
He took our infirmities and bore our diseases.
Matthew quotes Isaiah 53:4, the song of the suffering servant. Jesus does not heal from a distance; he takes our weakness on himself, and in the end he will carry it to the Cross.
ch: The Catechism quotes the centurion’s words in its teaching on preparing for Holy Communion (CCC 1386). St Augustine praised the centurion: by calling himself unworthy he showed himself worthy, so that Christ entered not his walls but his heart (in substance, Sermon 62). The warning about “the heirs of the kingdom” (v. 12) is said in the manner of the prophets, to shake anyone who presumes on privilege; the Church hears it as addressed to Christians too (7:21–23). It is not a judgment on the Jewish people, whom God has not rejected (CCC 839; Nostra Aetate 4).

rite: On Saturdays in Ordinary Time, when no obligatory memorial falls, the Latin Church may keep the memorial of the Blessed Virgin Mary. Today’s response, the Magnificat, fits it well: the Lord who asked Abraham “Is anything too wonderful for the Lord?” fulfilled his promise to Abraham in Mary’s Son.
study: Abraham ran to serve strangers in the heat of the day. Whom can I welcome this week, at home or in the parish, as if I were welcoming the Lord?
I say the centurion’s words before every Communion. What does it mean for me to say “only say the word” and truly mean it?

lead: The Thirteenth Sunday of Year B is about life stronger than death. The Book of Wisdom says plainly that God did not make death: he created all things to exist, and made us for incorruption. In the Gospel Mark weaves two stories into one: a woman who has bled for twelve years touches Jesus’ cloak and is healed, and the twelve-year-old daughter of Jairus, already dead, hears Jesus say, “Talitha cum,” and gets up. Psalm 30 gives thanks: “O Lord, you brought up my soul from Sheol.”

Between them St Paul asks the Corinthians to give generously to the poor church in Jerusalem, because Christ, though rich, became poor for our sake. The link is the same: the God of life gives himself, and those who receive life are called to share it.

set: The Book of Wisdom was written in Greek, probably in Alexandria in Egypt, during the century before Christ. Its author speaks in the person of Solomon, the wise king, but he writes for Jews living among Greeks, who were tempted to give up their faith. It is one of the latest books of the Old Testament, and it is part of the Catholic canon of Scripture.

Chapters 1–5 contrast the righteous and the ungodly. In chapter 2 the ungodly say that life is short, death is the end, so let us enjoy ourselves and crush the righteous man who rebukes us. The author answers that they are wrong about God and about death. Today’s verses come from the opening and from the answer.
str: 1:13: God did not make death and does not delight in it.
1:14: he created all things to exist; creation is wholesome; Hades has no rule on earth.
1:15: righteousness is immortal.
2:23: God created us for incorruption, in the image of his own eternity.
2:24: death entered through the devil’s envy, and those who belong to him experience it.
kw: Not decaying, not perishing. The word is used by St Paul for the resurrection body: “what is sown is perishable, what is raised is imperishable” (1 Corinthians 15:42).
“Righteousness is immortal” (1:15). Wisdom teaches that the souls of the righteous are in the hand of God (3:1). Life with God does not end at death.

The book says that death entered the world through the devil’s envy (2:24). Envy cannot bear another’s good. Many interpreters see here the serpent of Genesis 3, envious of the human beings made in God’s image.
vv: because God did not make death, and he does not delight in the death of the living.
A strong and simple statement. Death in its full sense, the death that separates from God, is not God’s work. Ezekiel had said the same: God has no pleasure in the death of anyone (Ezekiel 18:32).
For he created all things so that they might exist;
God’s will in creating is that things should be. Creation is good, as Genesis 1 repeats.
for God created us for incorruption, and made us in the image of his own eternity,
An echo of Genesis 1:27. Some Greek manuscripts read “image of his own nature” instead of “eternity”; both readings say that we are made to share God’s life.
but through the devil’s envy death entered the world,

This is one of the first texts in Scripture to link the serpent of Genesis with the devil. The Book of Revelation will call him “that ancient serpent, who is called the Devil and Satan” (Revelation 12:9).
ch: The Catechism quotes these verses: “God did not make death, and he does not delight in the death of the living… It was through the devil’s envy that death entered the world” (CCC 413). It teaches that death is a consequence of sin, and that God had destined man not to die (CCC 1008). It also teaches that behind the disobedience of our first parents lurks a seductive voice opposed to God, the fallen angel called Satan or the devil (CCC 391). The Church does not deny that the body dies according to nature; she proclaims that Christ has conquered death, and that the resurrection of the body is the fulfilment of the incorruption for which we were made.

r.h: Rich, yet for your sakes he became poor
set: Paul is organising a collection among his Gentile churches for the poor Christians of Jerusalem (compare Romans 15:25–27; Galatians 2:10). For him it is more than charity: it is a sign of the unity of Jewish and Gentile believers in one Church. The Corinthians had begun eagerly a year before but had not finished.
In chapters 8–9 Paul encourages them. He points to the churches of Macedonia, poor themselves, who gave beyond their means (8:1–5). Then he points to Christ.
str: v. 7: you excel in everything; excel also in this generous undertaking.
v. 9: the generous act of the Lord Jesus Christ: rich, he became poor, to make you rich.
vv. 13–14: not relief for others and pressure on you, but a fair balance.
v. 15: the manna: “The one who had much did not have too much, and the one who had little did not have too little.”
kw: Paul plays on this word through the chapter. The collection is a charis (v. 7, “generous undertaking”), and Christ’s self-giving is the charis of the Lord (v. 9, “generous act”). Our giving is a share in his grace.
He became a beggar, one who has nothing. Paul thinks of the whole mystery of the Son becoming man, as in Philippians 2:6–8.
Equality, fairness. Paul does not ask the Corinthians to become poor so that others may be rich; he asks for a balance in which abundance meets need.
vv: so we want you to excel also in this generous undertaking.
Paul does not command; he invites. Generosity is to be one more of the gifts in which the community shines.
though he was rich, yet for your sakes he became poor, so that by his poverty you might become rich.
One of the great Christ verses of the New Testament. The riches are the divine life; the poverty is his birth, his life and his Cross. The exchange is all to our advantage.
your present abundance and their need,
Today one community has more, tomorrow another. The Church is one body in which goods circulate.
The one who had much did not have too much, and the one who had little did not have too little.
Paul quotes Exodus 16:18. In the desert God gave manna to each according to need. Sharing in the Church is meant to reflect that divine providence.
ch: The Catechism quotes this verse when it teaches that the whole life of Christ is a mystery of redemption: by becoming poor he enriches us with his poverty (CCC 517). In its teaching on love for the poor it quotes St John Chrysostom: not to enable the poor to share in our goods is to steal from them and deprive them of life; the goods we possess are not ours, but theirs (CCC 2446). The collection at Mass, and the gifts given for the poor and for needy dioceses, continue Paul’s collection. They are not a tax but a share in the grace of Christ.

set: Jesus has just crossed back from the Gentile side of the lake, where he healed the man with the legion of demons (5:1–20). In chapters 4–5 Mark shows his power over the storm, the demons, sickness and death.

Mark often places one story inside another, so that each explains the other. Here the story of Jairus is interrupted by the woman with the haemorrhage. Both are called “daughter”, both involve the number twelve, and both turn on faith and touch. The shorter form of the reading keeps only Jairus’ story.
str: vv. 21–24: Jairus, a leader of the synagogue, begs Jesus to come to his dying daughter.
vv. 25–29: the woman who had suffered twelve years touches his cloak and is healed.
vv. 30–34: “Who touched my clothes?” She tells the whole truth. “Daughter, your faith has made you well.”
vv. 35–36: news of the girl’s death; “Do not fear, only believe.”
vv. 37–40: with Peter, James and John to the house; the mourners laugh.
vv. 41–43: “Talitha cum”; the girl gets up; give her something to eat.
kw: A respected lay leader who arranged the services. Jairus is an important man, yet he falls at Jesus’ feet. Grief and love make him humble.

Mark uses the same verb for healing and for salvation: Jairus asks that his daughter be “made well” (v. 23); the woman thinks “I will be made well” (v. 28); Jesus says “your faith has made you well” (v. 34). Bodily healing points to the salvation of the whole person.
Aramaic, the language Jesus spoke, kept by Mark and translated for his Greek readers: “Little girl, get up!” Many later manuscripts have the longer form koumi; the oldest have koum.
vv: My little daughter is at the point of death. Come and lay your hands on her, so that she may be made well, and live.
A father’s prayer, urgent and full of faith. He believes that Jesus’ touch can give life.
If I but touch his clothes, I will be made well.

The law of Leviticus 15 meant that her bleeding made her ritually unclean, and for twelve years she had lived with that and with her illness. She comes from behind, quietly. Her faith is real, though still timid.
Daughter, your faith has made you well; go in peace, and be healed of your disease.
Jesus will not let her slip away unseen. He calls her “daughter”, gives her peace, and confirms her healing before everyone. She is healed in body and restored in dignity.
Do not fear, only believe.
The word to Jairus is the word to every Christian in the face of death. Faith is asked for precisely when there seems nothing more to hope.
Talitha cum,
Jesus takes her by the hand. The verb “get up” is the same family of words used for the resurrection. The early Church heard in this a sign of the resurrection of all who belong to Christ.
ch: The Catechism lists the raising of Jairus’ daughter with that of the young man of Nain and of Lazarus as signs announcing Christ’s own Resurrection (CCC 994). It notes that Jesus hears the prayer of faith expressed in deeds, such as the woman who touches his clothes (CCC 2616), and that the sick try to touch him, for power comes from him and heals (CCC 1504). In the sacraments Christ continues to touch us: “power came forth from him” then, and it comes forth now in Baptism, the Eucharist and the Anointing of the Sick. The command to give the girl something to eat shows his care for ordinary needs, and the Church has often heard in it an echo of the food of life she gives her children.

qa: If God did not make death, why do we die?

The Church teaches that death entered as a consequence of sin (CCC 1008), not as part of God’s first plan. The body dies according to nature, but for those who are in Christ death has been changed: it becomes a passage to life with God. Christ did not take death away from this world; he went through it and opened the way to the resurrection.
Was the woman superstitious to think that touching his clothes would heal her?

Her faith was imperfect, perhaps mixed with ideas of magic, but Jesus accepted it and led it further. He calls her forward so that her trust in his clothes becomes a personal meeting with him. The Church honours relics and holy objects in the same spirit: never as magic, always as a way to the person of Christ and the saints.
Why does Paul ask for money in a letter that is Scripture?

Because love for the poor belongs to the heart of the Gospel. Paul’s collection was also a sign of unity between Gentile and Jewish Christians. He asks gently, without command, and he roots it in Christ’s own self-giving. Giving for the poor is part of worship, not a separate matter.
rite: In the Roman Rite the Thirteenth Sunday of Year B joins healing, resurrection and charity. Peter’s Pence, the gift of the faithful to the Holy Father for his works of charity, is traditionally linked with the solemnity of Saints Peter and Paul on Tuesday. Today is also a good day to pray for the sick of the parish and to bring them Holy Communion.
study: Wisdom says “God did not make death.” How does this change the way I think about illness, ageing and the death of those I love?
Paul says Christ became poor to make us rich. In what concrete way can my family share our “abundance” with someone in need this week?
The woman came from behind; Jesus called her forward. Is there something I bring to God quietly that he wants me to bring openly, perhaps in confession?
Jesus said to Jairus, “Do not fear, only believe.” Where do I need to hear that word today?

lead: Abraham walks with his three visitors towards Sodom, and the Lord shares his plan with him. Abraham then dares to intercede: will the Judge of all the earth sweep away the righteous with the wicked? From fifty down to ten, God agrees to spare the city. In the Gospel Jesus tells a would-be follower that the Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head, and tells another, “Follow me.” Psalm 103 sings of the Lord who is kind and merciful. Today the Church keeps the memorial of St Irenaeus, bishop and Doctor of the Church.

r.h: Shall not the Judge of all the earth do what is just?
set: The visitors who promised Isaac now look toward Sodom, the city of the plain whose sin had become notorious (13:13). God decides to share his purpose with Abraham, because Abraham is to teach his children “righteousness and justice”. What follows is the first great prayer of intercession in the Bible.

Scripture describes the sin of Sodom in more than one way: the violence and abuse against guests in chapter 19, and, in Ezekiel 16:49, pride, excess of food and prosperous ease, and failing to help the poor and needy.
str: vv. 16–19: God decides not to hide his plan from Abraham, chosen to teach justice.
vv. 20–21: the outcry against Sodom and Gomorrah.
vv. 22–25: Abraham stands before the Lord: “Will you indeed sweep away the righteous with the wicked?”
vv. 26–32: from fifty to forty-five, forty, thirty, twenty, ten; each time God agrees.
v. 33: the Lord goes his way; Abraham returns home.
kw: The cry of the oppressed for help, the same kind of cry as Israel’s in Egypt (Exodus 3:7–9). God hears the voice of the victims.
One who is right with God and with neighbour. Abraham’s question is whether the presence of a few righteous people can save a whole city.
Abraham knows how small he is before God (v. 27), yet he speaks. Humility and boldness go together in true prayer.
vv: Shall I hide from Abraham what I am about to do,
God treats Abraham as a friend, sharing his counsel with him. Later Scripture calls Abraham the friend of God (Isaiah 41:8; James 2:23).
Will you indeed sweep away the righteous with the wicked?
Abraham appeals to God’s own justice. He is not arguing against God but holding God to what God is.
Shall not the Judge of all the earth do what is just?
The key question of the chapter. God is the judge not only of Israel but of all nations, and his judgment is never unjust.
For the sake of ten I will not destroy it.
Abraham stops at ten, and the Lord would have spared the city for ten. The righteous few protect the many.
ch: The Catechism says that once God had confided his plan, Abraham’s heart was attuned to his Lord’s compassion for men, and he dared to intercede for them with bold confidence (CCC 2571). It adds that since Abraham, intercession, asking on behalf of another, has been characteristic of a heart attuned to God’s mercy (CCC 2635). The Church sees the fullness of this prayer in Christ, the one righteous man, for whose sake the many are spared, who “always lives to make intercession” for us (Hebrews 7:25).

set: Crowds press around Jesus, and he gives orders to cross the lake. Before he gets into the boat, two men speak to him about following. Matthew places these sayings just before the storm on the lake (8:23–27), where following Jesus will mean being in the boat with him in danger.
str: v. 18: Jesus gives orders to cross to the other side.
vv. 19–20: a scribe: “I will follow you wherever you go”; the Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head.
vv. 21–22: a disciple: “let me first bury my father”; “Follow me, and let the dead bury their own dead.”
kw: A teacher of the law. The scribe calls Jesus “Teacher” and offers to follow, with good will. Jesus wants him to know the cost.
Jesus’ favourite way of speaking of himself. Here it is used for the first time in Matthew, of his homelessness. The same title will be used of his suffering and of his coming in glory.
The word of discipleship. It appears in both scenes and again in v. 23, when the disciples follow him into the boat.
vv: Teacher, I will follow you wherever you go.
A generous promise. Jesus does not refuse him, but makes sure he knows where Jesus goes.
Foxes have holes, and birds of the air have nests; but the Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head.
The wild animals have more security than he does. To follow him is to share his poverty and his trust in the Father.
Follow me, and let the dead bury their own dead.

Burial of a father was among the most sacred duties in Jewish life. Jesus’ words are deliberately shocking, to show the urgency of the kingdom. Many Fathers and commentators take “the dead” to mean those who are spiritually dead, who have not yet heard the call.
ch: The Church does not read this Gospel as a rejection of care for parents, which the fourth commandment requires (CCC 2214–2220). She reads it as a call to put Christ first. The Catechism teaches that Jesus calls his disciples to prefer him to everything and everyone (CCC 2544). Priests, religious and missionaries who leave home and family live this saying in a visible way; every Christian lives it when the call of Christ comes before comfort.

rite: St Irenaeus was born in Asia Minor, probably at Smyrna, between about 130 and 140. As a young man he heard St Polycarp, who had known the apostle John, so he stands very close to the apostles. He became a priest at Lyons in Gaul and, after the martyrdom of Bishop Pothinus in 177, its bishop. His great work, usually called Against Heresies, defended the faith against the Gnostic teachers by pointing to Scripture, the rule of faith and the succession of bishops from the apostles, above all in the Church of Rome, which he called founded and organised by the two most glorious apostles, Peter and Paul (Against Heresies 3.3.2); the Catechism quotes the same passage on the communion of all the Churches with Rome (CCC 834). He wrote that “the glory of God is man fully alive” (CCC 294), and that the knot of Eve’s disobedience was loosed by Mary’s obedience (CCC 494). He is honoured as a martyr, though the details of his death are not known. In 2022 Pope Francis declared him a Doctor of the Church, calling him the Doctor of Unity. Like Abraham, he spoke for the whole Church; like the disciples in the Gospel, he left his homeland to follow Christ.
study: Abraham prayed boldly for a city that was not his own. For which town, nation or people can I pray with the same persistence this week?
What “first let me…” do I put between myself and Christ’s call?

lead: On the solemnity of Saints Peter and Paul the Church honours the two apostles who gave their lives in Rome and whom she calls her pillars. The first reading tells how the Lord rescued Peter from Herod’s prison while the church prayed for him. In the second, Paul, near the end, says, “I have fought the good fight, I have finished the race, I have kept the faith,” and trusts that the Lord will rescue him for his heavenly kingdom. In the Gospel Peter confesses Jesus as the Messiah, the Son of the living God, and Jesus answers, “you are Peter, and on this rock I will build my church.”

Psalm 34 joins the readings: “The angel of the Lord encamps around those who fear him, and delivers them.” Both apostles were rescued many times, and in the end both were delivered through martyrdom into the kingdom. The Vigil Mass has its own readings (Acts 3:1–10; Galatians 1:11–20; John 21:15–19).

r.h: The Lord has sent his angel and rescued me
set: King Herod here is Herod Agrippa I, grandson of Herod the Great, who ruled Judea from about 41 to 44 AD. He killed James, the brother of John, the first of the Twelve to be martyred, and then arrested Peter at the time of the Passover. Luke tells the story so that it recalls the first Passover: a night of deliverance, an angel of the Lord, a command to rise quickly with belt and sandals.

Luke writes that Herod saw that the killing of James “pleased the Jews”. In Acts this refers to the leaders and those in Jerusalem who at that moment opposed the apostles, not to the Jewish people as a whole. Peter, James and the whole Jerusalem church were themselves Jews, and Luke records that many thousands of Jews believed (Acts 21:20).
str: vv. 1–4: Herod kills James and imprisons Peter during the feast of Unleavened Bread.
v. 5: Peter is kept in prison; the church prays fervently for him.
vv. 6–7: the night before his trial, an angel wakes Peter; the chains fall off.
vv. 8–10: belt, sandals, cloak; through the guards and the iron gate.
v. 11: Peter comes to himself: “Now I am sure that the Lord has sent his angel and rescued me.”
kw: Stretched out, earnestly, without stopping. A related word describes Jesus’ prayer in Gethsemane (Luke 22:44). The whole church is at prayer while Peter sleeps.
The heavenly messenger who acts for God. The angel of the Lord also opened the prison doors for the apostles earlier (5:19).
Delivered, snatched out. The same verb is used by Stephen of God rescuing Joseph and Israel in Egypt (7:10, 34). Peter’s night is a small exodus.
vv: He had James, the brother of John, killed with the sword.
The first apostle to die for Christ. Jesus had told James and John that they would drink his cup (Mark 10:39).
While Peter was kept in prison, the church prayed fervently to God for him.
Two powers face each other: the prison of the king and the prayer of the church. Luke shows which one is stronger.
Peter, bound with two chains, was sleeping between two soldiers,
He sleeps on the night before his trial. Peter, who once slept in Gethsemane from weakness, now sleeps in peace, trusting God.
Fasten your belt and put on your sandals.
The words recall the Passover command: “your loins girded, your sandals on your feet” (Exodus 12:11). It happens during the same feast.
Now I am sure that the Lord has sent his angel and rescued me
Only when he stands in the street does Peter understand. Faith often recognises God’s action afterwards.
ch: The Church sees in this reading the power of prayer for the Pope and the bishops. The Catechism teaches that the Roman Pontiff, as Peter’s successor, is the perpetual and visible source and foundation of the unity both of the bishops and of the whole company of the faithful (CCC 882, quoting Lumen Gentium 23). In every Mass the Church names the Pope and the bishop of the diocese in the Eucharistic Prayer, praying for them as the Jerusalem church prayed for Peter. The angel’s rescue does not mean that Peter will never suffer. He will be rescued many times, and in the end will give his life, as Jesus foretold (John 21:18–19).

set: The Second Letter to Timothy presents Paul as a prisoner in Rome, near the end of his life, writing to his beloved disciple. It is one of the three Pastoral Letters. Many scholars think these letters were written by a disciple of Paul in his name after his death; others hold that Paul wrote them himself. The Church receives them as inspired Scripture, the voice of Paul to the Church.
Today’s verses are Paul’s farewell. He looks back on his life, and forward to the judgment, and remembers how the Lord stood by him when everyone else deserted him at his first defence (4:16).
str: v. 6: I am already being poured out as a libation; the time of my departure has come.
v. 7: the good fight, the race, the faith kept.
v. 8: the crown of righteousness, for me and for all who have longed for his appearing.
vv. 17–18: the Lord stood by me and gave me strength; he will rescue me for his heavenly kingdom. Glory to him.
kw: to be poured out as a libation
In ancient sacrifices wine or oil was poured out on the altar. Paul sees his coming death as an offering poured out to God (compare Philippians 2:17).
A word used for loosing a ship from its moorings or striking a tent. Death is a setting out, not an end.
The wreath given to the winner in the games. Paul has finished the race; the Lord, the just judge, will give the crown.
vv: As for me, I am already being poured out as a libation,
Paul’s life has been given to God day by day. His martyrdom will be the last drop of the offering.
I have fought the good fight, I have finished the race, I have kept the faith.
Three pictures: the athlete in the contest, the runner at the finishing line, and the steward who has kept safe what was entrusted to him. It is not pride, but thanksgiving for grace.
and not only to me but also to all who have longed for his appearing.
The crown is not only for apostles. It is promised to every believer who loves the Lord’s coming.
But the Lord stood by me and gave me strength,
When others left him, the Lord did not. Paul’s whole mission depended on that strength, so that “all the Gentiles might hear”.
To him be the glory forever and ever. Amen.
Paul ends with praise. Even in chains, the last word belongs to God.
ch: From the earliest times the Church has honoured Peter and Paul together. St Clement of Rome, writing to Corinth about the year 96, recalled the two great apostles who suffered in his own day; St Irenaeus spoke of the Church of Rome as founded and organised by the two most glorious apostles, Peter and Paul (Against Heresies 3.3.2). The Catechism calls martyrdom the supreme witness given to the truth of the faith (CCC 2473). In today’s Preface the Church praises God that Peter was foremost in confessing the faith and Paul its outstanding preacher, and that both, by different ways, gathered together the one family of Christ.

r.h: You are Peter, and on this rock I will build my church
set: Caesarea Philippi lay at the foot of Mount Hermon, near the sources of the Jordan, in the territory of Herod’s son Philip. It was a place of pagan shrines, built against a great rock face. There, far from Jerusalem, Jesus asks his disciples who he is.
Mark and Luke tell Peter’s confession too, but only Matthew gives Jesus’ answer to Peter with the blessing, the new name, the promise of the Church and the keys.
str: vv. 13–14: “Who do people say that the Son of Man is?” John the Baptist, Elijah, Jeremiah, a prophet.
vv. 15–16: “But who do you say that I am?” Peter: “You are the Messiah, the Son of the living God.”
v. 17: Blessed are you; my Father revealed this to you.
v. 18: you are Peter, and on this rock I will build my church; the gates of Hades will not prevail.
v. 19: the keys of the kingdom; binding and loosing.
kw: In Greek the name Peter (Petros) and the word rock (petra) are nearly the same. In Aramaic, which Jesus spoke, the word is the same, Kēpāʾ; that is why Paul often calls him Cephas (1 Corinthians 15:5; Galatians 2:9).
The assembly called together. In the Greek Old Testament it translates the Hebrew word for the assembly of Israel. Jesus speaks of “my church”, the people he gathers.

Isaiah 22:22 tells how the key of the house of David was given to Eliakim, the steward of the king’s palace: “he shall open, and no one shall shut.” The keys mean authority over the house in the name of the king.
vv: But who do you say that I am?
The question is addressed to every generation. Opinions about Jesus are not enough; he asks for a personal answer.
You are the Messiah, the Son of the living God.
Peter speaks for all the Twelve. The confession joins the hope of Israel, the Messiah, with the deepest truth of Jesus, the Son of God.
For flesh and blood has not revealed this to you, but my Father in heaven.
Faith is a gift from the Father, not a human discovery. The Catechism uses this verse to teach that faith is a grace (CCC 153).
you are Peter, and on this rock I will build my church, and the gates of Hades will not prevail against it.
Simon receives a new name that is a mission. The Church is Christ’s (“my church”), built by him on Peter. The powers of death will not overcome it.
whatever you bind on earth will be bound in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth will be loosed in heaven.

In Jewish teaching, to bind and loose meant to forbid and permit, and also to exclude from the community and to receive back. What Peter does in Christ’s name, heaven confirms. The same power is later given to the apostles together (18:18).
ch: The Catechism teaches that Peter’s confession of Jesus as the Christ, the Son of the living God, was the Father’s gift, and that on the rock of this faith confessed by St Peter Christ built his Church (CCC 424, 442). It teaches that Jesus entrusted a specific authority to Peter: the power of the keys designates authority to govern the house of God, which is the Church (CCC 553), and that the Lord made Simon alone the rock of his Church, while the office of binding and loosing was also given to the college of apostles united to its head (CCC 881). The Second Vatican Council teaches the same in Lumen Gentium 18 and 22. Peter’s authority comes from Christ, and it is a service of unity.

qa: Is the rock Peter himself or Peter’s faith?

Both, and the two are not opposed. Some Fathers emphasised Peter’s faith, others Peter himself. The Catechism says Christ built his Church “on the rock of this faith confessed by St Peter” (CCC 424), and also that the Lord “made Simon alone… the rock of his Church” (CCC 881). The rock is Peter the believer, confessing the faith given by the Father, and his successors who keep that faith for the whole Church.
Why are Peter and Paul celebrated on the same day?

Because tradition holds that both gave their lives in Rome under Nero, Peter by crucifixion and Paul by the sword, and the Church of Rome has kept their memory together since ancient times. A Roman calendar of the fourth century already lists 29 June. The two were very different, the fisherman from Galilee and the learned Pharisee from Tarsus, and they even disagreed openly once (Galatians 2:11–14), but they were united in Christ and in martyrdom.
What does this feast mean for Christians who do not accept the Pope’s authority?

Orthodox and many other Christians also honour Peter and Paul and keep this feast. The Catholic Church holds that Christ gave Peter and his successors a ministry of unity. St John Paul II, aware that the papacy has also been a difficulty for other Christians, invited them to help find a way of exercising this ministry that all could recognise (Ut Unum Sint 95). On this feast Catholics pray for the Pope and for the unity of all who believe in Christ.
rite: In the Latin Church today is a solemnity. In Rome the Holy Father blesses the pallia, the woollen bands worn by metropolitan archbishops as a sign of their communion with the Successor of Peter, for the archbishops appointed in the past year. Peter’s Pence, the offering of the faithful for the Pope’s works of charity, is traditionally linked with this day. Tomorrow the Church remembers the first martyrs of Rome, who died under Nero in the same persecution. The bones honoured as St Peter’s lie beneath the high altar of St Peter’s Basilica, and St Paul’s tomb is venerated in the basilica of St Paul Outside the Walls.
study: Jesus asks, “But who do you say that I am?” How would I answer in my own words, today?
The church prayed fervently for Peter in prison. Do I pray regularly for the Pope and my bishop? How could my family make this a habit?
Paul says, “I have kept the faith.” What have I received in faith that I must hand on to my children or to others?
Peter and Paul were very different men. What can our parish learn from them about unity among people who are not alike?

lead: Isaac is born and weaned, and Sarah demands that Hagar and her son be sent away. Abraham, distressed, obeys God and sends them into the wilderness of Beer-sheba. When the water runs out and Hagar cannot bear to watch the child die, God hears the voice of the boy and opens her eyes to a well. In the Gospel Jesus crosses to Gentile land, delivers two men possessed by demons, and the townspeople, instead of rejoicing, ask him to leave. Psalm 34 answers both: “The Lord hears the cry of the poor.” Today the Church may remember the first martyrs of the Church of Rome.

r.h: God has heard the voice of the boy
set: The promise has been fulfilled: Isaac is born when Abraham is a hundred. At the feast of his weaning, Sarah sees Ishmael, the son of Hagar the Egyptian slave woman, “playing” with Isaac, and fears for her son’s inheritance. The story is painful and honest. Scripture does not hide the jealousy and harshness in the family of the patriarchs.

Hagar had once run away into the wilderness before Ishmael’s birth, and the angel had met her there and named the child “God hears” (16:7–14). Now she is in the wilderness again, sent away, and God hears once more.
str: vv. 5, 8: Isaac born; the feast of his weaning.
vv. 9–10: Sarah demands that Hagar and her son be cast out.
vv. 11–13: Abraham is distressed; God tells him to listen, and promises that Ishmael too will be a nation.
vv. 14–16: bread and a skin of water; the wilderness; Hagar weeps at a bowshot’s distance.
vv. 17–20a: God hears; the angel calls; the well; God is with the boy.
kw: The text never names Ishmael in this passage; he is “the boy”, “the child”, “your offspring”. But the story keeps saying that God “heard”, the meaning of his name.
“God heard the voice of the boy” (v. 17). In Scripture God hears the cry of the weak, as he heard Israel in Egypt (Exodus 3:7).
Water in the desert means life. God opens Hagar’s eyes to see what was already there.
vv: The matter was very distressing to Abraham on account of his son.
Abraham loves Ishmael. The father of faith is not shown as cold; he suffers.
As for the son of the slave woman, I will make a nation of him also, because he is your offspring.
God’s promise reaches beyond the line of the covenant. Ishmael is not abandoned.
And God heard the voice of the boy;
Hagar wept, but it is the boy’s voice that God hears. The angel says “Do not be afraid”, as angels so often do in Scripture.
Then God opened her eyes and she saw a well of water.
Despair had hidden the well from her. God’s help often comes as the opening of our eyes.
ch: St Paul uses Hagar and Sarah in an allegory about slavery and sonship in Galatians 4:21–31. That allegory concerns living by grace, not a verdict on any people, and the Church is careful never to use it against the Jewish people, to whom “belong the adoption, the glory, the covenants” (Romans 9:4; CCC 839). The Second Vatican Council notes that Muslims link their faith with Abraham, and asks Christians and Muslims to forget past quarrels and work together for justice and peace (Nostra Aetate 3). Psalm 34 gives the Church’s reading of today’s story: the Lord hears the cry of the poor, of the outcast mother and the thirsty child.

r.h: They begged him to leave their neighbourhood
set: Jesus has just calmed the storm on the lake (8:23–27). He lands on the eastern shore, in the region of the Decapolis, mostly Gentile country, where pigs were kept. Mark and Luke tell the same story with one man; Matthew has two, as he does elsewhere (compare 20:30). The place name differs in the manuscripts: Gadarenes, Gerasenes or Gergesenes.
str: v. 28: two fierce demoniacs come out of the tombs.
v. 29: “What have you to do with us, Son of God? Have you come here to torment us before the time?”
vv. 30–32: the demons beg to enter the swine; “Go!”; the herd rushes into the sea.
vv. 33–34: the swineherds tell the town; the townspeople ask Jesus to leave.
kw: People under the power of evil spirits. They live among the tombs, the place of death, and no one can pass that way.
The demons know that a time of judgment is coming when their power will end. In Jesus that end has already begun.
The same verb is used of the demons begging (v. 31) and of the townspeople begging Jesus to leave (v. 34). Both want him at a distance.
vv: What have you to do with us, Son of God?
The demons recognise who Jesus is before the disciples fully do. Knowing is not the same as believing (compare James 2:19).
And he said to them, “Go!”
One word is enough. Jesus does not struggle with the demons; he commands them.
when they saw him, they begged him to leave their neighborhood.
They count the loss of the pigs and are afraid. The healing of two men matters less to them than their property and their quiet.
ch: The Catechism teaches that Jesus’ exorcisms release people from the domination of demons and anticipate his great victory over “the ruler of this world” (CCC 550). The Church continues this ministry: in baptism she prays for deliverance from evil, and in grave cases a priest authorised by the bishop may perform a solemn exorcism (CCC 1673). The Gospel also asks a hard question: do I prefer my comfort, my possessions or my routine to the presence of Christ who changes things?

rite: Today the Church may keep the memorial of the First Martyrs of the Holy Roman Church. After the great fire of Rome in the year 64, the emperor Nero blamed the Christians, and the Roman historian Tacitus records that a vast multitude were put to death with cruel tortures. St Clement of Rome later spoke of “a great multitude of the elect” who suffered there (in substance). They are remembered on the day after Saints Peter and Paul, who died in the same persecution. Their names are unknown, but like Hagar’s child, their cry was heard by God. Christians in many lands still suffer for their faith; we pray for them, and for those who wrong them.
study: When have I, like Hagar, been unable to see the “well” God had placed near me? Who helped open my eyes?
Is there any part of my life where I have quietly asked Jesus to “leave”, because his presence would cost me something?
